blocks.text: Never put other people's work, or code copied from the internet or produced by AI, in your portfolio as if you made it yourself. Always credit sources. Being caught passing off work is far worse than having a smaller portfolio.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A portfolio is a collection of your best work that proves your skills.
Include school projects, personal projects, clubs, competitions and volunteering.
TechFirst replaced CyberFirst in 2026; the TechFirst Girls Competition is for Year 9 girls in NI.
Bebras, CTFs, hackathons and Sentinus Young Innovators are great experience.
For each piece: problem, users, what you did, what you would improve.

check.q: What is a portfolio?
o: A collection of your best work that shows your skills
A list of your exam grades
check.why: A portfolio shows evidence of what you can do.

check.q: Which programme replaced CyberFirst in 2026?
check.why: CyberFirst became part of the larger TechFirst programme, with the NCSC leading the cyber pathway.

check.q: What is a hackathon?
o: An illegal attack on a website
A team event to build a solution in a short time
check.why: Hackathons are short, intense building events, usually in teams.

check.q: Which year group in NI is the TechFirst Girls Competition aimed at?
check.why: In NI it is for Year 9 girls (Year 8 in England and Wales).

practice.q: Suggest **three** things a Year 10 pupil could add to a digital portfolio.
practice.a: Any three: school project (1); personal project (1); club work (1); competition certificate/result (1); volunteering/work experience (1).

practice.q: Describe what should be included when explaining a piece of work in a portfolio.
practice.a: Any three: the problem (1); who it was for/users (1); what you did (1); how you tested/refined it or what you would improve (1).

practice.q: Explain why you should never present AI-generated or copied code as your own work.
practice.a: It is dishonest/plagiarism/breaks copyright (1) and could lose you a place or job if discovered / does not show your real skills (1).

pages.spec: Explain how your digital footprint and online reputation can affect your future, and how to behave professionally online
pages.summary: Your digital footprint is the trail of data you leave online, and it shapes your online reputation. Universities and employers may look you up, so think before you post and use online spaces professionally.

diagram.title: Before you post: the think-first check
diagram.caption: Follow the questions. If any answer is a problem, do not post.

nodes.label: I want to post something
nodes.detail: A photo, comment, video or message.

nodes.label: Would I be happy for a future employer to see it?
nodes.detail: Imagine it on a big screen at a job interview.

nodes.label: Is it kind, true and fair to others?
nodes.detail: Does it embarrass, upset or mislead anyone? Do I have permission for photos of others?

nodes.label: Does it share private information?
nodes.detail: Address, school, passwords, location, other people's details.

nodes.label: Do not post it
nodes.detail: Change it, keep it private or leave it. Deleted posts can still have been copied.

nodes.label: OK to post
nodes.detail: Still check your privacy settings and who can see it.

blocks.text: Everything you do online leaves a trace: posts, likes, comments, photos you are tagged in, game usernames and more. This is your **[[Digital footprint]]**.

Your **[[Online reputation]]** is what people think of you based on what they can find. When you apply for a part-time job, a course or an apprenticeship, the person deciding may search for your name.
Why it matters for your career

items: Posts can be **screenshotted and shared**, so 'deleted' does not mean gone.
Something you post at 14 could still be found when you are 18 and applying for jobs.
Offensive jokes, bullying or posts about illegal behaviour can cost people places and jobs.
A **positive** footprint helps: a project you shared, a club you helped run or a competition you entered.

blocks.text: Professionalism online
**[[Professionalism]]** means behaving in a way that is reliable, respectful and appropriate for work or study. Online that means:

head: Unprofessional
Professional
rows: Email address based on your name, e.g. **aoife.byrne@...**
Message to a teacher: *'hey wheres the homework'*
*'Hello Mr Butler, could you tell me where this week's homework is? Thank you, Aoife.'*
Disagreeing politely, or not replying at all
Public profile with location and school shown
Privacy settings checked; personal details kept private
Using someone else's work without credit
blocks.caption: Online behaviour that helps or harms your reputation

blocks.title: Worked example: what would an employer think?
blocks.context: Eoin applies for a Saturday job in an Enniskillen computer shop. The manager searches his name and finds (a) a gaming video where he swears at other players, and (b) a website he built for his local GAA club. What impression does each give?
steps: (a) Shows poor self-control and disrespect: a **negative** impression for a customer-facing job.
(b) Shows real web skills, community involvement and reliability: a **positive** impression.
Eoin should make the video private or delete it, check what else is public, and mention the GAA website in his application.
blocks.answer: The same search can help or harm you; you control much of what people find.

blocks.text: Privacy settings help, but they are not a guarantee. Friends can share your posts, and companies can change their settings. The safest rule: if you would not want a future employer to see it, do not post it.

Search your own name (with a parent or carer) once in a while to see what others can find. Also check the minimum age in a site's terms before you join it: most social media sites require users to be at least 13.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Your digital footprint is the trail of data you leave online.
Your online reputation is what people think of you from what they find.
Posts can be copied, so deleted is not always gone.
Use a sensible email address and polite, clear messages.
Build a positive footprint by sharing work you are proud of.

check.q: What is a digital footprint?
o: The trail of data you leave online
A fingerprint scanner on a phone
check.why: Posts, likes, comments and tags all add to your digital footprint.

check.q: Which email address is most professional for a job application?
check.why: An address based on your name looks professional.

check.q: Why is 'I deleted it' not always enough?
o: Deleted posts always come back after a week
Others may already have screenshotted or shared it
check.why: Once posted, content can be copied and shared.

check.q: Which of these would build a POSITIVE online reputation?
o: Sharing a friend's photo without asking
Sharing a website you built for a local club
check.why: Showing your work and community involvement creates a positive footprint.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a **digital footprint** and an **online reputation**.
practice.a: Digital footprint: the trail of data/content you leave online (1). Online reputation: what people think of you based on that content (1).

practice.q: Give **two** ways a pupil could improve their online reputation before applying for a job.
practice.a: Any two: delete/hide unsuitable posts (1); check privacy settings (1); use a professional email (1); share positive work/projects (1).

practice.q: Rewrite this message so it is professional: 'hey cant come 2 work tmrw im sick'.
practice.a: Polite greeting and sign-off with name (1); clear, correctly spelt message, e.g. 'Hello Mrs Kelly, I'm sorry but I am unwell and won't be able to work tomorrow. ...' (1).

pages.spec: Write a skills-based CV and plan a personal statement for a tech course or job
pages.summary: A skills-based CV puts your skills and evidence first, which suits young people with little work experience. A personal statement explains why you want a course and how you have prepared; UCAS now asks three questions in 4,000 characters.

diagram.title: Personal statement character counter
diagram.caption: UCAS gives you 4,000 characters in total across three answers. Change the lengths to see how many characters you have left.

inputs.label: Answer 2: how your studies prepared you
Answer 3: what else you have done

blocks.text: A **[[CV]]** (curriculum vitae) is a short document, usually no more than two pages, that summarises your skills, education and experience for an employer. You will need one for part-time jobs, work experience and apprenticeships.
What is a skills-based CV?

A traditional CV lists jobs you have had. At 15 or 16 you probably have not had many! A **[[Skills-based CV]]** puts your **skills first**, each backed by evidence from school, clubs, hobbies or volunteering.

head: Section
What to include
rows: Name, phone number and a professional email address. Your town is enough: you do not need your full address.
Two or three sentences: who you are, what you are good at and what you are looking for.
Three to five skills, each with a short example as evidence (use STAR ideas).
Your school and the GCSE subjects you are taking or have taken.
Part-time jobs, work experience, volunteering, helping run a club.
Competitions, awards, projects, sports, music: things that show something about you.
Say *'References available on request'*, and ask a teacher's permission before naming them.
blocks.caption: Sections of a skills-based CV

blocks.title: Worked example: improving a 'Key skills' entry
blocks.context: Sinéad's CV says: 'IT skills: good with computers.' Improve it.
steps: The original is vague: *every* applicant could say it.
Name specific skills: programming in Python, spreadsheets, web design.
Add evidence: *'Built a spreadsheet to track sales for our school tuck shop, using formulas and charts to show the best-selling items.'*
blocks.answer: 'Digital skills: Python programming and spreadsheets. Built a tuck shop spreadsheet with formulas and charts that helped choose which snacks to stock.'

blocks.text: Check spelling and grammar carefully. Spelling mistakes on a CV suggest you are careless, which is especially bad for a job that needs attention to detail, such as testing software. And never lie on a CV.
Personal statements

A **[[Personal statement]]** is a piece of writing where you explain why you want a course or job and why you would be good at it. You will write one for university applications (through **UCAS**) and often for apprenticeships.
For courses starting from 2026, UCAS replaced the single long essay with **three questions**, answered in **4,000 characters in total**:

items: Why do you want to study this course or subject?
How have your qualifications and studies helped you to prepare for this course or subject?
What else have you done to prepare outside of education, and why are these experiences useful?

blocks.text: For a tech course, strong answers mention real projects, what you learned from your GCSE and A level coursework, competitions, clubs, reading about technology and work experience. Specific beats general every time.
Start a *'useful for my CV'* note now. Write down projects, competitions, roles and achievements as they happen. In Year 13 you will be glad you did.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A CV summarises your skills, education and experience, usually in two pages or fewer.
A skills-based CV puts skills and evidence first: ideal when you have little work experience.
Use a professional email, check spelling and never lie.
A personal statement explains why you want a course and how you have prepared.
UCAS now asks three questions, 4,000 characters in total.

check.q: What does a skills-based CV put first?
o: A list of every job you have had
check.why: Skills-based CVs focus on what you can do, which suits young people.

check.q: How many characters does UCAS allow in total for the personal statement?
check.why: 4,000 characters across the three questions.

check.q: Which is the best 'Key skills' entry?
o: Python: wrote a quiz program and tested it with Year 8 pupils.
check.why: It names a skill and gives specific evidence.

check.q: Before naming a teacher as a referee you should...
check.why: Always ask before naming someone as a referee.

practice.q: List **four** sections you would include in a skills-based CV.
practice.a: Any four: contact details, personal profile, key skills, education, experience, achievements/interests, references (1 each).

practice.q: Explain why a skills-based CV suits a Year 11 pupil better than a traditional CV.
practice.a: They have little or no work history (1), so putting skills with evidence from school/clubs/hobbies first shows what they can do (1).

practice.q: Write a two-sentence personal profile for a CV for a Saturday job in a computer shop.
practice.a: Who you are and key strengths (1); what you are looking for / why this job (1).

pages.spec: Explain why diversity matters in technology and challenge myths and stereotypes about who 'does' computing
pages.summary: Women and other groups are under-represented in tech: in 2025 only about 22% of UK IT specialists were women. Diverse teams build better, fairer products, and the stereotype of who 'does' computing is simply wrong.

diagram.title: Myth or reality?
diagram.caption: Common myths about who works in computing, and what is actually true.

states.label: Myths
points: Computing is for boys
You must be a maths genius
Tech people work alone and never talk
You need to have coded since you were six

states.label: Reality
points: Women have shaped computing from the very start
Problem solving and practice matter more than genius
Tech is teamwork: lots of talking, planning and explaining
Many people start coding at school, college or later

blocks.text: A **[[Stereotype]]** is a fixed, over-simple idea about what a group of people is like. The stereotype of a programmer is a young man alone in a dark room. It puts many people off before they have even tried, and it is not true.
The numbers

According to BCS, The Chartered Institute for IT, about **22%** of IT specialists in the UK workforce in **2025** were women. That means roughly **one in five**. Women make up about half the population, so they are clearly **under-represented**.

blocks.title: Worked example: what does 22% mean?
blocks.context: A Belfast tech company has 150 IT specialists. If it matched the UK figure of 22% women, how many would be women? How many would there be at 50%?
steps: The difference is 75 − 33 = **42** people.
blocks.answer: 33 at 22%, compared with 75 if the team matched the population.

blocks.text: Women who shaped computing

head: Person
What she did
rows: Wrote notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, including what is often called the first published computer program.
US Navy computer scientist who helped develop early compilers and the COBOL language. She helped popularise the word *debugging*.
NASA mathematician whose calculations helped send astronauts into orbit and to the Moon.
Led the team that wrote the on-board flight software for the Apollo Moon missions.
British computer scientist whose ideas about weighting words are still used by search engines.
blocks.caption: Some women who changed computing

blocks.text: Why diversity matters
**[[Diversity]]** means including people of different genders, backgrounds, ethnicities, ages, abilities and ways of thinking. In tech this is not just about fairness: it makes products better.

items: A team that all thinks alike can miss problems that affect other users.
AI trained on data from only one group of people can work badly, or unfairly, for everyone else.
A team that includes disabled people is more likely to build **accessible** products.
Different ideas lead to more creative solutions.

blocks.text: Do not let a stereotype decide your GCSE choices for you. If you enjoy solving problems, making things or helping people, there is a place for you in tech, whoever you are.
Programmes such as the **TechFirst Girls Competition** exist to encourage girls to try computing early, and many NI tech companies run events aimed at girls and under-represented groups.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A stereotype is a fixed, over-simple idea about a group.
In 2025 about 22% of UK IT specialists were women.
Women such as Ada Lovelace, Grace Hopper and Margaret Hamilton shaped computing.
Diverse teams build fairer, more accessible and more creative products.
You do not need to be a genius or start at six: practice matters most.

check.q: About what percentage of UK IT specialists were women in 2025?
check.why: BCS reported about 22%, roughly one in five.

check.q: Who wrote what is often called the first published computer program?
check.why: Ada Lovelace wrote it for Babbage's Analytical Engine in the 1840s.

check.q: Why can a lack of diversity make AI systems worse?
o: AI needs a person of every age to switch it on
AI trained on data from one group can work badly for others
check.why: Biased data can lead to biased results.

check.q: Which statement is a myth?
o: Tech work involves lots of teamwork
You must be a maths genius to work in tech
Many people learn to code at school or later
Women have shaped computing from the start
check.why: Problem solving and practice matter more than genius.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by a **stereotype**, using an example from computing.
practice.a: A fixed, over-simple idea about what a group is like (1), e.g. that programmers are all boys who work alone (1).

practice.q: Give **two** reasons why diverse tech teams can build better products.
practice.a: Any two: spot problems affecting different users (1); fairer AI/less biased data (1); more accessible products (1); more creative ideas (1).

practice.q: Name **one** woman who made an important contribution to computing and describe what she did.
practice.a: Name (1) and correct contribution (1), e.g. Margaret Hamilton led the Apollo flight software team.

pages.spec: Create a personal careers plan with SMART targets for your next steps
pages.summary: A careers plan sets out where you might like to go and the steps to get there. Use SMART targets, gain work experience, talk to the Careers Service and review your plan as your interests change.

diagram.title: Example careers plan: Caoimhe, Year 10
diagram.caption: One pupil's plan from Year 10 to Year 14. Click each stage to see her targets.

items.label: Year 10: explore
items.detail: Choose GCSEs including Digital Technology and maths. Join the school coding club. Enter Bebras in November.

items.label: Year 11: build
items.detail: Make a personal website to hold her portfolio. Volunteer to help at the school open night tech stand.

items.label: Year 12: test it out
items.detail: Work experience in an IT department. Meet a Careers Service adviser. Finish her Unit 5 controlled assessment project.

items.label: Years 13 and 14: decide
items.detail: A level Digital Technology. Compare university courses with Higher Level Apprenticeships; apply to both.

items.label: After school
items.detail: A software development HLA or a computing degree. Review the plan every year.

blocks.text: You do not need to know your exact future job in Year 10. Most adults change jobs several times, and some of the jobs you will do have not been invented yet. But a **[[Careers plan]]** helps you make good choices now and keeps your options open.
Step 1: know yourself

items: What do I **enjoy**? (Making things, solving puzzles, helping people, design, data...)
What am I **good at**? (Look at reports, feedback and projects.)
What **matters** to me? (Working with people, being creative, helping the environment, earning well, staying in Fermanagh...)

blocks.text: Step 2: explore options

items: Research the six career areas on pages 2 and 3, and look at real job adverts to see what they ask for.
Talk to your careers teacher and a **Careers Service** adviser.
Ask family and friends who work with technology what their job is really like.
Look at college, university and apprenticeship course pages to see entry requirements.

blocks.text: Step 3: set SMART targets

A **[[SMART target]]** is a goal that is **S**pecific, **M**easurable, **A**chievable, **R**elevant and **T**ime-bound. *'Get better at coding'* is not SMART. *'Finish the first ten Python challenges on our class site by the Easter holidays'* is.

head: Weak target
SMART target
rows: Join the school coding club and attend every week until June.
Email three local businesses by 1 March asking about a week of work experience in Year 12.
Put my three best KS3 projects, with descriptions, into a portfolio by the end of Year 10.
Get at least 70% in each GCSE Unit 4 practice paper by the end of Year 11.
blocks.caption: Making targets SMART

blocks.text: Step 4: get experience

**[[Work experience]]** means spending time in a real workplace to see what a job is like. Schools often arrange it in Year 12 or Year 13, but you can also gain experience through part-time jobs, volunteering, open days and online taster events.

blocks.title: Worked example: is it SMART?
blocks.context: Decide whether each target is SMART and fix it if not. (a) 'Learn about cyber security.' (b) 'Enter the TechFirst Girls Competition with my friends this November and complete every challenge.'
steps: (a) Not SMART: not specific, not measurable and no deadline. Better: *'Complete three beginner cipher challenges and write up what I learned in my portfolio by the end of term.'*
(b) SMART: specific (one named competition), measurable (every challenge), achievable, relevant to a cyber interest, and time-bound (this November).
blocks.answer: (a) needs rewriting; (b) is already SMART.

blocks.text: A careers plan is not a contract. If you discover you love UX design instead of networking, change the plan! Review it at least once a year, for example when you get your report.
Keep your options open by choosing GCSEs you enjoy and are good at. Digital Technology combined with subjects such as maths, a science, art or English keeps many tech routes available.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A careers plan helps you make good choices now and keeps options open.
Know yourself, explore options, set SMART targets, get experience.
SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.
Work experience shows you what a job is really like.
Review and change your plan as your interests change.

check.q: What does the T in SMART stand for?
check.why: SMART targets have a deadline.

check.q: Which target is SMART?
o: Join the coding club and attend every week until June
check.why: It is specific, measurable and has a time limit.

check.q: What is work experience?
o: Time spent in a real workplace to see what a job is like
A job you are paid a full salary for
check.why: Work experience lets you try a job before you choose it.

check.q: How often should you review your careers plan?
o: Never: it is fixed once written
At least once a year, and whenever your interests change
Only if a teacher forces you
check.why: Plans should change as you learn more about yourself and your options.

practice.q: What does SMART stand for?
practice.a: Specific, Measurable (1); Achievable, Relevant (1); Time-bound (1).

practice.q: Rewrite 'get some work experience' as a SMART target.
practice.a: Specific action (e.g. email three named businesses) (1) with a deadline / measurable outcome (1).

practice.q: Give **two** ways a Year 10 pupil could find out more about careers in digital technology.
practice.a: Any two: Careers Service adviser/careers teacher (1); research job adverts/course pages (1); ask people who work in tech (1); clubs/competitions/open days (1).

chapters.title: Computational Thinking and Algorithms
chapters.intro: How computer scientists think about problems before they write any code: decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithms, then flowcharts, pseudocode, trace tables, searching, sorting and debugging.

pages.spec: Explain what computational thinking is and name its four parts
pages.summary: Computational thinking is a way of solving problems so that a person or a computer could carry out the solution. It has four parts: decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithms.

diagram.title: The four parts of computational thinking
diagram.caption: Click each part. Real problem solving often goes round more than once.

items.label: Decomposition
items.detail: Break a big problem into smaller problems that are easier to solve, e.g. a school trip becomes transport, money, permission slips and lunch.

items.label: Pattern recognition
items.detail: Spot what the smaller problems have in common, so one solution can be reused, e.g. every class needs a room, a teacher and a subject.

items.label: Abstraction
items.detail: Ignore the detail that does not matter and keep only what you need, e.g. the London Underground map shows stations and lines, not streets.

items.label: Algorithms
items.detail: Write clear, step-by-step instructions that solve the problem, e.g. a flowchart or pseudocode for making toast.

blocks.text: Computers are very fast, but they cannot think for themselves. They only do exactly what they are told. **[[Computational thinking]]** is the skill of working out a problem so clearly that the steps could be handed to a computer (or to another person) and carried out without any guessing.

It is not about thinking *like* a computer. It is about thinking like a **computer scientist**: being organised, logical and precise. You already do it every day when you plan your homework, pack your PE bag or work out the quickest way to the canteen.
The four parts

head: Part
What it means
Making toast
rows: Breaking a big problem into smaller, more manageable parts.
Get the bread, toast it, butter it, serve it.
Spotting similarities, so you can reuse a solution you already have.
Toasting a bagel or a crumpet works in the same way as toasting bread.
Removing detail that does not matter so you can focus on what does.
The brand of bread and the colour of the toaster do not matter. How long to toast it does.
Writing precise step-by-step instructions to solve the problem.
1. Put bread in toaster. 2. Push lever down. 3. Wait until golden. 4. Butter it.
blocks.caption: Computational thinking applied to making toast

blocks.text: Remember the four parts with **D-P-A-A**: "**D**ogs **P**lay **A**ll **A**fternoon" (Decomposition, Pattern recognition, Abstraction, Algorithms).

blocks.title: Worked example: planning a class party
blocks.context: Your form class wants to hold an end-of-term party in the form room. Use computational thinking to plan it.
steps: **Decomposition:** split the job into smaller problems: food, music, decorations, permission from the form tutor, tidying up.
**Pattern recognition:** food, music and decorations all follow the same pattern: decide what is needed, find out who can bring it, make a list. Solve that once and reuse it.
**Abstraction:** ignore detail that does not matter right now (the exact colour of the balloons) and keep what does (how many pupils, what time the party is, any allergies).
**Algorithm:** write the plan as clear, ordered steps that anyone in the class could follow on the day.
blocks.answer: Each part of computational thinking makes a big, messy job smaller and clearer, until it becomes a set of steps that anyone could follow.

blocks.text: The four parts are not always used in a strict order. You might decompose a problem, spot a pattern, then go back and decompose one part further. What matters is that you end up with a clear algorithm.
Why does it matter?

items: Programmers use it before they write a single line of code. In Year 10 you will turn algorithms into C# programs.
It works for problems that have nothing to do with computers: planning a sports day, revising for exams or organising a fundraiser.
Employers value people who can break problems down and explain solutions clearly.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Computational thinking is a way of solving problems clearly enough that a computer or person could follow the solution.
Decomposition: break a problem into smaller parts.
Pattern recognition: spot similarities and reuse solutions.
Abstraction: remove unnecessary detail.
Algorithms: write precise, step-by-step instructions.

check.q: Which part of computational thinking means breaking a problem into smaller parts?
check.why: Decomposition breaks a big problem into smaller, more manageable ones.

check.q: Ignoring the brand of bread when writing instructions for making toast is an example of...
check.why: Abstraction removes detail that does not matter to the problem.

check.q: Which statement about computational thinking is true?
o: It only matters when you use a computer
It means thinking as fast as a computer
It is a way of solving problems clearly and logically
check.why: It is a problem-solving approach, useful with or without a computer.

check.q: Realising that toasting a crumpet is the same process as toasting bread is...
check.why: You spotted a similarity so you can reuse a solution.

practice.q: Name the **four** parts of computational thinking.
practice.a: Decomposition (1); pattern recognition (1); abstraction (1); algorithms / algorithmic thinking (1).

practice.q: Your Year 8 class is organising a cake sale for charity. Explain how **decomposition** and **abstraction** could help with the planning.
practice.a: Decomposition: break the cake sale into smaller tasks (1), e.g. baking, pricing, posters, setting up the table (1). Abstraction: ignore details that do not matter (1), e.g. focus on how many cakes and the price, not the colour of the plates (1).

practice.q: Explain what is meant by an **algorithm**.
practice.a: A set of step-by-step instructions (1) to solve a problem or complete a task (1).

pages.spec: Use decomposition to break down a problem and pattern recognition to spot similarities
pages.summary: Decomposition breaks a big problem into smaller sub-problems that can each be solved on their own. Pattern recognition spots what those sub-problems have in common, so one solution can be reused.

diagram.title: Decomposing the school timetable
diagram.caption: Click each box. Each sub-problem can be broken down again until it is easy to solve.

nodes.label: Make the school timetable
nodes.detail: A huge problem: hundreds of pupils, dozens of teachers and rooms, and every period of the week.

nodes.label: Year groups
nodes.detail: Split the school into Years 8 to 14. Each year group is a smaller problem.

nodes.label: Subjects
nodes.detail: Each year needs a set number of periods of English, Maths, Digital Technology and so on.

nodes.label: Rooms and teachers
nodes.detail: Each lesson needs a free room of the right type (a computer room for Digital Technology, a lab for Science) and a free teacher.

nodes.label: One class, one week
nodes.detail: Small enough to solve: fill every period of the week for 8A without clashes.

blocks.text: Decomposition

**[[Decomposition]]** means breaking a large, complex problem into smaller parts called **[[Sub-problem]]s**. Each sub-problem is easier to understand, solve and check than the whole thing. If a sub-problem is still too big, you break it down again.

Think about the school timetable. Making it in one go would be impossible: hundreds of pupils, dozens of teachers and rooms, and not a single clash allowed. Decomposed, it becomes a set of much smaller jobs that can be tackled one at a time.

blocks.title: Worked example: decomposing a Year 8 trip to the Ulster Museum
blocks.context: Your form tutor asks the class to help plan a day trip to Belfast. Break the problem down.
steps: **Transport:** book a bus, work out the leaving and return times.
**Money:** find the cost of the bus and entry, divide by the number of pupils.
**Permission:** write a consent letter, collect the replies, keep a list.
**On the day:** register pupils on the bus, plan groups and a meeting point, pack lunches.
Any part that is still too big is decomposed again, e.g. **Permission** becomes: write letter, print copies, hand out, collect, chase missing replies.
blocks.answer: Five smaller problems that could be shared out between different people and solved separately.

blocks.text: Decomposition makes teamwork easy: different people can work on different sub-problems at the same time. Large software such as a video game is built this way by teams of hundreds.
Pattern recognition

**[[Pattern recognition]]** means looking for similarities, or **patterns**, between problems or within a problem. Once you spot a pattern you can reuse the same solution instead of starting from scratch every time.

head: Situation
The pattern
How it helps
rows: Every lesson needs a class, a teacher, a room and a period.
One method for placing a lesson works for every lesson in the school.
Every pupil gets the same letter with only the name changed.
Write one letter and change the name, rather than writing 28 letters.
Every sandwich is: two slices of bread, butter, filling, cut in half.
Learn the steps once and repeat them for each sandwich.
You can predict the next value (15) without being told.
blocks.caption: Spotting patterns

blocks.text: Patterns lead straight to **loops** in algorithms. If the same steps are repeated for every sandwich, an algorithm can say "repeat these steps 28 times" instead of writing them out 28 times.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Decomposition breaks a big problem into smaller sub-problems.
Sub-problems can be broken down again until each is easy to solve.
Decomposition lets different people work on different parts.
Pattern recognition spots similarities so a solution can be reused.
Repeated patterns often become loops in an algorithm.

check.q: What is a sub-problem?
o: A smaller part of a bigger problem
check.why: Decomposition produces sub-problems.

check.q: Every lesson needs a teacher, a room, a class and a period. Noticing this is...
check.why: It is a similarity shared by every lesson.

check.q: Why is decomposition useful for a team?
o: It removes the need to test
Different people can work on different parts at the same time
It means only one person does the work
check.why: Sub-problems can be shared out.

check.q: What comes next in 4, 8, 12, 16, ...?
check.why: The pattern is add 4, so 16 + 4 = 20.

practice.q: Define **decomposition** and give **one** benefit of using it.
practice.a: Breaking a problem down into smaller sub-problems (1). Benefit: each part is easier to solve / parts can be shared between a team / easier to test (1).

practice.q: The PE department is organising sports day. Decompose this problem into **four** sub-problems.
practice.a: Any four sensible sub-problems (1 each), e.g. choosing events; entering pupils into events; timing and recording results; awarding points to houses; equipment and staff; first aid.

practice.q: Explain how **pattern recognition** could save time when writing reports for every pupil in a class.
practice.a: Every report follows the same structure / has the same sections (1), so one template can be reused and only the details changed for each pupil (1).

pages.spec: Use abstraction to remove unnecessary detail, using the London Underground map as an example
pages.summary: Abstraction means hiding or removing detail that is not needed, so you can focus on what matters. The London Underground map is a famous abstraction: it shows the order of stations and where lines meet, not real distances.

diagram.title: Street map or Tube map?
diagram.caption: Two ways to show the same city. Which one would you use to get from King's Cross to Oxford Circus?

states.label: Real street map
points: Every street, building and park
Real distances and real directions
Curvy, accurate railway lines
Great for walking, too detailed for planning a Tube journey

states.label: Tube map (abstraction)
points: Only stations, lines and interchanges
Straight lines at neat angles
Stations spaced evenly, not by real distance
Perfect for planning which train to take and where to change

blocks.text: **[[Abstraction]]** means removing (or hiding) detail that is not needed to solve a problem, so you can concentrate on the detail that is. What you are left with is a simpler **[[model]]** of the real thing.
The London Underground map

Early maps of the London Underground were drawn to scale on top of the streets. In the centre the stations were crammed together and hard to read; at the edges they were miles apart. In **1931** an electrical draughtsman called **Harry Beck** had an idea: passengers underground do not care about the streets above them. They only need to know **which line to take, the order of the stops, and where to change**.

head: Kept (needed)
Removed (not needed)
rows: The order of stations on each line
The real shape and bends of each line
Each line in its own colour
Real compass directions (they are only roughly right)
blocks.caption: What Harry Beck kept and removed

blocks.text: His map was printed in 1933 and was an instant success. The same idea is still used for metro maps all over the world. Only one real feature survived: a simplified River Thames, to help people get their bearings.
Abstraction does not mean making something up. Everything left on the Tube map is **true**: the stations, their order and the connections. Only the unnecessary detail has gone.
Abstraction around school

items: **The school timetable** is an abstraction of your week: it shows subject, room and teacher, not what you will learn or who you sit beside.
**A fire exit plan** on the classroom wall shows corridors, doors and exits, not desks, displays or the colour of the walls.
**A football game** such as EA FC turns a real player into a few numbers (pace, shooting, passing) instead of every detail of their life.
**A satnav** shows roads and your route, but not every house you pass.

blocks.title: Worked example: an abstraction for a bus timetable app
blocks.context: The school wants an app that tells pupils when their bus leaves. Decide what to keep and what to remove.
steps: Ask: what problem is the app solving? Pupils need to know **which bus** and **when it leaves**.
Keep: bus number, departure time, bay number, destination.
Remove: the driver's name, the colour of the bus, the registration plate, the exact route through every village.
Check: could a pupil still catch the right bus with only the kept details? Yes.
blocks.answer: Bus number, bay, destination and time: four details instead of dozens.

blocks.text: A good test for abstraction: "Would removing this detail stop the problem being solved?" If not, it can go.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Abstraction removes unnecessary detail to focus on what matters.
The result is a simpler model of the real thing.
Harry Beck's 1931 Tube map kept stations, order and interchanges, and removed real distances and streets.
What you keep depends on the problem you are trying to solve.
Timetables, fire exit plans and satnavs are everyday abstractions.

check.q: What does abstraction mean?
o: Removing detail that is not needed
check.why: Abstraction hides or removes unnecessary detail.

check.q: Which detail is **kept** on the London Underground map?
o: The exact bends of each tunnel
The order of stations on each line
check.why: Passengers need the order of stops, not real distances.

check.q: Who designed the famous Tube map in 1931?
check.why: Harry Beck, an electrical draughtsman.

check.q: An app tells pupils when their bus leaves. Which detail is best removed?
check.why: It does not help anyone catch the bus.

practice.q: Explain why the London Underground map is a good example of **abstraction**.
practice.a: It removes unnecessary detail such as streets / real distances / real bends (1); it keeps only what passengers need: stations, the order of stops, lines and interchanges (1); this makes it simpler and easier to use for planning a journey (1).

practice.q: A game designer is creating a racing game. State **two** details about a real car that should be kept and **two** that could be removed.
practice.a: Kept (any two, 1 each): top speed, acceleration, handling/steering, braking. Removed (any two, 1 each): the radio, seat fabric, the glovebox, cup holders, the owner's manual, etc.

practice.q: Your school map for new Year 8 pupils is an abstraction. Describe what it should show and what it should leave out.
practice.a: Show: buildings/corridors, room numbers, key places such as the canteen, office and toilets (1). Leave out: furniture, displays, car parking spaces or other detail new pupils do not need (1).

pages.spec: Define an algorithm and represent one as a flowchart using the standard symbols
pages.summary: An algorithm is a precise, ordered set of steps that solves a problem. A flowchart shows an algorithm as a diagram using standard symbols: terminator, process, decision, input/output and arrows.

diagram.title: Flowchart: making toast
diagram.caption: Click each symbol. The decision loops back until the toast is golden.

nodes.label: Start
nodes.detail: Terminator: every flowchart begins here.

nodes.label: Put bread in toaster
nodes.detail: Process: an action to carry out.

nodes.label: Push lever down
nodes.detail: Process: another action.

nodes.label: Wait 30 seconds
nodes.detail: Process: an action that involves waiting.

nodes.label: Is the toast golden?
nodes.detail: Decision: a Yes/No question. No: go back and wait again. Yes: carry on.

nodes.label: Butter the toast
nodes.detail: Process: the toast is ready to butter.

nodes.label: Stop
nodes.detail: Terminator: the algorithm ends here.

blocks.text: What is an algorithm?

An **[[algorithm]]** is a precise, step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem or completing a task. A recipe, the instructions for a flat-pack wardrobe and the directions to the sports hall are all algorithms. A computer program is an algorithm written in a programming language.
A good algorithm must be:

items: **Precise and unambiguous:** each step has only one possible meaning. "Add some milk" is vague; "add 100 ml of milk" is precise.
**In the correct order:** "butter the toast" before "toast the bread" gives a very different result.
**Finite:** it must finish. Instructions that go on forever are not a useful algorithm.

blocks.text: Algorithms come before programs. You plan the algorithm first (as a flowchart or in pseudocode), then turn it into code in any language: C#, Python or micro:bit blocks.
Flowchart symbols
A **[[flowchart]]** shows an algorithm as a diagram. Everyone uses the same shapes, so anyone can read anyone else's flowchart.

head: Symbol
Shape
Used for
Example
rows: The start and end of the algorithm
A Yes/No (True/False) question with two exits
Data going in (from the user) or coming out (to the screen)
Joins the symbols and shows the direction to follow
From Start down to the first step
blocks.caption: The standard flowchart symbols

blocks.text: A decision diamond must have **two** arrows coming out of it, labelled **Yes** and **No** (or True and False). A process box has only **one** arrow out.

blocks.title: Worked example: a flowchart for the Year 10 trip
blocks.context: Pupils can only go on the trip if they are 14 or older. Describe a flowchart that asks for a pupil's age and says whether they can go.
steps: **Terminator:** Start.
**Input/output** (parallelogram): INPUT age.
**Decision** (diamond): Is age >= 14?
**Yes** arrow to an **output** parallelogram: OUTPUT "You can go on the trip".
**No** arrow to an **output** parallelogram: OUTPUT "Sorry, you are too young".
Both arrows join up and lead to the **terminator**: Stop.
blocks.answer: Start, input, one decision, two outputs, Stop: five kinds of symbol used correctly.

blocks.text: Draw flowcharts from top to bottom, use a ruler for arrows, and keep the wording inside each shape short.

blocks.title: Key points
items: An algorithm is a precise, ordered, finite set of steps to solve a problem.
Terminator (rounded rectangle): Start and Stop.
Process (rectangle): an action or calculation.
Decision (diamond): a Yes/No question with two labelled exits.
Input/output (parallelogram): data in or out. Arrows show the direction of flow.

check.q: Which flowchart symbol is a diamond?
check.why: A decision asks a Yes/No question.

check.q: Which symbol would you use for OUTPUT "Well done"?
check.why: Input and output both use the parallelogram.

check.q: Which instruction is the most precise?
check.why: It has only one possible meaning.

check.q: How many arrows should leave a decision symbol?
check.why: One for Yes and one for No.

practice.q: Define the term **algorithm**.
practice.a: A set of precise / step-by-step instructions (1) to solve a problem or complete a task (1).

practice.q: Name the flowchart symbol used for each of the following: (a) Start (b) Is score > 100? (c) INPUT password (d) total = total + 5
practice.a: (a) Terminator (1). (b) Decision (1). (c) Input/output (1). (d) Process (1).

practice.q: Draw a flowchart for an algorithm that asks the user for a number and outputs "Even" if it can be divided by 2 exactly, or "Odd" if not.
practice.a: Start and Stop terminators (1); INPUT number in a parallelogram (1); decision diamond asking whether the number divides by 2 exactly (1); Yes and No labelled exits (1); two output parallelograms: "Even" on Yes, "Odd" on No, both leading to Stop (1).

pages.spec: Write simple pseudocode using sequence, selection and iteration
pages.summary: Pseudocode writes an algorithm in structured, code-like English that is not tied to any one language. Every algorithm is built from three building blocks: sequence, selection and iteration.

diagram.title: Which building block?
diagram.caption: Match each piece of pseudocode to the building block it shows.

blocks.text: What is pseudocode?

**[[Pseudocode]]** (say *soo-doh-code*) is a way of writing an algorithm that looks a bit like a program but is written in simple, structured English. It is not a real programming language, so it will not run on a computer, and it does not matter if you make a tiny spelling slip. It lets you plan the logic before you worry about the exact rules of C#, Python or blocks.

head: Pseudocode
Meaning
rows: Get a value from the user and store it in `name`.
Display text and values on the screen.
Store 0 in `score`. Read the arrow as *becomes*.
Equal to, not equal to, less than, greater than, less than or equal to, greater than or equal to.
Repeat while a condition is true.
Repeat a set number of times.
A note for humans; it is ignored when the algorithm runs.
blocks.caption: The pseudocode used in this topic

blocks.text: Indent (move in) the lines inside an IF or a loop. It shows clearly which lines belong to it.
1. Sequence
**[[Sequence]]** means the steps are carried out one after another, in order, from top to bottom.

blocks.title: Sequence: area of a rectangle
blocks.code:
// Work out the area of a rectangle
INPUT length
INPUT width
area ← length * width
OUTPUT "The area is ", area
blocks.output:
If the user enters 6 and 4:
The area is 24

blocks.text: 2. Selection

**[[Selection]]** means the algorithm makes a choice. It checks a **[[condition]]** (something that is either true or false) and follows a different path depending on the answer. In a flowchart, selection is a decision diamond.

blocks.title: Selection: pass or try again
blocks.code:
INPUT mark
IF mark >= 50 THEN
    OUTPUT "Pass"
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Try again"
ENDIF
blocks.output:
Mark 63: Pass
Mark 50: Pass
Mark 49: Try again

blocks.text: For more than two paths, use `ELSEIF`. The conditions are checked from the top, and only the **first** true one runs:

blocks.title: Selection with ELSEIF: house points
blocks.code:
INPUT points
IF points >= 100 THEN
    OUTPUT "Gold award"
ELSEIF points >= 50 THEN
    OUTPUT "Silver award"
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Keep going!"
ENDIF
blocks.output:
120 points: Gold award
75 points: Silver award
30 points: Keep going!

blocks.text: 3. Iteration
**[[Iteration]]** means repeating steps, also called **looping**. There are two kinds:

blocks.title: Count-controlled: the 3 times table
blocks.code:
FOR i ← 1 TO 5
    OUTPUT i * 3
NEXT i

blocks.title: Condition-controlled: keep asking for the password
blocks.code:
password ← ""
WHILE password <> "Dragon"
    INPUT password
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT "Welcome"
blocks.output: Keeps asking until the user types Dragon, then shows Welcome.

head: FOR loop
WHILE loop
rows: You know how many times, e.g. 5 times table rows
You do not know how many times, e.g. password attempts

blocks.title: Key points
items: Pseudocode is structured English for planning algorithms; it is not a real language.
Sequence: steps run in order, one after another.
Selection: IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF chooses a path using a condition.
Iteration: FOR ... NEXT repeats a set number of times; WHILE ... ENDWHILE repeats while a condition is true.
Read ← as "becomes"; = means "is equal to" and <> means "is not equal to".

check.q: What does `FOR i ← 1 TO 4` followed by `OUTPUT i * 2` and `NEXT i` output?
check.why: i is 1, 2, 3, 4 and each is doubled.

check.q: Which building block makes a choice?
check.why: Selection uses IF to choose a path.

check.q: You do not know how many guesses a user will need. Which loop is best?
check.why: A condition-controlled loop repeats until the condition changes.

check.q: Using the house points pseudocode, what is output for 50 points?
check.why: 50 is not >= 100, but it is >= 50.

practice.q: Name and describe the **three** basic building blocks of an algorithm.
practice.a: Sequence (1): instructions carried out one after another in order (1). Selection (1): a decision/condition decides which path is followed, e.g. IF (1). Iteration (1): steps are repeated / a loop, e.g. FOR or WHILE (1).

practice.q: Write pseudocode that asks for the temperature and outputs "Wear a coat" if it is below 10, otherwise outputs "No coat needed".
practice.a: INPUT temperature (1); IF temperature < 10 THEN (1); OUTPUT "Wear a coat" (1); ELSE OUTPUT "No coat needed" ENDIF (1).

practice.q: Explain the difference between a **count-controlled** loop and a **condition-controlled** loop.
practice.a: A count-controlled loop (FOR) repeats a fixed / known number of times (1). A condition-controlled loop (WHILE) repeats until a condition changes / while a condition is true, so the number of repeats may not be known (1).

pages.spec: Use variables in algorithms and trace an algorithm with a trace table
pages.summary: A variable is a named store for a value that can change while the algorithm runs. A trace table records the value of every variable step by step, so you can work out exactly what an algorithm does.

diagram.title: The adding-up loop
diagram.caption: Click each step, then follow it round the loop four times with the trace table below.

nodes.label: Start
nodes.detail: The algorithm begins.

nodes.label: total ← 0, count ← 1
nodes.detail: Both variables are given a starting value (initialised).

nodes.label: Is count <= 4?
nodes.detail: The condition is checked before every pass of the loop.

nodes.label: total ← total + count
nodes.detail: Add the current count onto the running total.

nodes.label: count ← count + 1
nodes.detail: Move count on by 1, or the loop would never end.

nodes.label: OUTPUT total
nodes.detail: Shows 10 on the screen.

nodes.label: Stop
nodes.detail: The algorithm ends.

blocks.text: Variables

A **[[variable]]** is a named store (like a labelled box) that holds a value while the algorithm runs. It is called a variable because the value can **vary**: a game's `score` starts at 0 and goes up every time you collect a coin.

items: Give variables **meaningful names**: `score`, `total`, `pupilName`, not `x` or `thing`.
No spaces in a name. Join words together, e.g. `highScore`.
A variable holds **one value at a time**. Putting a new value in replaces the old one.

blocks.text: Putting a value into a variable is called **[[assignment]]**. In our pseudocode it uses the arrow `←`, read as *becomes*:

blocks.title: Assignment
blocks.code:
score ← 0          // score becomes 0
score ← score + 5  // score becomes 0 + 5, so 5
score ← score + 5  // score becomes 5 + 5, so 10
OUTPUT score

blocks.text: `score ← score + 5` looks strange in maths, but it is not an equation. Work out the right-hand side **first** using the old value, then store the answer back in `score`.
Trace tables

A **[[trace table]]** is a table with a column for each variable (plus conditions and output). You work through the algorithm by hand, one line at a time, writing down every value. This is called a **[[dry run]]**. It shows exactly what the algorithm does and helps you find mistakes.

blocks.title: Algorithm to trace: adding up 1 to 4
blocks.code:
total ← 0
count ← 1
WHILE count <= 4
    total ← total + count
    count ← count + 1
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT total

head: Pass
count (at check)
count <= 4?
total becomes
count becomes
OUTPUT
blocks.caption: Trace table: the loop runs 4 times and outputs 10

blocks.title: Worked example: tracing a FOR loop
blocks.context: Trace this algorithm: `score ← 0`, then `FOR i ← 1 TO 3`, `score ← score + i * 2`, `NEXT i`, then `OUTPUT score`.
steps: Before the loop: score = 0.
The loop has run 3 times, so it ends. OUTPUT 12.
blocks.answer: The output is **12**.

blocks.text: Double-check every row: use the **old** value on the right-hand side, and only update one thing at a time. Most trace table mistakes come from rushing ahead.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A variable is a named store whose value can change.
Assignment (←) puts a value into a variable, replacing the old value.
Work out the right-hand side first, then store the result.
A trace table records every variable's value as you dry run an algorithm by hand.
Trace tables show what an algorithm outputs and help find errors.

check.q: score is 7. After `score ← score + 3`, what is score?
check.why: 7 + 3 = 10, which replaces the old value.

check.q: What is a trace table used for?
o: Recording variable values step by step while dry running an algorithm
check.why: It tracks every value as you work through by hand.

check.q: How many times does the loop body run in `WHILE count <= 4` if count starts at 1 and goes up by 1 each pass?
check.why: count = 1, 2, 3, 4 pass; 5 fails.

check.q: Which is the best variable name for a pupil's test mark?
check.why: Meaningful, no spaces, does not start with a number.

practice.q: What is a **variable**? Give an example of a variable that a quiz game might use.
practice.a: A named store / location in memory that holds a value which can change while the algorithm runs (1). Example: score, lives, questionNumber, playerName (1).

practice.q:
Complete a trace table for this algorithm and state the output.

`x ← 3`
`y ← 10`
`WHILE y > x`
`    y ← y - 2`
`    x ← x + 1`
`ENDWHILE`
`OUTPUT x, y`
practice.a: Start: x = 3, y = 10. Pass 1: 10 > 3 True, y = 8, x = 4 (1). Pass 2: 8 > 4 True, y = 6, x = 5 (1). Pass 3: 6 > 5 True, y = 4, x = 6 (1). Check: 4 > 6 False, loop ends; OUTPUT 6, 4 (1).

practice.q: Explain why a programmer would dry run an algorithm using a trace table.
practice.a: To check what the algorithm does / what it outputs (1) and to find logic errors before (or without) running it on a computer (1).

pages.spec: Describe and carry out a linear search and a binary search
pages.summary: A linear search checks each item in turn from the start and works on any list. A binary search repeatedly checks the middle item and throws away half of the list each time, but the list must be sorted first.

diagram.title: How a binary search works
diagram.caption: Click each step. Every time round the loop, half of the remaining list is thrown away.

nodes.label: Start
nodes.detail: The list must already be sorted. low = 1, high = the last position.

nodes.label: Is low <= high?
nodes.detail: If low has passed high, there is nothing left to search.

nodes.label: mid ← (low + high) DIV 2
nodes.detail: Find the middle position. DIV divides and throws away any remainder, so (7 + 8) DIV 2 = 7.

nodes.label: Is list[mid] the target?
nodes.detail: Check the middle item.

nodes.label: Found!
nodes.detail: Output the position and stop.

nodes.label: Is list[mid] < target?
nodes.detail: Is the target bigger than the middle item?

nodes.label: low ← mid + 1
nodes.detail: Throw away the lower half, including mid.

nodes.label: high ← mid - 1
nodes.detail: Throw away the upper half, including mid.

nodes.label: Not found
nodes.detail: The target is not in the list.

blocks.text: Searching means finding whether an item is in a **[[list]]** and, if so, where. Computers search all the time: finding your name in the register, a song in a playlist or a product on a shop's website. Two well-known searching algorithms are **linear search** and **binary search**.
In this topic the first item in a list is at **position 1**. (Many programming languages, including C#, count from 0. The idea is the same.)
Linear search
A **[[linear search]]** starts at the first item and checks each one in turn until it finds the target or reaches the end of the list. It is simple and works on **any** list, sorted or not.

blocks.title: Worked example: linear search for 19
steps: Position 1: 12. Not 19, move on.
Position 2: 5. Not 19, move on.
Position 3: 31. Not 19, move on.
Position 4: 8. Not 19, move on.
Position 5: 19. Found!
blocks.answer: 19 is at **position 5**, found after **5** checks. Searching for 50 would check all 7 items and then report "Not found".

blocks.title: Linear search
blocks.code:
found ← FALSE
position ← 1
WHILE found = FALSE AND position <= LENGTH(list)
    IF list[position] = target THEN
        found ← TRUE
    ELSE
        position ← position + 1
    ENDIF
ENDWHILE
IF found = TRUE THEN
    OUTPUT "Found at position ", position
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Not found"
ENDIF
blocks.output:
Searching 12, 5, 31, 8, 19, 44, 27 for 19:
Found at position 5

blocks.text: Binary search

A **[[binary search]]** only works on a **sorted** list. It checks the **middle** item. If that is the target, it stops. If the target is bigger, it throws away the lower half; if smaller, it throws away the upper half. It keeps halving until it finds the target or runs out of items. It is how you find a word in a dictionary: open in the middle, then decide which half to look in.

blocks.title: Worked example: binary search for 42
steps: low = 1, high = 11. mid = (1 + 11) DIV 2 = **6**. Item 6 is **31**. 42 > 31, so throw away positions 1 to 6: low = 7.
low = 7, high = 11. mid = (7 + 11) DIV 2 = **9**. Item 9 is **50**. 42 < 50, so throw away positions 9 to 11: high = 8.
low = 7, high = 8. mid = (7 + 8) DIV 2 = **7** (15 ÷ 2 = 7.5, round down). Item 7 is **36**. 42 > 36, so low = 8.
low = 8, high = 8. mid = (8 + 8) DIV 2 = **8**. Item 8 is **42**. Found!
blocks.answer: 42 is at **position 8**, found after **4** checks. A linear search would have needed 8 checks.

blocks.text: Binary search **only works on a sorted list**. On an unsorted list it could throw away the half that contains the target. Sort the list first, or use a linear search.
If there is an even number of items there are two middles. Our rule `(low + high) DIV 2` always picks the **left** one. Stick to one rule throughout a question.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Linear search checks every item in turn from the start.
Linear search works on sorted or unsorted lists but can be slow on long lists.
Binary search checks the middle item and throws away half the list each time.
Binary search only works on a sorted list.
mid = (low + high) DIV 2, rounding down.

check.q: What must be true about a list before you use a binary search?
o: It must have fewer than 100 items
check.why: Halving only works if the items are in order.

check.q: A linear search for 8 in 4, 9, 8, 2 checks how many items?
check.why: It checks 4, then 9, then finds 8 at the third check.

check.q: In a binary search, low = 1 and high = 10. Which position is checked first?
Which search works on an unsorted list?
check.why: Binary search needs a sorted list; linear search does not.

practice.q: Describe how a **linear search** finds an item in a list.
practice.a: Start at the first item (1); compare each item with the target in turn / move to the next item if it does not match (1); stop when the item is found, or report not found when the end of the list is reached (1).

practice.q: Show the steps of a binary search for **20** in this sorted list: 3, 7, 12, 18, 24, 31, 36, 42, 50, 57, 63.
practice.a: mid = (1 + 11) DIV 2 = 6, item 31, 20 < 31 so high = 5 (1). mid = (1 + 5) DIV 2 = 3, item 12, 20 > 12 so low = 4 (1). mid = (4 + 5) DIV 2 = 4, item 18, 20 > 18 so low = 5; mid = 5, item 24, 20 < 24 so high = 4 (1). low (5) > high (4), so 20 is not in the list (1).

practice.q: Give **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of binary search compared with linear search.
practice.a: Advantage: much faster / fewer checks on a long list, because half is removed each time (1). Disadvantage: the list must be sorted first / more complicated to write (1).

pages.spec: Carry out a bubble sort on a list, pass by pass
pages.summary: A bubble sort compares each pair of neighbouring items and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. It repeats these passes through the list until a whole pass makes no swaps.

diagram.title: Bubble sort: 5, 2, 8, 1, 4
diagram.caption: Click each pass to see the list after it. The largest unsorted item bubbles to the end each time.

items.label: Start
items.detail: 5, 2, 8, 1, 4: unsorted.

items.label: Pass 1: 3 swaps
items.detail: 2, 5, 1, 4, **8**. The 8 has bubbled to the end.

items.label: Pass 2: 2 swaps
items.detail: 2, 1, 4, **5, 8**. The 5 is now in place.

items.label: Pass 3: 1 swap
items.detail: 1, 2, 4, 5, 8. It looks sorted, but the algorithm does not know yet.

items.label: Pass 4: 0 swaps
items.detail: 1, 2, 4, 5, 8. No swaps in a whole pass, so the list is sorted. Stop.

blocks.text: Sorting means putting items into order. **[[Ascending order]]** goes from smallest to largest (1, 2, 3 or A to Z); descending order goes from largest to smallest. Sorted lists are easier for people to read (a class register in alphabetical order) and they let computers use a fast binary search.
How a bubble sort works

items: Start at the beginning of the list.
Compare the first two items. If they are in the wrong order, **[[swap]]** them.
Move along one place and compare the next pair. Keep going to the end of the list. That is one **[[pass]]**.
After each pass, the largest unsorted item has "bubbled" up to its correct place at the end.
Repeat passes until a whole pass makes **no swaps**. The list is then sorted.

blocks.text: It is called a **[[bubble sort]]** because the big values rise to the end of the list like bubbles rising to the top of a fizzy drink.
Worked example, pass by pass
Sort **5, 2, 8, 1, 4** into ascending order. Each pass makes 4 comparisons (a list of 5 items has 4 neighbouring pairs).

head: Pass
Compare
Swap?
List after
blocks.caption: Bubble sort of 5, 2, 8, 1, 4: 4 passes, 6 swaps in total

blocks.text: After pass 3 the list *looks* sorted, but the algorithm only knows it is finished when a **whole pass makes no swaps**. That is why pass 4 is needed.
Swapping two values
To swap two items you need a **temporary** variable. Imagine swapping the drinks in two full cups: you need an empty third cup to pour one into first.

blocks.title: Bubble sort
blocks.code:
swapped ← TRUE
WHILE swapped = TRUE
    swapped ← FALSE
    FOR i ← 1 TO LENGTH(list) - 1
        IF list[i] > list[i + 1] THEN
            temp ← list[i]           // empty cup
            list[i] ← list[i + 1]
            list[i + 1] ← temp
            swapped ← TRUE
        ENDIF
    NEXT i
ENDWHILE

blocks.text: In an exam, write the whole list out again after **every pass** (or every swap if asked). Tick off each pair as you compare it so you do not skip one.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A bubble sort compares neighbouring pairs and swaps them if they are in the wrong order.
One trip through the whole list is a pass.
After each pass the largest unsorted item is in its correct place at the end.
The sort stops when a whole pass makes no swaps.
Swapping needs a temporary variable.

check.q: In a bubble sort, what happens to the largest item in pass 1?
o: It moves to the end of the list
check.why: It is swapped along every time until it reaches the end.

check.q: When does a bubble sort stop?
o: When the first item is the smallest
When a whole pass makes no swaps
check.why: No swaps in a pass means everything is in order.

check.q: What is 3, 1, 2 after one pass of a bubble sort (ascending)?
check.why: 3 and 1 swap (1, 3, 2), then 3 and 2 swap (1, 2, 3).

check.q: Why is a temporary variable needed to swap two values?
o: So one value is not lost when it is overwritten
check.why: Like the empty cup when swapping two drinks.

practice.q: Show the list after **each pass** of a bubble sort to put **6, 3, 9, 2** into ascending order.
practice.a: Pass 1: 3, 6, 2, 9 (1). Pass 2: 3, 2, 6, 9 (1). Pass 3: 2, 3, 6, 9 (1). Pass 4: 2, 3, 6, 9 with no swaps, so the sort stops (1).

practice.q: Explain how a bubble sort knows that a list is sorted.
practice.a: It makes a full pass through the list (1) without making any swaps (1).

practice.q: Describe how a bubble sort works.
practice.a: Compare the first two / each pair of neighbouring items (1); swap them if they are in the wrong order (1); repeat passes through the list until a pass makes no swaps (1).

pages.spec: Compare algorithms that solve the same problem in terms of efficiency
pages.summary: Different algorithms can solve the same problem, but some take far fewer steps. Efficiency is about how much time (number of steps) and memory an algorithm needs, especially as the amount of data grows.

diagram.title: How many checks does binary search need?
diagram.caption: Change the number of items in a sorted list. A linear search could need to check every one of them.

blocks.text: There is often more than one algorithm that solves a problem. They might all give the right answer, but one might take a second and another might take an hour. Computer scientists compare algorithms by their **[[efficiency]]**: how much **time** (number of steps) and **memory** they need.
Counting steps

We do not time algorithms with a stopwatch, because a faster computer would give a different answer. Instead we count the **steps**, such as the number of comparisons. We usually look at the **[[worst case]]**: the most steps the algorithm could ever need.

head: Items in sorted list
Linear search (worst case)
Binary search (worst case)
blocks.caption: Doubling the list adds only one extra check to a binary search

blocks.text: Every check in a binary search halves what is left, so doubling the size of the list adds just **one** more check. A linear search on a list twice as long could take **twice** as many checks.

head: Linear search
Binary search
rows: Fast: halves the list each time

blocks.text: Binary search is not always the winner. If the list is not sorted you would have to sort it first, which takes time. For a short list, or one you only search once, a linear search is perfectly sensible.
Two algorithms, one problem
Problem: add up all the whole numbers from 1 to 100. Both algorithms below are correct.

blocks.title: Algorithm A: loop
blocks.code:
total ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 100
    total ← total + i
NEXT i
OUTPUT total
blocks.output: 5050 (after 100 additions)

blocks.title: Algorithm B: formula
blocks.code:
n ← 100
total ← n * (n + 1) / 2
OUTPUT total
blocks.output: 5050 (one calculation)

blocks.title: Worked example: which is more efficient?
blocks.context: Compare algorithms A and B for adding 1 to n.
steps: Algorithm A does **one addition for every number**: 100 additions for n = 100, a million for n = 1,000,000.
Algorithm B does **the same small calculation** whatever n is: 100 × 101 ÷ 2 = 5050.
Both give the correct answer, so compare the steps.
As n gets bigger, A gets slower and slower but B stays the same.
blocks.answer: Algorithm B is more efficient. Algorithm A is easier to understand, but its number of steps grows with n.

blocks.text: Sorting algorithms differ too. **Bubble sort** is easy to understand but slow on big lists, because it keeps passing through the whole list. Faster methods, such as **merge sort**, are used for big jobs like sorting every pupil in Northern Ireland by exam result.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Efficiency is how much time (steps) and memory an algorithm uses.
Compare algorithms by counting steps, often in the worst case.
Binary search needs far fewer checks than linear search on a long sorted list.
The most efficient algorithm is not always best: binary search needs a sorted list.
Bubble sort is simple but slow on large lists.

check.q: What does the efficiency of an algorithm describe?
o: Which language it is written in
How much time and memory it uses
check.why: Efficient algorithms use fewer steps and less memory.

check.q: A sorted list has 1,000 items. What is the most checks a binary search needs?
check.why: Halving 1,000 repeatedly takes at most 10 checks.

check.q: When might a linear search be the better choice?
o: The list is huge and sorted
The list is short or unsorted
When the target is in the middle
check.why: No sorting needed, and on a short list the difference is tiny.

check.q: What is the worst case for a linear search on a list of 50 items?
check.why: The target is last, or missing, so every item is checked.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by the **efficiency** of an algorithm.
practice.a: How much time / how many steps it takes (1) and how much memory it uses (1) to solve a problem.

practice.q: A library has 100,000 books sorted by title. Explain why a binary search would be more efficient than a linear search for finding a book.
practice.a: Linear search might have to check every one of the 100,000 titles (1). Binary search halves the number of books left with each check (1), so it needs at most about 17 checks (1).

practice.q: Algorithm A uses a loop to add the numbers 1 to n. Algorithm B uses the formula n × (n + 1) ÷ 2. Which is more efficient for large values of n? Explain your answer.
practice.a: Algorithm B (1). It does the same small number of steps whatever n is, while A needs one addition for every number, so it gets slower as n grows (1).

pages.spec: Find and fix errors in an algorithm using tracing and test data
pages.summary: A bug is an error that stops an algorithm working correctly. Debugging means testing, tracing to find the bug, fixing it and testing again; logic errors are the hardest to spot because the algorithm still runs.

diagram.title: The debugging cycle
diagram.caption: Click each stage. Keep going round until the tests all pass.

items.label: Test
items.detail: Run the algorithm with test data where you already know the correct answer.

items.label: Spot
items.detail: Compare the actual output with the expected output. Different? There is a bug.

items.label: Find
items.detail: Use a trace table to dry run the algorithm line by line and see where the values first go wrong.

items.label: Fix
items.detail: Change the faulty line. Change one thing at a time.

items.label: Retest
items.detail: Run all the tests again, to check the fix worked and has not broken anything else.

blocks.text: Almost no algorithm works perfectly first time. An error in an algorithm or program is called a **[[bug]]**, and finding and fixing bugs is called **[[debugging]]**. Good programmers expect bugs and test carefully to find them.
Two kinds of error

head: Syntax error
Logic error
rows: Breaks the rules (grammar) of the language, e.g. a spelling mistake in a keyword or a missing bracket
Follows the rules but gives the wrong result
No: the program will not run until it is fixed
Yes, but the output is wrong
The editor or translator points to the line
Testing and tracing with a trace table

blocks.text: A **[[syntax error]]** is usually easy to find. A **[[logic error]]** is harder, because nothing tells you it is there. You only notice when the answer is wrong, which is why we test.
Common bugs

head: Bug
Example
Fix
rows: A WHILE loop where count never changes
OUTPUT total before the loop that adds it up
Move the OUTPUT after ENDWHILE or NEXT
blocks.caption: Bugs to look out for

blocks.text: Worked example: fixing a broken average
This algorithm should read in five test marks and output the average. Testing with the marks 6, 8, 10, 7 and 9 (total 40, so the average should be **8**) gives **1.8**. Something is wrong.

blocks.title: Broken algorithm
blocks.code:
total ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 5
    INPUT mark
    total ← mark
NEXT i
average ← total / 5
OUTPUT average
blocks.output: Marks 6, 8, 10, 7, 9 give 1.8 (expected 8)

blocks.title: Worked example: trace, find, fix
blocks.context: Trace the broken algorithm with marks 6, 8, 10, 7, 9.
steps: i = 1: mark = 6, total = **6**.
i = 2: mark = 8, total = **8**. The 6 has gone! The total should be 14.
This is where it first goes wrong: `total ← mark` **replaces** the total instead of adding to it.
Carry on: after i = 5, total = 9, so average = 9 / 5 = 1.8. That matches the wrong output.
Fix: change the line to `total ← total + mark`. Retest: total = 6 + 8 + 10 + 7 + 9 = 40, average = 40 / 5 = **8**. Correct.
blocks.answer: The bug was a logic error on line 4. The fixed line is `total ← total + mark`.

blocks.text: Choosing test data
Good **[[test data]]** checks more than just the obvious. For "pass if the mark is 50 or more" (marks out of 100):

head: Type
Example
Why
rows: Typical values the algorithm should handle easily.
Values right at the edge, where `>` and `>=` bugs show up.
blocks.caption: Normal, boundary and erroneous test data

blocks.text: Work out the **expected** output before you test. If you do not know what the right answer is, you cannot tell whether the algorithm got it wrong.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A bug is an error; debugging is finding and fixing it.
Syntax errors break the language rules and stop it running.
Logic errors run but give the wrong result, so testing and tracing are needed.
Common bugs: wrong comparison, off-by-one, infinite loops, wrong order, variables not updated.
Test with normal, boundary and erroneous data, then retest after every fix.

check.q: An algorithm runs but gives the wrong answer. What type of error is this?
check.why: It follows the rules but the logic is wrong.

check.q: `count ← 1`, then `WHILE count <= 3` with `OUTPUT count` inside and nothing else. What happens?
check.why: count never changes, so it is an infinite loop.

check.q: The rule is "pass if 50 or more". Which pair is boundary test data?
check.why: They sit either side of the edge of the rule.

check.q: `WHILE count < 10` should output 1 to 10 but stops at 9. What kind of bug is this?
check.why: It runs one time too few; `<=` fixes it.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a **syntax error** and a **logic error**.
practice.a: Syntax error: breaks the rules/grammar of the language, so the program will not run (1). Logic error: the program runs but produces the wrong result / does not do what was intended (1).

practice.q:
This algorithm should output the numbers 1 to 5, but it never stops. Identify the bug and write the corrected algorithm.

`count ← 1`
`WHILE count <= 5`
`    OUTPUT count`
`ENDWHILE`
practice.a: count is never increased, so count <= 5 is always true / infinite loop (1). Add `count ← count + 1` (1) inside the loop, after `OUTPUT count` and before `ENDWHILE` (1).

practice.q: An algorithm gives a cinema discount to anyone **aged 12 or under**. Give **one** normal, **one** boundary and **one** erroneous test value, and the expected result for each.
practice.a: Normal, e.g. 8: discount / 30: no discount (1). Boundary, e.g. 12: discount or 13: no discount (1). Erroneous, e.g. -4 or "ten": rejected / error message (1).

chapters.title: Cyber Security
chapters.intro: Learn how criminals try to attack computers and accounts, and, more importantly, how to stop them: from spotting phishing and building strong passwords to encryption, firewalls, backups, the law and careers in cyber security.

pages.spec: Explain why data and computer systems are valuable and describe the CIA triad
pages.summary: Cyber security protects computers, networks, accounts and data. Good security keeps data Confidential, keeps it correct (Integrity) and keeps it Available when it is needed: the CIA triad.

diagram.title: Which part of CIA is broken?
diagram.caption: Decide which part of the CIA triad each attack damages, then click to check.
head: What happened
CIA part
Why
rows: A pupil reads the teacher's markbook over their shoulder
Someone saw data they were not allowed to see
Someone changes their own test score from 45% to 95%
The data has been altered, so it can no longer be trusted
Ransomware locks every file on the school server
Staff and pupils cannot get to the data when they need it
A hacker posts the school's pupil addresses online
Private personal data has been exposed
The online homework site is flooded with fake traffic and crashes
The system is down, so nobody can use it
Malware swaps the bank details on a supplier's invoice
Data was secretly changed so money goes to the wrong place

blocks.text: Think about everything stored about you in school: your name, address, date of birth, medical notes, attendance, reports and exam results. Now think about your phone: photos, messages, game accounts and saved passwords. All of this is **data**, and to the wrong person it is worth a lot.
**[[Cyber security]]** is the set of methods, tools and habits used to protect computers, networks, accounts and data from being attacked, damaged or accessed without permission.
Why is data so valuable?

head: Who wants it?
What they might do with it
rows: Sell stolen passwords and personal details, steal money, or use your identity to open accounts.
Lock an organisation's files and demand payment to unlock them.
Use data about what you like to target adverts (legally, if they follow the rules).
Take over a social media or game account to embarrass the owner.
Spy on governments and businesses, or disrupt hospitals, power and transport.
blocks.caption: Why people want your data and systems

blocks.text: Systems are valuable too. If a hospital's computers stop working, operations are cancelled. If a school's network is down, registers, lessons and exams are disrupted. Attacking the **system** can do as much harm as stealing the **data**.
The CIA triad
Security experts describe what they are protecting using three ideas, called the **[[CIA triad]]** (nothing to do with the American spy agency!).

head: Letter
Meaning
School example
rows: Only the right people can **see** the data.
Only your teachers and parents can see your report.
The data is **correct** and has not been changed without permission.
Nobody can secretly change your exam marks.
The data and systems **work** when the right people need them.
The register system works at 9 am every morning.
blocks.caption: The three parts of the CIA triad

blocks.title: Worked example: a stolen teacher password
blocks.context: Someone guesses a teacher's password and logs in to the school's management system. Which parts of the CIA triad are at risk?
steps: They can **see** pupils' private details: confidentiality is broken.
They could **change** marks or attendance: integrity is at risk.
They could **delete** records or lock the account: availability is at risk.
