nodes.label: Inputs
nodes.detail: Values you can change, e.g. distance 18 km, average speed 40 km/h, 12 stops.

nodes.label: Rules
nodes.detail: Formulas or code that describe how the system behaves, e.g. time = distance ÷ speed × 60 + stops × 0.5.

nodes.label: Outputs
nodes.detail: The answers the model produces, e.g. journey time 33 minutes.

nodes.label: Decide
nodes.detail: Use the output to make a decision, or change an input and run the model again (a what-if).

blocks.text: Every computer model, from a weather forecast to a game, is made of the same four parts.

head: Part
What it is
School bus example
rows: A value fed into the model that you can change
Distance 18 km, average speed 40 km/h, 12 stops
A formula or instruction describing how the system behaves
Driving time = distance ÷ speed × 60; each stop adds half a minute
A value that stays the same every time the model runs
blocks.caption: The parts of a model

blocks.text: A **[[variable]]** is a named value that can change, such as *speed* or *number of stops*. Inputs and outputs are both variables: when an input variable changes, the outputs change too. That is the whole point of a model.

blocks.title: Worked example: the school bus model
blocks.context: A bus brings pupils 18 km to school from the far side of Lough Erne. Its average speed is 40 km/h and it makes 12 stops, each taking 0.5 minutes. How long is the journey?
steps: Rule 1: driving time = distance ÷ speed × 60 = 18 ÷ 40 × 60 = **27 minutes**.
Rule 2: stop time = stops × time per stop = 12 × 0.5 = **6 minutes**.
Output: journey time = 27 + 6 = **33 minutes**.
blocks.answer: The model predicts a 33-minute journey.

blocks.title: Worked example: change one variable
blocks.context: What if roadworks slow the bus to an average of 30 km/h? Everything else stays the same.
steps: Driving time = 18 ÷ 30 × 60 = **36 minutes**.
Stop time is still 12 × 0.5 = 6 minutes.
Journey time = 36 + 6 = **42 minutes**.
blocks.answer: Changing one input (speed) changed the output from 33 to 42 minutes.

blocks.text: Choosing data types
Each variable stores a particular kind of value, called its **[[data type]]**. Choosing the right one matters in spreadsheets and in code, because it decides what you can do with the value.

head: Data type
What it stores
Model example
rows: Number of stops: 12; pupils on the bus: 48
Time per stop: 0.5 minutes; ticket price: 2.75
Is it snowing? FALSE; Bus full? TRUE
blocks.caption: Data types in a model

blocks.text: Do not store a count of people as a float. You cannot have **48.5 pupils** on a bus! Counts of whole things should be **integers**. Money and measurements usually need **floats**.
A **Boolean** input is a great way to switch part of a model on or off. For example, *Snowing? = TRUE* could add 15 minutes to the journey using an IF rule.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Inputs go in, rules are applied, outputs come out.
A variable is a value that can change; a constant stays the same.
Changing an input variable changes the outputs.
Integer = whole number, float = decimal, string = text, Boolean = TRUE/FALSE.
Pick the data type that matches the real value.

check.q: In the bus model, which is an input?
check.why: Speed is a value you can change and feed in.

check.q: Which data type should store whether it is raining?
check.why: It can only be TRUE or FALSE.

check.q: A bus travels 18 km at 30 km/h and makes 12 stops of 0.5 minutes. What is the journey time?
What is a constant in a model?
o: A value that stays the same every time
A value the user changes often
A detail that has been left out
check.why: e.g. 60 minutes in an hour.

practice.q: A model works out the cost of a pizza order. Identify **one** input, **one** rule and **one** output.
practice.a: Input, e.g. number of pizzas / price per pizza / delivery charge (1). Rule, e.g. total = number × price + delivery (1). Output, e.g. total cost (1).

practice.q: State the most suitable data type for each variable: (a) number of pupils on a trip; (b) cost per pupil in pounds; (c) whether a pupil has paid.
practice.a: (a) Integer (1). (b) Float / real (1). (c) Boolean (1).

practice.q: A bus travels 24 km at 40 km/h and makes 12 stops of 0.5 minutes. Calculate the journey time. Show your working.

pages.spec: Build a spreadsheet model with formulas and use it to answer 'what if' questions
pages.summary: In a spreadsheet model the inputs are cells, the rules are formulas that refer to those cells, and the outputs recalculate automatically. Changing one input to see the effect is a what-if question.

diagram.title: Try it: the Year 9 disco model
diagram.caption: Change the inputs and watch the profit. Costs are £150 for the DJ, £40 for decorations, plus snacks for each pupil.

blocks.text: Spreadsheets are one of the most common tools for building models, because a formula **recalculates automatically** whenever a value it uses changes. If you have studied the Spreadsheets topic, this page builds on it.
Example: the Year 9 Christmas disco
The Year 9 council is running a disco to raise money for charity. They need to know whether it will make a profit. Here is their model.

head: A
B
blocks.caption: Inputs in B1:B5, outputs in B7:B10

blocks.title: Worked example: checking the outputs
blocks.context: Check each output by hand.
steps: Profit = 900 − 406 = **£494**, so B10 shows *Profit*.
blocks.answer: The model is working correctly: £494 profit.

blocks.text: Asking 'what if?'
A **[[what-if question|What-if question]]** changes one input and looks at the effect on the outputs. Change only **one** input at a time, so you know which change caused the difference.

head: What if...?
Input changed
Income
Costs
Profit
blocks.caption: Four what-if questions, one input changed each time

blocks.title: Worked example: only 120 pupils come
blocks.context: Snow is forecast and the council worries only 120 will come. What happens to the profit?
steps: Change B2 from 180 to 120. Nothing else changes.
blocks.answer: The disco still makes a profit, but £228 less than planned.

blocks.text: Never **[[hard-code|Hard-coding]]** values into formulas, e.g. `=5*180`. If the price changes, that formula will not update and your model gives the wrong answer. Always refer to the input cells: `=B1*B2`.
Colour your **input cells** (for example light yellow) and keep them together at the top. Anyone using the model can see straight away which cells they are allowed to change.

The DJ and decorations are **fixed costs**: they stay the same however many pupils come. Snacks are a **variable cost**: they go up with every ticket sold. Spotting which is which is a key part of building a money model.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Inputs are cells; rules are formulas that refer to those cells; outputs recalculate.
A what-if question changes one input to see the effect.
Change one input at a time so you know what caused the change.
Never hard-code numbers into formulas.
Label and colour the input cells.

check.q: In the disco model, which cell is an output?
check.why: B9 is calculated by a formula; B1, B2 and B5 are inputs.

check.q: Tickets are £5, 180 are sold, fixed costs are £190 and snacks are £1.20 each. What is the profit?
Why is =5*180 a poor formula for income?
o: It will not update if the price or tickets change
check.why: Hard-coded values do not change when the inputs change.

check.q: Why should you change only one input at a time in a what-if?
o: Excel can only recalculate one cell
So you know which change caused the effect
Changing two inputs causes an error
check.why: One change at a time shows clearly what each input does.

practice.q: Using the disco model, calculate the profit if 200 tickets are sold at £5. Show your working.
Write the formula for cell B8 (total costs) in the disco model, and explain why it uses cell references.
practice.a: =B3+B4+B5*B2 (1). So the total updates automatically if any cost or the number of tickets changes (1).

practice.q: Explain the difference between a **fixed cost** and a **variable cost**, using the disco as an example.
practice.a: Fixed cost stays the same however many come, e.g. DJ hire £150 (1). Variable cost depends on the number of pupils, e.g. snacks £1.20 each (1).

pages.spec: Use Goal Seek and scenarios to explore a spreadsheet model
pages.summary: Goal Seek works backwards: you choose the answer you want and it finds the input needed. Scenarios save whole sets of inputs, such as worst case, expected and best case, so you can compare them.

diagram.title: What-if vs Goal Seek
diagram.caption: Both use the same model, but they work in opposite directions.

states.label: What-if (forwards)
points: You choose the input
The model works out the output
e.g. What profit if 120 come?
Answer: £266

states.label: Goal Seek (backwards)
points: You choose the output you want
Excel finds the input needed
e.g. How many must come to break even?
Answer: 50 tickets

blocks.text: A what-if question works **forwards**: change an input, see the output. Sometimes you want to work **backwards** instead: *"How many tickets must we sell to raise £600?"* You could keep guessing, but Excel has a tool for it.
Goal Seek
**[[Goal Seek]]** finds the input value that makes an output reach a target. In Excel it is on the **Data** tab: **What-If Analysis > Goal Seek**. It asks three things:

head: Goal Seek box
Meaning
Disco example
blocks.caption: Goal Seek settings to find the break-even point

blocks.text: The point where income exactly equals costs, so profit is £0, is called **[[break-even|Break-even point]]**.

blocks.title: Worked example: the break-even point
blocks.context: Tickets are £5, fixed costs are £190 (DJ + decorations) and snacks cost £1.20 per pupil. How many tickets must be sold to break even?
steps: Each ticket brings in £5 but costs £1.20 in snacks, so each pupil adds 5 − 1.20 = **£3.80** towards the fixed costs.
The fixed costs are £190, so we need 190 ÷ 3.80 = **50** tickets.
Check: income 5 × 50 = £250; costs 190 + 1.20 × 50 = £250; profit = £0.
blocks.answer: Goal Seek gives 50 tickets: any more and the disco makes a profit.

blocks.title: Worked example: a target of £600
blocks.context: The council wants to raise £600. Use Goal Seek on B9 = 600 by changing B2.
steps: Need 3.80 × tickets − 190 = 600, so 3.80 × tickets = 790.
You cannot sell 0.89 of a ticket, and 207 tickets would fall just short, so **round up**.
blocks.answer: They need to sell 208 tickets.

blocks.text: Goal Seek often gives a decimal answer like **207.89**. For people, tickets or buses you must think about whether to round **up** or down. Rounding 207.89 down to 207 would miss the target.
Scenarios

A **[[scenario]]** is a saved set of input values that describes one possible situation. Planners often compare a **worst case**, an **expected case** and a **best case**. In Excel, **Data > What-If Analysis > Scenario Manager** stores scenarios and can produce a summary table.

head: Scenario
Tickets sold
Snacks per pupil
Income
Costs
Profit
blocks.caption: Three disco scenarios (ticket price £5, fixed costs £190 in each)

blocks.text: Even in the worst case the disco makes £160, so the council can go ahead with confidence. That is exactly the kind of decision a model is for.
A scenario can change **several** inputs at once, because in real life bad news often comes together: on a snowy night fewer pupils come **and** the shop may charge more for last-minute snacks.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Goal Seek works backwards from a target output to the input needed.
Set cell = output, To value = target, By changing cell = input.
Break-even is where income equals costs (profit £0).
Round Goal Seek answers sensibly, often up.
Scenarios save sets of inputs such as worst, expected and best case.

check.q: What does Goal Seek do?
o: Finds the input needed to reach a target output
Draws a chart of the outputs
check.why: It works backwards from the answer you want.

check.q: Each pupil adds £3.80 and fixed costs are £190. What is the break-even number of tickets?
Goal Seek says 207.89 tickets are needed to reach a target. How many should be sold?
check.why: You cannot sell part of a ticket and 207 falls short, so round up.

check.q: What is a scenario?
o: A saved set of input values for one possible situation
check.why: e.g. worst case, expected case, best case.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a what-if question and Goal Seek.
practice.a: What-if: you change an input and see the output (1). Goal Seek: you set the output you want and Excel finds the input needed (1).

practice.q: Tickets cost £6, fixed costs are £190 and snacks cost £1.20 per pupil. Calculate the break-even number of tickets. Show your working.
Give **one** reason why planners compare a worst case, expected case and best case scenario.
practice.a: To check the plan still works if things go badly / to see the range of possible results / to plan for risks (1).

pages.spec: Carry out a simulation step by step over time and explain how changing a variable changes the outcome
pages.summary: A simulation over time applies the model's rules again and again, one time step after another, and each new row is worked out from the row before. Small changes to a variable can make a huge difference.

diagram.title: Test yourself: the sickness bug simulation
diagram.caption: Each pupil who catches the bug passes it to 2 new pupils the next day. Click a hidden cell to check.
head: Day
New cases
Total so far

blocks.text: Many real systems change **over time**: a population grows, a bug spreads, money in a savings account builds up. A simulation handles this by working in **[[time steps|Time step]]**: it applies the rules to get from one day (or minute, or year) to the next, then does it again and again. This repetition is a kind of **[[iteration]]**.
Example: a sickness bug in Year 9
One pupil in a year group of **120** comes in with a sickness bug. The model's rules are:

items: Each new case passes the bug to **2** new pupils the next day (the **spread rate**).
New cases today = new cases yesterday × spread rate.
Total so far = yesterday's total + today's new cases.

blocks.title: Worked example: run the simulation
blocks.context: Start on day 0 with 1 case. Work out each day until day 6.
steps: Day 1: new = 1 × 2 = 2; total = 1 + 2 = 3.
Day 2: new = 2 × 2 = 4; total = 3 + 4 = 7.
Day 4: new = 16; total = 31. Day 5: new = 32; total = 63.
blocks.answer: By day 6 the model says 127 pupils have caught it. But there are only 120 in the year group!

blocks.text: A result of **127 out of 120** shows the model has broken. Our rules forgot that pupils who have already had the bug cannot catch it again, so there are fewer and fewer people left to infect. Always ask: **does this output make sense in real life?**
Building it in a spreadsheet

head: A
B
C
blocks.caption: Spread rate (2) is stored in F1. Row 3 is filled down to make more days.

blocks.text: Each row uses the row above it, so you write row 3 once and drag it down. The spread rate is in **one input cell**, F1, with an absolute reference `$F$1`, so you can change it and the whole simulation reruns instantly.
Change one variable

head: Spread rate
Total by day 3
Total by day 5
What it could mean
blocks.caption: Changing one variable changes the outcome enormously

blocks.text: With a spread rate of 1, only 6 pupils have had it by day 5. With a rate of 3, the model passes the whole year group by day 5. This is why health experts focus so much on reducing how many people each case passes an illness to.
Real disease models used by scientists are far more detailed. They track who is healthy, ill and recovered, and they include randomness. But the idea is the same: rules applied step by step.
A spreadsheet chart of the *Total so far* column makes the pattern obvious: a curve that gets steeper and steeper. This is called **exponential growth**.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A simulation over time applies rules one time step after another.
Each row is calculated from the row before.
In a spreadsheet: write one row, store variables in input cells, fill down.
A small change to a variable can make a huge difference over time.
Check outputs make sense: impossible results show a missing rule.

check.q: In a simulation over time, what is a time step?
o: The total time the simulation takes
One jump forward, such as one day
The first row of the spreadsheet
check.why: The rules are applied once per time step.

check.q: New cases double each day, starting with 1 on day 0. How many new cases are there on day 4?
The sickness model said 127 out of 120 pupils were ill. What does this show?
o: A rule is missing, so the model has broken
check.why: Pupils who have had it cannot catch it again; the model ignored this.

check.q: Why is the spread rate stored in $F$1?
o: Excel will not multiply by a number
So every row uses it when filled down and it can be changed in one place
So the spread rate changes on every row
check.why: The $ signs keep the reference fixed when the formula is copied.

practice.q: A model of rabbits on a farm starts with 20 rabbits. Each year the number of rabbits doubles. Work out how many rabbits there are after 3 years, showing each year.
Explain why simulations over time are often built in a spreadsheet by filling a formula down.
practice.a: Each row is one time step calculated from the row above (1); writing one formula and filling down repeats the rule for as many steps as needed without retyping (1).

practice.q: The sickness model predicted more pupils were ill than there were in the year group. Suggest how the rules could be improved.
practice.a: Add a rule that only pupils who have not yet had it can catch it / limit new cases to the number of healthy pupils left (1) so the total can never be more than 120 (1).

pages.spec: Explain why some simulations use random numbers and why they are run many times
pages.summary: Real life involves chance, so some simulations use random numbers. Each run gives a different result, so the simulation is run many times and the results are averaged to give a reliable prediction.

diagram.title: Chance of at least one six
diagram.caption: Change the number of dice rolls. The model works out the chance of rolling at least one six.

result.label: Chance of at least one six

blocks.text: Some things are not certain. A penalty taker does not score every time; it does not rain every day in Fermanagh (even if it feels like it). To model **chance**, a simulation uses **[[random numbers|Random number]]**.
Random numbers in a spreadsheet

head: Formula
What it does
Example result
rows: A random decimal from 0 up to (but not including) 1
A random whole number from 1 to 6, like rolling a dice
Gives Goal about 75% of the time
blocks.caption: Excel's random functions

blocks.text: These cells give a new value every time the sheet recalculates. In Excel you can press **F9** to force a recalculation and "run" the simulation again.
One run is not enough

Roll a dice 6 times and you might get no sixes, or three. A single run of a random simulation can be very lucky or unlucky. So we run it **many times** and look at the average or the overall pattern. The more runs, the closer the result gets to the true [[probability]].

head: Rolls simulated
Sixes
Fraction that were sixes
blocks.caption: One computer run (results change every time). The true probability is 1 ÷ 6 ≈ 0.167.

blocks.title: Simulating 1,000 dice rolls in Python
blocks.output: e.g. 171 sixes out of 1000 rolls. Run it again and you will get a slightly different number, usually somewhere near 167.

blocks.title: Worked example: penalty shoot-out
blocks.context: Ciara scores 75% of her penalties. A simulation of 5 penalties uses =IF(RAND()<0.75,"Goal","Miss") five times. Run 1 gave 5 goals, run 2 gave 3 goals. How many goals should the coach expect, on average?
steps: Two runs gave very different answers, so neither on its own is a good prediction.
On average she scores 0.75 goals per penalty.
Expected goals = 5 × 0.75 = **3.75**.
If the simulation is run 1,000 times, the average number of goals will be very close to 3.75.
blocks.answer: About 3.75 goals out of 5. Many runs give a reliable average; one run does not.

blocks.text: Weather forecasts do this too

The weather is very sensitive to tiny changes. Forecasters such as the **Met Office** run their weather model **many times**, each with slightly different starting conditions. If almost every run shows rain tomorrow, they are confident. If the runs disagree, the forecast is less certain. This is where a forecast like *"60% chance of rain"* comes from.
Do not judge a random simulation on **one run**. A single run that says "the team scores 5 out of 5" is just luck. Look at the results of many runs.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Random numbers let a simulation model chance.
RAND() gives a decimal from 0 up to 1; RANDBETWEEN(1,6) gives a whole number 1 to 6.
Each run of a random simulation gives a different result.
Run it many times and average the results.
More runs give a more reliable prediction.

check.q: Why do some simulations use random numbers?
o: To model events that happen by chance
Because computers cannot do exact maths
check.why: e.g. a penalty that goes in only some of the time.

check.q: What can =RANDBETWEEN(1,6) give?
check.why: It simulates rolling a normal dice.

check.q: Why is a random simulation run many times?
o: Excel needs several runs to start
One run might be lucky or unlucky
Every run gives the same answer
check.why: The average of many runs is a more reliable prediction.

check.q: A player scores 75% of penalties. How many goals would you expect from 8 penalties, on average?

practice.q: Write a spreadsheet formula that simulates a coin toss, showing *Heads* or *Tails*.
practice.a: =IF(RAND()<0.5,"Heads","Tails") or using RANDBETWEEN(1,2) with an IF (1 for the random part, 1 for the correct IF with both outcomes).

practice.q: A simulation of 10 dice rolls gave 4 sixes. Explain why this does not mean the chance of a six is 4 in 10.
practice.a: 10 rolls is a small number of runs, so the result can be lucky/unlucky (1). Running it many more times (e.g. 1,000) would give a fraction close to 1/6 (1).

practice.q: Explain why a weather forecaster runs the same model many times with slightly different starting values.
practice.a: Small changes in starting conditions can change the weather a lot (1); if most runs agree the forecast is confident, if they differ it is uncertain / it gives a percentage chance (1).

pages.spec: Test a model's predictions against real data and refine the model to improve it
pages.summary: Testing checks the model's formulas work as intended; validating checks its predictions against what really happens. If they do not match, refine the rules or assumptions and test again.

diagram.title: Validating a model
diagram.caption: Click each stage. If the prediction is not close enough, refine the model and go round again.

nodes.label: Predict
nodes.detail: Run the model, e.g. the bus journey will take 33 minutes.

nodes.label: Collect real data
nodes.detail: Time the real bus every day for a week.

nodes.label: Compare
nodes.detail: How far apart are the prediction and reality? Is the model always too high or too low?

nodes.label: Refine
nodes.detail: Change a rule or assumption, e.g. add 5 minutes for town traffic, then predict again.

nodes.label: Use
nodes.detail: Close enough? Use the model to make decisions, and keep checking.

blocks.text: A model is only useful if its predictions are close to what really happens. There are two different checks.

head: Testing
Validating
rows: Does the model do what I designed it to do?
Does the model match the real world?
Work out answers by hand with test data and compare with the spreadsheet
Compare the model's predictions with real measurements
Mistakes in formulas, e.g. a wrong cell reference

blocks.text: **[[Validation]]** means comparing a model's predictions with **real data**. The difference between them is the model's **[[error|Prediction error]]**.

blocks.title: Worked example: validating the bus model
blocks.context: The bus model predicts 33 minutes. A pupil times the real bus for a week: Mon 38, Tue 41, Wed 36, Thu 52 (heavy snow), Fri 37 minutes.
steps: Find each error (real − predicted): 5, 8, 3, 19, 4 minutes. The model is **always too low**.
Thursday was very unusual (snow), so look at it separately. The other four days average (38 + 41 + 36 + 37) ÷ 4 = **38 minutes**.
On a normal day the model is about 5 minutes short. Something is missing: the bus crawls through traffic in Enniskillen at 8:30.
Refine: add a new rule, *town traffic = 5 minutes*. New prediction: 33 + 5 = **38 minutes**.
blocks.answer: After refining, the model matches normal days. A Boolean input *Snowing?* could add extra time for days like Thursday.

head: Day
Predicted (old)
Real
Error
Predicted (refined)
blocks.caption: The refined model is much closer on normal days (times in minutes)

blocks.text: What makes a fair comparison?

items: Use **real data that the model was not built from**, so it is a genuine test.
Collect **enough** data: one day could just be a fluke.
Look for a **pattern** in the errors. Always too low? Something is missing.
Note unusual events (like snow) separately rather than ignoring them.

blocks.text: Do not change a model just to match **one** odd result. If you added 19 minutes to make Thursday fit, the model would then be wrong on every normal day.
Professional modellers do this all the time. Weather forecasters check every forecast against what actually happened, and this is one reason forecasts have become much more accurate over the years.
Each time round the loop (predict, compare, refine) the model should get a little better. This is the same **plan, build, test, refine** cycle used in all software development.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Testing checks the formulas work; validating checks the model matches reality.
Error = real value − predicted value.
A pattern in the errors points to a missing rule or a wrong assumption.
Refine the model, then test it again.
Use enough real data, and treat unusual events separately.

check.q: What does it mean to validate a model?
o: Check the spelling of the labels
Compare its predictions with real data
Make the inputs a different colour
check.why: Validation asks whether the model matches the real world.

check.q: A model predicts 33 minutes; the real journey took 41. What is the error?
A model's predictions are too low every single day. What does this most likely show?
o: The real data must be wrong
A rule or factor is missing from the model
check.why: A consistent pattern in the errors points to something the model leaves out.

check.q: Which is the best thing to do with one very unusual result, such as a snow day?
o: Change the model to match it exactly
Delete the whole set of results
Note it and consider it separately
Use it as the main prediction
check.why: Changing the model to fit one odd day would make it worse on normal days.

practice.q: Explain the difference between **testing** a model and **validating** a model.
practice.a: Testing checks the formulas / model work as designed, e.g. by comparing with hand-worked answers (1). Validating compares the model's predictions with real-world data (1).

practice.q: The disco model predicted 180 pupils. Only 152 came. Calculate the error and suggest **one** reason the prediction might have been wrong.
practice.a: Error 152 − 180 = −28 / 28 fewer pupils (1). Any sensible reason, e.g. bad weather, a clash with another event, assumption based on last year's numbers (1).

practice.q: Describe how a model can be improved after it has been validated.
practice.a: Look for patterns in the differences between predictions and reality (1); change / add rules or assumptions and then test it again against new data (1).

pages.spec: Evaluate the limitations, trade-offs and possible bias of models, including AI models, and ask who a model works for
pages.summary: Every model leaves things out, so it has limits. A model can be unfair if its data or assumptions leave some people out. AI models are models too: they learn patterns from data, so biased data gives biased results.

diagram.title: What went wrong with the model?
diagram.caption: Match each problem to an example.
pairs: A bus model still uses last year's timetable
A sickness model says 127 out of 120 pupils are ill
Face recognition trained mostly on one group of people
Crash tests that only use a dummy the size of an average man
A queue model assuming every pupil takes exactly 15 seconds
A typing mistake enters 1,800 tickets instead of 180

blocks.text: The statistician George Box famously said: *"All models are wrong, but some are useful."* Because every model is a simplification, it will never be perfect. A good modeller knows the **limits** of their model and asks **who it works for**, not just whether it works.
Common limitations

items: **Missing factors**: abstraction left out something that turned out to matter.
**Assumptions** that are not true for everyone or every day.
**Data quality**: old, incomplete or wrongly typed data. *Garbage in, garbage out* (**[[GIGO]]**).
**The unexpected**: no model can predict every event, like a sudden storm or a pandemic.
**People change**: if a model says *"traffic is quiet on this road"*, everyone's sat nav sends them there and it fills up.

blocks.text: Trade-offs
Building a model always involves **[[trade-offs|Trade-off]]**: gaining one thing means giving up another.

head: Trade-off
One side
The other side
rows: Quick to build, easy to understand
More accurate, but slow and hard to check
Waiting hours for a better answer
blocks.caption: Trade-offs in modelling

blocks.title: Worked example: the disco price
blocks.context: A council member adds a rule: *for every £1 the ticket price goes up, 25 fewer pupils come* (300 − 25 × price). With fixed costs of £190 and snacks at £1.20, which price is best?
steps: The model says £7 makes the most money, but 75 fewer pupils come than at £4.
blocks.answer: Best for the charity: about £7. Best for pupils who cannot afford £7: £4. The model gives the numbers; people must decide what is fair.

blocks.text: Bias: who gets left out?
A model is **[[biased|Bias]]** if it gives results that are unfair to some groups of people, often because of the data or assumptions it was built on.

items: **Crash test dummies**: for many years the standard dummy was based on an average-sized man. Research has found that women are more likely to be seriously injured in similar crashes. In 2022, researchers in Sweden presented a crash test dummy based on an average woman.

**Exam grades in 2020**: when exams were cancelled because of Covid-19, a statistical model was used across the UK, including by CCEA in Northern Ireland, to work out grades, partly using schools' past results. Many pupils felt it marked them down unfairly because of their school's history rather than their own work. After protests, teachers' predicted grades were used instead (A level pupils kept the calculated grade if it was higher).

blocks.text: AI models are models too

An **[[AI model]]** is a model that has **learned patterns from a large set of data** (its **[[training data]]**) so it can make predictions or generate content. Like any model, it is a simplification, and it can only be as good as its data. If the data leaves some people out, the AI's predictions will be worse for them. For example, studies found some face recognition systems were much less accurate for people with darker skin, because they had been trained mostly on photos of lighter-skinned faces.
A computer's answer is **not automatically fair or correct** just because a computer worked it out. Ask: what data was it built from, what did it leave out, and who could lose out?

blocks.title: Key points
items: All models are simplifications, so all have limits.
Garbage in, garbage out: bad data gives bad predictions.
Modelling involves trade-offs such as simple vs accurate.
Biased data or assumptions can make a model unfair to some people.
AI models learn from training data, so they can carry its bias.
Always ask who a model works for, and who it leaves out.

check.q: What does garbage in, garbage out mean?
o: Bad input data leads to bad output
Old models should be thrown away
Outputs are always more accurate than inputs
check.why: A model can only be as good as the data put into it.

check.q: Why were older crash test dummies a problem?
o: They were too expensive to use
They were based on an average-sized man
They could only test slow crashes
check.why: Models based on one body type can be less safe for others.

check.q: How does an AI model learn?
o: A programmer writes every rule by hand
It copies a human brain exactly
It uses no data at all
It finds patterns in a large set of training data
check.why: AI models learn patterns from data, so their data matters.

check.q: A model shows the highest profit comes from a £7 ticket, but fewer pupils can afford it. This is an example of...
check.why: Gaining more money means fewer pupils can go.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by **bias** in a model, and give an example.
practice.a: When a model gives results that are unfair to / less accurate for some groups of people (1). Example, e.g. crash test dummies based on men; face recognition trained mostly on lighter-skinned faces; 2020 grades model (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** limitations of using a computer model to make decisions.
practice.a: Any two: it is a simplification so may leave out important factors (1); assumptions may be wrong (1); depends on accurate data / garbage in, garbage out (1); cannot predict unexpected events (1).

practice.q: An AI system is trained to predict which pupils will do well at GCSE using data from only one school. Explain why its predictions might be unfair for pupils at other schools.
practice.a: It has only learned patterns from one school's pupils / training data is not representative (1), so it may not work for pupils with different backgrounds, subjects or circumstances / results would be biased (1).

pages.spec: Plan, build, test and evaluate a model of your own to answer a real question
pages.summary: Building a good model follows a cycle: plan the question, inputs, rules, outputs and assumptions; build it; test and validate it; then evaluate how well it works and who it works for, and refine it.

diagram.title: The modelling cycle
diagram.caption: Most models go round this loop more than once.

items.label: Plan
items.detail: Write the question, the user, the success criteria, the inputs, rules, outputs and assumptions.

items.label: Build
items.detail: Create the spreadsheet or program. Label and colour the inputs. Use cell references, not typed numbers.

items.label: Test and validate
items.detail: Check outputs against hand calculations, then compare predictions with real data.

items.label: Evaluate and refine
items.detail: Did it meet the success criteria? Who does it work for? Improve it and go round again.

blocks.text: Now it is your turn. Building your own model uses everything in this topic, and it follows the same cycle of **planning, development, testing and refinement** used to build any software.
1. Plan
Before you open Excel, plan on paper. A clear plan saves a lot of time later.

head: Plan section
Hot chocolate stall at the school Christmas fair
rows: What price should we charge to make at least £100 for charity?
Price per cup (float), cups sold (integer), cost per cup (float), stall hire (float)
Income = price × cups; costs = stall hire + cost per cup × cups; profit = income − costs
Same number sold at any price; no cups wasted; everyone pays
Profit is correct when checked by hand; answers the price question; inputs are clearly labelled
blocks.caption: A model plan

blocks.text: 2. Build

items: Put all **inputs together** at the top, labelled and coloured.
Write **rules as formulas** using cell references.
Format money as currency, and use sensible data types.
Add an IF output to make the answer obvious, e.g. =IF(B9>=100,TRUE,FALSE).

blocks.text: 3. Test and validate

blocks.title: Worked example: test with hand-worked data
blocks.context: Inputs: price £1.50, 120 cups sold, cost 40p per cup, stall hire £20. What should the model show?
steps: Profit = 180 − 68 = **£112**, so *Target met?* should be TRUE.
If the spreadsheet shows anything different, a formula is wrong.
blocks.answer: Expected outputs: £180, £68, £112, TRUE.

blocks.text: Use **[[test data|Test data]]** that includes normal values, extreme values (0 cups sold) and values right on the target. With 0 cups sold the profit should be **−£20** (just the stall hire). After the fair, **validate** by comparing the model's prediction with what was really sold.
4. Evaluate and refine
An **evaluation** judges how well your model met its success criteria and what could be improved. Use evidence, not just "it works".

items: **Did it answer the question?** e.g. it showed £1.50 meets the target if 120 cups sell.
**How accurate was it?** e.g. predicted 120 cups, really sold 95.
**What were its limits?** e.g. it assumed the same sales at any price.
**Who does it work for?** e.g. could pupils with less money still buy a drink?
**Improvements**: e.g. add a demand rule, a scenario for a rainy day, or a chart.

blocks.text: Good project ideas: a canteen queue, your savings towards a new phone, a school sports day timetable, a fundraising event, the spread of a rumour through a year group, or a simple game with random dice rolls.
Do not write *"My model is perfect."* Every model has limitations. Naming them, with a sensible improvement, is what earns the best marks in an evaluation.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Plan first: question, user, inputs, rules, outputs, assumptions, success criteria.
Build with labelled inputs and formulas that use cell references.
Test with hand-worked answers, then validate with real data.
Evaluate against the success criteria, using evidence.
Name limitations, think about who it works for, and refine.

check.q: What should you do first when building a model?
o: Draw a chart of the results
Plan the question, inputs, rules and outputs
check.why: Planning first saves time and mistakes later.

check.q: Price £1.50, 120 cups, 40p per cup, stall hire £20. What is the profit?
What are success criteria?
o: Statements used to judge whether the model does its job
The formulas used in the model
The random numbers in a simulation
check.why: You evaluate against them at the end.

check.q: Which is the best evaluation comment?
o: It predicted 120 cups but 95 sold, as it ignored the weather
check.why: A good evaluation uses evidence and names a limitation.

practice.q: A pupil plans a model of their savings for a £300 bike. List **two** inputs, **one** rule and **one** output for the model.
practice.a: Inputs, e.g. money saved already, pocket money per week, money from a part-time job / birthday (2). Rule, e.g. total = saved + weekly amount × weeks (1). Output, e.g. weeks needed / date they can buy it (1).

practice.q: Explain why test data should include extreme values as well as normal values.
practice.a: Extreme values (e.g. 0 cups sold) check the model still gives sensible answers at the limits (1) and can reveal errors that normal values do not show (1).

practice.q: Write **two** sentences evaluating the hot chocolate model, using the fact that it predicted 120 cups but only 95 were sold.
practice.a: One mark for using the evidence (prediction 120 vs real 95, so the model was too high / profit was lower than predicted) (1); one mark for a reason or improvement, e.g. it assumed the same sales at any price / did not include weather, so add a demand rule or a rainy-day scenario (1).

chapters.title: Networks and the Internet
chapters.intro: Find out what really happens when you send a message, open a website or download a game: the hardware, layouts, addresses and rules that make networks and the internet work.

pages.spec: Explain what a network is, why computers are networked, and the difference between a LAN and a WAN
pages.summary: A network is two or more devices connected so they can share data and resources. A LAN covers a small area like a school; a WAN covers a large area and the internet is the biggest WAN of all.

diagram.title: Stand-alone vs networked
diagram.caption: What changes when you join computers together?

states.label: Stand-alone computer
points: Files only on that computer
Needs its own printer
Software installed one machine at a time
Viruses cannot spread to other machines

states.label: Networked computer
points: Log on anywhere and open your files
Shares printers and the internet connection
Updates installed on every machine at once
Needs security to stop viruses and hackers

blocks.text: When you log on in the computer room, your work is not saved on the computer in front of you. It is saved on a **server** somewhere else in the school, and you can open it from any computer in the building. That only works because the computers are joined together in a **[[Network]]**.

A network is **two or more computers or devices connected together** so that they can communicate and share data and resources. The connection can be a cable or a wireless signal. A computer that is not connected to anything is called a **[[Stand-alone computer]]**.
Why do we network computers?

items: **Share files:** pupils and teachers can save work centrally and open it on any computer.
**Share hardware:** thirty pupils can use one printer instead of needing thirty printers.
**Share an internet connection:** every device uses the same connection to the outside world.
**Communicate:** email, Teams messages and video calls all travel over networks.
**Central management:** the technician can install software or updates on every computer at once, and back up everyone's work in one go.
**Security and logins:** each user has their own username and password, and can only see the files they are allowed to.

blocks.text: Are there any drawbacks?

head: Drawback
Why it matters
rows: Servers, switches, cables and wireless access points all cost money to buy and install.
Large networks need a trained technician or network manager to run them.
Malware on one computer can travel across the network to others.
If the main server goes down, nobody can get to their files.
A network that is connected to the internet can be attacked from outside, so it needs security such as a firewall.
blocks.caption: Disadvantages of networking

blocks.text: LAN or WAN?

head: LAN
WAN
rows: Large: towns, countries, the whole world
The organisation itself, e.g. the school
The school network; your home Wi-Fi
The internet; a bank linking all its branches

blocks.title: Worked example: LAN or WAN?
blocks.context: A supermarket chain has a network in each of its 40 shops. The tills in every shop send sales data to head office in Belfast each night. Which networks are LANs and which is a WAN?
steps: Inside a single shop, the tills, office PCs and printer are all on one site, so each shop has a **LAN**.
The shops are spread across Northern Ireland, so the connections linking all 40 LANs to head office cover a large area.
A network linking LANs across a large area is a **WAN**.
blocks.answer: Each shop is a LAN; the network joining the shops to head office is a WAN.

blocks.text: The **[[Internet]]** is a giant WAN: millions of LANs (homes, schools, businesses) joined together all over the world. When you browse from school, your request leaves the school LAN and travels across the internet.
In Year 8 you met the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web. In this topic we look under the bonnet at **how** networks actually move data around.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A network is two or more connected devices that can share data and resources.
Networks let us share files, printers and an internet connection, and manage computers centrally.
Drawbacks include cost, the spread of viruses and dependence on the server.
LAN = small area (one site); WAN = large area, often linking LANs.
The internet is the largest WAN in the world.

check.q: What is a network?
o: A single computer with lots of storage
Two or more devices connected so they can share data and resources
check.why: A network needs at least two connected devices.

check.q: Which of these is a LAN?
o: A bank linking branches in five countries
check.why: One school site is a small area, so it is a LAN.

check.q: Which is a **disadvantage** of networking computers?
o: Viruses can spread from one computer to others
Work can be backed up centrally
check.why: Being connected means malware can travel between computers.

check.q: What is the largest WAN in the world?
check.why: The internet links millions of networks worldwide.

practice.q: State **three** advantages of connecting the computers in a school to a network.
practice.a: Any three: share files / log on and open work from any computer (1); share printers or other hardware (1); share one internet connection (1); communicate, e.g. email/messages (1); install software or updates centrally (1); back up all users' work centrally (1); individual logins control who can access what (1).

practice.q: Explain the difference between a LAN and a WAN. Give an example of each.
practice.a: LAN covers a small geographical area / one site (1); e.g. a school or home network (1). WAN covers a large geographical area / links LANs together (1); e.g. the internet or a company linking branches (1).

practice.q: Give **two** disadvantages of a network.
practice.a: Any two: cost of hardware/cabling (1); need a technician to manage it (1); viruses can spread across it (1); if the server fails users cannot access files (1); risk of hacking (1).

pages.spec: Identify the main pieces of network hardware and describe what each one does
pages.summary: Every device needs a NIC to join a network. Switches connect devices inside a LAN, routers connect networks together, wireless access points add Wi-Fi, and modems convert signals. Data travels through Ethernet or fibre optic cables.

diagram.title: Match the hardware
diagram.caption: Click to match each device with its job.
pairs: Lets a device connect to a network; has a MAC address built in
Connects devices inside a LAN and sends data only to the right one
Connects different networks, such as a LAN and the internet
Lets laptops and phones join a wired network by Wi-Fi
Converts digital data into signals for a phone line or cable
Carries data as pulses of light over long distances

blocks.text: A network needs more than just computers. Special hardware connects the devices and moves data between them. If you look in the cupboard in the corner of a computer room you will often find a **cabinet** full of flashing lights and cables: that is network hardware at work.
The main devices

head: Hardware
What it does
Where you might see it
rows: Lets a device connect to a network. Every NIC has a unique **MAC address** built in. It can be wired (with an Ethernet socket) or wireless.
Built into every laptop, phone, games console and smart TV
Connects lots of devices together **inside a LAN**. It reads where each piece of data is going and sends it **only to the device it is meant for**.
The network cabinet in school, with dozens of cables plugged in
Connects **different networks together**, for example the school LAN to the internet. It forwards packets towards their destination using **IP addresses**.
Your broadband box at home; the school's link to the outside world
Lets wireless devices join a wired network using Wi-Fi.
White boxes on classroom ceilings or corridor walls
Converts the computer's digital data into signals that can travel along a phone line or cable, and converts incoming signals back. (Short for **mo**dulator **dem**odulator.)
Usually built into a home broadband router
blocks.caption: Network hardware

blocks.text: A quick way to remember: a **switch** works **within** one network; a **router** works **between** networks.
Your home router is several devices in one

The box your internet provider sends you is usually called a router, but it actually contains a **router**, a **switch** (the yellow Ethernet sockets on the back), a **wireless access point** (for Wi-Fi) and often a **modem** (to talk to the phone line or fibre). In a school these are separate, bigger devices because there are hundreds of users.
Cables

head: Ethernet (copper)
Fibre optic
rows: Electrical signals along twisted pairs of copper wire
Pulses of light along thin strands of glass
Can be affected by electrical interference
More expensive and harder to fit
Connecting PCs to the switch in a classroom
Linking buildings on a school site; broadband to homes and streets

blocks.title: Worked example: following the journey out of school
blocks.context: You click a link in a lesson. Which pieces of hardware does your request pass through to get from your PC to the internet?
steps: The **NIC** in your PC turns the request into signals and sends them down the **Ethernet cable**.
The cable runs to a **switch** in the network cabinet, which passes the data on towards the school router.
The **router** sees the data is for a computer outside the school and forwards it onto the internet (often via a **fibre optic** link).
blocks.answer: NIC, Ethernet cable, switch, router, then out onto the internet.

blocks.text: You may also hear of a **hub**. It is an older, simpler device that sends every piece of data to every device connected to it. Switches replaced hubs because they are cleverer and cause less wasted traffic.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A NIC lets a device connect to a network and holds its MAC address.
A switch connects devices within a LAN and sends data only to the right device.
A router connects networks together and forwards data using IP addresses.
A wireless access point adds Wi-Fi to a wired network; a modem converts signals for phone lines or cables.
Ethernet uses copper and electricity; fibre optic uses glass and light, and is faster over longer distances.

check.q: Which device connects a school LAN to the internet?
check.why: Routers connect different networks together.

check.q: What does a switch do?
o: Connects devices within a LAN and sends data to the correct device
Gives each device a MAC address
check.why: A switch works inside one network.

check.q: How does a fibre optic cable carry data?
o: As pulses of light in glass
check.why: Fibre uses light, so it is fast and unaffected by electrical interference.

check.q: Which piece of hardware must every networked device have?
check.why: Without a NIC, a device cannot connect to any network.

practice.q: Describe the purpose of a **router** and a **switch**.
practice.a: Router: connects different networks together / connects the LAN to the internet (1); forwards packets towards their destination using IP addresses (1). Switch: connects devices together within a LAN (1); sends data only to the device it is intended for (1).

practice.q: A school is linking its main building to a new sports hall 400 metres away. Explain why fibre optic cable would be chosen instead of Ethernet cable.
practice.a: Any three: Ethernet only works up to about 100 m (1); fibre works over many kilometres (1); fibre is faster / higher bandwidth (1); fibre is not affected by electrical interference (1).

practice.q: What is the job of a wireless access point?
practice.a: It allows wireless devices to connect to a wired network using Wi-Fi (1).

pages.spec: Compare wired and wireless connections, including Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and choose a suitable one for a task
pages.summary: Wired connections are faster, more reliable and more secure. Wireless connections (Wi-Fi and Bluetooth) give freedom to move and need no cables, but are slower, have limited range and can suffer from interference.

diagram.title: Which connection?
diagram.caption: Decide, then click to check.
head: Situation
Best connection
Reason
rows: Desktop PCs in the computer room
They never move and need speed and reliability
Smartwatch sending steps to a phone
Close together and needs very little battery power
Pupils using laptops in the library
They move around and need internet access
Linking two school buildings 500 m apart
Too far for Ethernet or Wi-Fi; fibre is fast over long distances
Short range, low power, two devices
Must be as fast, reliable and secure as possible

blocks.text: Devices can connect to a network in two ways: with a **cable** (wired) or using **radio waves** (wireless). Most schools use both. The desktop PCs in the computer room are wired, while laptops, iPads and phones connect wirelessly.
Wired vs wireless

head: Wired (e.g. Ethernet)
Wireless (e.g. Wi-Fi)
rows: Usually slower; drops as you move away or more people join
Harder to intercept: someone needs to plug in
Signals travel through the air, so must be encrypted and password protected
Cables must be run through walls and ceilings
Quick to set up; no trailing cables

blocks.text: Wi-Fi

**[[Wi-Fi]]** uses radio waves to connect devices to a wireless access point or home router. A typical indoor range is **a few tens of metres**, and the signal gets weaker through thick walls and floors. To join a Wi-Fi network you usually need its name and a password (the **key**), which also **encrypts** the data so people nearby cannot read it.
Bluetooth

**[[Bluetooth]]** is also wireless, but it is designed for **short-range** connections (usually up to about **10 metres**) directly between two devices. It uses very little power, which makes it perfect for small battery-powered gadgets. Devices are **paired** once and then reconnect automatically.

head: Wi-Fi
Bluetooth
rows: Fast enough to stream films and games
Laptops and phones on the school or home network; internet access
Wireless earbuds, game controllers, smartwatches, sending a photo to a friend's phone
blocks.caption: Wi-Fi compared with Bluetooth

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing a connection
blocks.context: The school is setting up three things: (a) a new server in the network cabinet, (b) iPads for a geography field trip around the school grounds, (c) a wireless speaker for the PE department's phone. Which connection suits each?
steps: (a) A server must be fast and reliable and it never moves, so use a **wired Ethernet** (or fibre) connection.
(b) Pupils will walk around, so the iPads need **Wi-Fi**, with access points covering the grounds.
(c) A phone and a speaker a few metres apart only need a short-range, low-power link, so use **Bluetooth**.
blocks.answer: Server: wired. iPads: Wi-Fi. Speaker: Bluetooth.

blocks.text: Free public Wi-Fi in cafés is often **not encrypted**. Avoid logging in to anything important, such as a bank account, on it.
If your games console keeps lagging online, try plugging it straight into the router with an Ethernet cable. A wired link is usually faster and steadier than Wi-Fi.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Wired connections are faster, more reliable and more secure, but you cannot move around.
Wireless connections give freedom to move and need no cables, but are slower and can suffer interference.
Wi-Fi connects devices to a network over tens of metres.
Bluetooth connects two devices directly over about 10 metres using very little power.
Wireless data should be encrypted with a password so others cannot read it.

check.q: Which is an advantage of a wired connection over Wi-Fi?
o: You can walk around with your device
It is usually faster and more reliable
check.why: Cables give a steady, fast connection.

check.q: What is the typical range of Bluetooth?
check.why: Bluetooth is designed for short-range links.

check.q: Which would be the best use of Bluetooth?
o: Connecting wireless earbuds to a phone
check.why: Short range, low power, two devices: ideal for Bluetooth.

check.q: Why should a Wi-Fi network have a password?
o: To stop strangers joining and to encrypt the data
check.why: The key controls who can join and scrambles the data.

practice.q: Give **two** advantages and **two** disadvantages of using Wi-Fi rather than cables in a classroom.
practice.a: Advantages, any two: pupils can move around / use laptops anywhere (1); no trailing cables / safer (1); cheaper and quicker to install (1); easy to add new devices (1). Disadvantages, any two: slower (1); less reliable / interference from walls or other devices (1); limited range (1); less secure / signals can be intercepted (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** differences between Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
practice.a: Any two: Bluetooth has a shorter range (about 10 m) than Wi-Fi (tens of metres) (1); Bluetooth uses less power (1); Bluetooth is slower (1); Bluetooth connects two devices directly while Wi-Fi connects devices to a network/the internet (1).

pages.spec: Describe star, bus and mesh network topologies and give an advantage and a disadvantage of each
pages.summary: A topology is the layout of a network. In a star, every device connects to a central switch. In a bus, every device shares one backbone cable. In a mesh, devices connect to many others so there are lots of routes.

diagram.title: Star, bus and mesh
diagram.caption: Click each layout to compare them.

states.label: Star
points: Every device cabled to a central switch
One broken cable affects only one device
Switch fails = whole network fails
Used in most schools and offices

states.label: Bus
points: All devices on one backbone cable
Cheap: needs little cable
Backbone breaks = whole network fails
Data can collide when two devices send at once

states.label: Mesh
points: Devices connected to several others
Many routes, so very reliable
Lots of cable: expensive to set up
The internet and mesh Wi-Fi work this way

blocks.text: A **[[Topology]]** is the **shape or layout** of a network: how the devices are connected to each other. Different layouts suit different jobs, and each has strengths and weaknesses.
Star topology
In a **[[Star topology]]**, every computer has **its own cable to a central switch**. This is how most school and office networks are built, including the computer rooms in our school.

items: **Advantage:** if one cable breaks, only that one computer loses its connection; everyone else carries on.
**Advantage:** it is fast, because the switch sends data only to the computer it is meant for.
**Advantage:** it is easy to add a new computer: just plug another cable into the switch.
**Disadvantage:** if the central switch fails, the whole network goes down.
**Disadvantage:** it needs a lot of cable, because every device has its own.

blocks.text: Bus topology

In a **[[Bus topology]]**, every device is connected to **one main cable**, called the **backbone**, with a **terminator** at each end to stop signals bouncing back. Data sent by one device travels along the whole backbone, and each device checks whether it is meant for them. Bus networks are rarely used today, but they help explain why star networks took over.

items: **Advantage:** cheap and simple, because it needs less cable.
**Disadvantage:** if the backbone cable breaks, the **whole network fails**.
**Disadvantage:** only one device can send at a time. If two send at once their data **collides**, so it gets slower as more devices are added.
**Disadvantage:** every device can see all the data, which is less secure.

blocks.text: Mesh topology

In a **[[Mesh topology]]**, devices are connected to **several other devices**. In a **full mesh** every device connects to every other one; in a **partial mesh** some do. Because there are lots of routes, if one link breaks the data simply takes another path. **The internet is a giant partial mesh** of routers. Many homes now use **mesh Wi-Fi**, where several small units around the house pass data between each other to cover every room.

items: **Advantage:** very reliable: there is no single point of failure.
**Advantage:** data can take the quickest or least busy route.
**Disadvantage:** a wired mesh needs huge amounts of cable and is expensive to set up and manage.

blocks.title: Worked example: how much cable does a full mesh need?
blocks.context: A full mesh network has 5 computers, each connected directly to every other one. How many cables are needed? How many would a star network with 5 computers need?
steps: Each computer connects to the other 4, so 5 x 4 = 20 connection ends.
Each cable has two ends (it joins two computers), so divide by 2: 20 / 2 = **10 cables**.
A star needs one cable from each computer to the switch: **5 cables**.
Check: with 6 computers a full mesh needs 6 x 5 / 2 = 15 cables, while a star needs 6. The mesh grows much faster.
blocks.answer: Full mesh: 10 cables. Star: 5 cables. This is why wired full meshes are rare in schools.

blocks.text: Exam questions often ask: *what happens if one cable fails?* Star: only that device is affected. Bus: the whole network if it is the backbone. Mesh: data takes another route.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Topology = the layout of a network.
Star: each device connects to a central switch; one cable failing only affects one device, but the switch is a single point of failure.
Bus: all devices share one backbone; cheap, but a break stops everything and data can collide.
Mesh: many connections and routes; very reliable but expensive. The internet is a mesh.
Most school networks use a star topology.

check.q: In a star topology, what is at the centre?
check.why: Every device has its own cable to the central switch.

check.q: What happens in a bus network if the backbone cable breaks?
check.why: Every device relies on the single backbone.

check.q: Why is a mesh network very reliable?
o: There are many routes, so data can go around a broken link
check.why: No single point of failure.

check.q: Which topology is most like the internet?
check.why: The internet is a huge partial mesh of routers.

practice.q: Describe a star topology and give **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of it.
practice.a: Each device has its own cable to a central switch (1). Advantage, any one: if one cable fails only that device is affected / fast / easy to add devices (1). Disadvantage, any one: if the switch fails the whole network fails / uses a lot of cable, so more expensive (1).

practice.q: Explain why a mesh topology is more reliable than a bus topology.
practice.a: In a mesh, devices have several connections / there are many routes, so if one link fails data takes another route (1). In a bus, all devices rely on one backbone cable, so if it breaks the whole network fails (1).

practice.q: A full mesh network has 4 computers. How many cables are needed? Show your working.
practice.a: 4 x 3 = 12 connection ends, divided by 2 (1) = 6 cables (1).

pages.spec: Compare client-server and peer-to-peer networks and decide which is suitable for a given situation
pages.summary: In a client-server network, clients ask central servers for files, logins and services, so it is easy to manage and secure. In a peer-to-peer network every computer is equal and shares directly, which is cheap and simple but harder to manage.

diagram.title: Client-server or peer-to-peer?
diagram.caption: Decide, then click to check.
head: Situation
Best model
Reason
rows: A school with 900 pupils who log on anywhere
Two friends swapping photos with AirDrop
A family sharing a printer between two laptops
A bank with thousands of staff
Watching a video on a website
Your browser is a client asking a web server
A small shop with one till and one office PC
Cheap and simple for two computers

blocks.text: As well as a physical layout, every network has a way of **organising who does what**. There are two main models: **client-server** and **peer-to-peer**.
Client-server

In a **[[Client-server network]]**, one or more powerful computers called **[[servers|Server]]** provide services, and the other computers, called **[[clients|Client]]**, request them. The school network (C2k) is client-server: when you log on, your PC (the client) asks a server to check your username and password, and then loads your files from a file server.

head: Type of server
What it does
School example
rows: Stores users' files and controls who can open them
Your documents and the shared Year 9 folder
Manages a queue of print jobs for shared printers
Choosing a printer in the computer room
Stores web pages and sends them to browsers that ask for them
Checks usernames and passwords when people log on
Logging on at the start of the lesson
blocks.caption: Common types of server

blocks.text: Peer-to-peer

In a **[[Peer-to-peer network]]** (P2P) there is **no central server**. Every computer, called a **peer**, is equal. Each one stores its own files and can share them directly with the others. Sending a photo to a friend's phone with Bluetooth or AirDrop, or connecting two laptops to swap a file, are simple examples. Some online games and file-sharing apps also use P2P.

head: Client-server
Peer-to-peer
rows: Each user must back up their own computer
Central logins and permissions; easier to control
Harder to control; each user sets their own sharing
Clients are fine unless it is the server
Only that computer's files are lost to others
Homes, very small offices, sharing between friends

blocks.title: Worked example: which model?
blocks.context: A hairdresser has two computers: one at the reception desk for bookings and one in the back office for accounts. A grammar school has 600 computers and 1,000 users. Which model suits each?
steps: The hairdresser only has two computers and probably no IT technician. Buying a server would be expensive and unnecessary, so **peer-to-peer** is suitable: the two computers can share files and a printer directly.
The school has hundreds of users who need to log on anywhere, have their work backed up and be kept out of each other's files. This needs central control, so **client-server** is suitable.
blocks.answer: Hairdresser: peer-to-peer. School: client-server.

blocks.text: When you visit a website, your browser is acting as a **client** and the computer storing the website is a **web server**. So the internet itself relies on the client-server model millions of times every second.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Client-server: clients request services from central servers.
Servers can store files, manage printing, host websites, handle email and check logins.
Peer-to-peer: no server; every computer is equal and shares directly.
Client-server is easier to secure, back up and manage, but costs more.
Peer-to-peer is cheap and simple, so suits homes and very small businesses.

check.q: What is a client?
o: A computer that provides services to others
A computer that requests services from a server
check.why: Clients ask; servers provide.

check.q: Which network model has no central server?
check.why: In P2P every computer is equal.

check.q: Why does a school use a client-server network?
o: Logins, security and backups can be managed centrally
check.why: Central control suits hundreds of users.

check.q: Which server checks your username and password when you log on?
check.why: Authentication means checking who you are.

practice.q: Describe **two** differences between a client-server network and a peer-to-peer network.
practice.a: Any two differences, each explained for both sides (2 marks each, max 4): client-server has a central server, P2P has none / all computers equal (2); client-server stores files centrally, P2P stores files on each computer (2); client-server is backed up centrally, P2P each user backs up their own (2); client-server security controlled centrally, P2P harder to control (2); client-server more expensive, P2P cheaper (2).

practice.q: State **three** types of server and what each does.
practice.a: Any three, 1 mark each for type with correct job: file server, stores users' files (1); print server, manages print jobs/queue (1); web server, stores and sends web pages (1); email server, sends/receives/stores email (1); authentication server, checks usernames and passwords (1).

pages.spec: Explain how data is split into packets and sent across a network using packet switching
pages.summary: Data is split into small packets. Each packet has a header with the sender's and receiver's addresses and a packet number. Routers send each packet by the best route available, and the receiving computer puts them back in order and asks for any missing ones again.

diagram.title: A packet's journey
diagram.caption: Click each step to follow a file across the internet.

nodes.label: Split
nodes.detail: The sender's computer splits the file into numbered packets and adds a header to each.

nodes.label: Send
nodes.detail: Packets leave through the router onto the internet.

nodes.label: Route
nodes.detail: Each router reads the destination address and sends each packet by the best route at that moment.

nodes.label: Reorder
nodes.detail: Packets arrive, possibly out of order; they are sorted using their packet numbers.

nodes.label: Check and rebuild
nodes.detail: Any missing or damaged packet is requested again, then the file is put back together.

blocks.text: When you send a photo to a friend, it is not sent as one big lump. It is chopped into lots of small pieces called **[[packets|Packet]]**. Each packet travels across the internet on its own, and the pieces are put back together at the other end.
What is in a packet?

head: Part
What it contains
Like on a parcel...
rows: The sender's IP address, the destination IP address, the packet number (e.g. 3 of 50) and the protocol being used
The address label and return address
The actual piece of data: part of your photo, message or web page
A check value used to spot if the data was damaged on the way, and a marker for the end of the packet
A seal showing it has not been tampered with
blocks.caption: The parts of a packet

blocks.text: Packet switching

The internet uses **[[Packet switching]]**. Each packet is sent separately. At every **router** it reaches, the router reads the destination address in the header and sends the packet onwards along whichever route is **best at that moment**. If one route is busy or broken, the next packet can be sent a different way. This means packets from the same file can travel by **different routes** and arrive **out of order**.

blocks.title: Worked example: sending a photo from Enniskillen to Australia
blocks.context: Orla emails a 2 MB photo to her cousin in Sydney. To keep it simple, imagine it is split into just 6 packets. Packet 4 goes missing on the way. What happens?
steps: Orla's computer splits the photo into packets 1 to 6 and adds a **header** to each one with her IP address, her cousin's mail server's IP address and the packet number.
The packets leave through her router. Routers along the way send each packet by the best route at that moment: packets 1, 2 and 5 go via London and New York; 3 and 6 go via Amsterdam and Singapore.
They arrive in the order 1, 3, 2, 6, 5. The receiving computer uses the **packet numbers** to put them back in order: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6.
It notices packet 4 is missing, so it asks for packet 4 to be **sent again**.
Packet 4 arrives, the photo is reassembled perfectly, and an acknowledgement is sent back.
blocks.answer: The packets travel separately, are reordered using their numbers, and any missing packet is resent, so the photo arrives complete.

blocks.text: Why use packets?

items: **Reliable:** if a route breaks, packets simply go another way, and lost packets can be resent.
**Efficient:** many people share the same cables at once, because packets from different users take turns.
**Only damaged parts are resent:** if one packet is damaged, only that small packet is sent again, not the whole file.
**Fast:** packets can avoid busy routes.

blocks.text: Protocols

For this to work, every device in the world must follow the same rules. A set of rules for communicating is called a **[[Protocol]]**. **TCP/IP** is the main set of protocols for the internet: **TCP** splits data into packets, numbers them and checks they all arrive; **IP** handles the addressing and routing. **HTTP** and **HTTPS** are the protocols for sending web pages.
Think of a jigsaw sent through the post in several envelopes. Each envelope is numbered, they may arrive on different days, but you can still build the picture using the numbers.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Data is split into small packets before it is sent.
Each packet has a header (sender and destination addresses, packet number), a payload and a trailer.
Routers send each packet by the best available route, so packets may arrive out of order.
The receiver reorders packets using their numbers and asks for missing ones to be resent.
A protocol is a set of rules for communication; TCP/IP is the main one for the internet.

check.q: Which part of a packet contains the destination address?
check.why: The header is like the address label on a parcel.

check.q: Why might packets arrive in the wrong order?
o: They are sent by different routes
check.why: Each packet may take a different route, some quicker than others.

check.q: What happens if a packet goes missing?
o: The receiver asks for that packet to be sent again
The other packets are thrown away
check.why: Only the missing packet needs resending.

check.q: What is a protocol?
o: A set of rules for how devices communicate
check.why: Everyone follows the same rules, so devices can understand each other.

practice.q: State **three** items of information found in the header of a packet.
practice.a: Any three: sender's/source IP address (1); destination IP address (1); packet number / sequence number (1); total number of packets (1); protocol used (1).

practice.q: Describe how a file is sent across the internet using packet switching.
practice.a: Any four: the file is split into packets (1); each packet is given a header with addresses and a packet number (1); routers send each packet by the best route available / packets can take different routes (1); packets may arrive out of order (1); the receiver reassembles them in order using the packet numbers (1); missing or damaged packets are requested again (1).

pages.spec: Explain what IP addresses and MAC addresses are and the difference between them
pages.summary: An IP address identifies a device on a network so data can be routed to it, and it can change. A MAC address is a unique, permanent address built into a device's NIC when it is made.

diagram.title: IP or MAC?
diagram.caption: Click to match each address fact with its description.
pairs: A much longer address created because IPv4 ran out
12 hexadecimal digits fixed in the NIC by the manufacturer
Uses IP addresses to send packets between networks
Uses MAC addresses to send data within a LAN

blocks.text: For a packet to reach the right device, every device needs an **address**, just as every house needs an address for the post to arrive. Networked devices actually have **two** kinds: an **IP address** and a **MAC address**.
IP addresses
An **[[IP address]]** (Internet Protocol address) identifies a device on a network so that data can be **routed** to it. Routers use IP addresses to decide where to send packets.

items: **IPv4** addresses are four numbers, each from **0 to 255**, separated by dots, e.g. `192.168.1.25`. That gives about 4.3 billion different addresses.

There are now far more devices than that, so **IPv6** was created. IPv6 addresses are much longer and written in hexadecimal, e.g. `2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334`. There are enough for every grain of sand on Earth to have many.
IP addresses are usually given out automatically by the router when a device joins a network, so **they can change**. Your phone gets a different IP address at home, at school and in a café.

blocks.title: Worked example: is this a valid IPv4 address?
blocks.context: Which of these are valid IPv4 addresses? (a) 10.0.15.200 (b) 192.168.1.256 (c) 172.16.4 (d) 8.8.8.8
steps: Rule: exactly **four** numbers separated by dots, each from **0 to 255**.
(a) 10, 0, 15, 200: four numbers, all 0 to 255, so **valid**.
(b) 256 is bigger than 255, so **not valid**.
(c) Only three numbers, so **not valid**.
(d) 8, 8, 8, 8: four numbers, all in range, so **valid**.
blocks.answer: (a) and (d) are valid; (b) and (c) are not.

blocks.text: MAC addresses

A **[[MAC address]]** (Media Access Control address) is **built into the NIC** of a device when it is manufactured. It is **unique** in the world and **does not normally change**. It is written as **12 hexadecimal digits** in pairs, e.g. `3C:22:FB:9A:41:07`. Switches use MAC addresses to send data to the right device **within a LAN**.
IP vs MAC

head: IP address
MAC address
rows: A device's location on a network
The NIC of one particular device
Yes: it changes when you join a different network
No: fixed when the NIC is made
Routers, to send data between networks
Switches, to send data within a LAN

blocks.text: Think of a MAC address as your **name**: it stays with you wherever you go. An IP address is like your **postal address**: if you move house, it changes.

Devices on a home or school LAN usually have **private** IP addresses (often starting 192.168 or 10). The router has one **public** IP address that the rest of the internet sees, and it keeps track of which device inside asked for what.

blocks.title: Key points
items: An IP address identifies a device on a network so data can be routed to it.
IPv4 = four numbers 0 to 255 separated by dots; IPv6 is longer and has far more addresses.
IP addresses are usually assigned by the router and can change.
A MAC address is unique, set in the NIC when it is made, and does not change.
Routers use IP addresses; switches use MAC addresses.

check.q: Which is a valid IPv4 address?
check.why: Four numbers, each 0 to 255.

check.q: Where is a MAC address stored?
o: In the NIC, when it is made
check.why: The manufacturer builds it into the network interface card.

check.q: Why was IPv6 introduced?
o: The world was running out of IPv4 addresses
check.why: IPv4 only has about 4.3 billion addresses.

check.q: Your phone connects to Wi-Fi at school, then at home. What happens?
o: Its IP address will probably change but its MAC address stays the same
check.why: IP addresses depend on the network; MAC addresses are fixed.

practice.q: Describe **two** differences between an IP address and a MAC address.
practice.a: Any two differences, each explained for both sides (2 marks each, max 4): IP can change / MAC is permanent (2); IP is assigned by the router/network / MAC is set by the manufacturer (2); IP is used to route data between networks / MAC is used to identify a device within a LAN (2); IPv4 is four denary numbers / MAC is 12 hexadecimal digits (2).

practice.q: Explain why 192.168.0.260 is not a valid IPv4 address.
practice.a: Each number in an IPv4 address must be between 0 and 255, and 260 is greater than 255 (1).

pages.spec: Describe, step by step, what happens when you type a URL into a browser, including the role of DNS
pages.summary: Computers find each other using IP addresses, but people remember names. When you type a URL, a DNS server looks up the IP address for the domain name, then the browser contacts the web server at that address and the page arrives as packets.

diagram.title: Typing a URL: step by step
diagram.caption: Click each step to see what happens.

nodes.label: Type the URL
nodes.detail: You type www.bbc.co.uk and press Enter.

nodes.label: IP address in cache?
nodes.detail: The browser checks whether it already knows the IP address from a recent visit.

nodes.label: Ask a DNS server
