practice.q: Explain the difference between a **row** and a **column** in a spreadsheet.
practice.a: A row runs across/horizontally and is labelled with a number (1). A column runs down/vertically and is labelled with a letter (1).

practice.q: Give **two** examples of how a spreadsheet could be used in a school.
practice.a: Any two, e.g. recording/averaging pupils' test marks (1); a school trip budget (1); tuck shop sales and profit (1); sports day results/league table (1); recording science experiment results (1).

practice.q: Using the tuck shop sheet, state the cell reference of the cell holding the number of chocolate bars sold, and state how many cells are in the range A1:D7.
practice.a: C3 (1). 4 columns × 7 rows = 28 cells (1).

pages.spec: Enter different types of data and format cells so a spreadsheet is clear to read
pages.summary: Cells can hold text, numbers, currency, percentages and dates. Formatting (bold, borders, number formats, column width) changes how data looks, not its value, and makes a sheet easier to read.

diagram.title: Which data type?
diagram.caption: Decide the best data type for each item, then click to check.
head: Data
Data type
rows: Price of a bottle of water: £0.75

blocks.text: Every cell holds one piece of data. Excel works out its **[[data type]]** from what you type, and that decides what you can do with it: you can add numbers, but you cannot add names!

head: Data type
Example
Notes
rows: Lines up on the **left** of the cell. Used for headings and names.
Lines up on the **right**. Can be used in calculations.
A number shown with a £ sign and 2 decimal places.
Stored as a number (days since 1 Jan 1900), so you can work out the days between two dates.
blocks.caption: Common data types in Excel

blocks.text: Quick test: if Excel puts your number on the **left** of the cell, it has treated it as text and will not calculate with it. This often happens if you type a space or a letter O instead of a zero.
Formatting
**[[Formatting]]** changes how a cell *looks* without changing what is stored in it. Most tools are on the **Home** tab.

items: **Bold, font size and fill colour** for headings, so they stand out.
**Borders** to show where the table starts and ends.
**[[Currency format]]** (the £ button, or Format Cells > Currency) to show money with 2 decimal places.
**Increase/Decrease Decimal** to control how many decimal places are shown.
**Merge & Center** to put a title across the top of several columns.
**Wrap Text** and **column width** so that long labels fit.

blocks.title: Worked example: formatting does not change the value
blocks.context: Cell B2 holds the number 0.6. It is formatted as currency so it shows £0.60. Cell C2 holds 25. What does =B2*C2 give?
steps: The formatting only adds the £ and the extra 0; the value stored is still 0.6.
If D2 is also formatted as currency it shows £15.00.
blocks.answer: =B2*C2 gives 15, shown as £15.00.

blocks.text: If a cell shows **#####**, the number is too wide for the column. Nothing is wrong with your data: double-click the line between the column headings to widen it.
Never type the £ sign or units like *kg* as part of a number (e.g. *25kg*). Excel will treat it as text. Type 25 and use formatting instead.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Data types include text, number, currency, percentage and date.
Text lines up left; numbers line up right.
Formatting changes how a value looks, not the value itself.
Use currency format for money, not a typed £ sign.
##### means the column is too narrow.

check.q: A cell shows £0.75. What value is actually stored?
check.why: Currency is just a format; the stored value is the number 0.75.

check.q: What does ##### in a cell usually mean?
check.why: Widen the column and the number appears.

check.q: Which would Excel treat as text, not a number?
check.why: Adding a word makes the whole entry text.

check.q: Excel stores 25% as…
check.why: A percentage is stored as a decimal: 25% = 0.25.

practice.q: Describe **two** ways of formatting a spreadsheet to make it easier to read.
practice.a: Any two, e.g. bold/larger headings (1); borders around the table (1); fill/background colour for headings (1); currency format for money (1); widening columns so data fits (1); merge and centre a title (1).

practice.q: A pupil types **£2.50** into a cell as the letters and symbols on the keyboard, but later finds another pupil's sheet shows 2.5 with a currency format. Explain why the second method is better.
practice.a: If typed as text, it may not be used in calculations (1). With currency format the cell stores a number, so formulas work, and it is still displayed as £2.50 (1).

practice.q: State the most suitable data type for: (a) a pupil's surname (b) the cost of a school trip (c) the date of the trip.
practice.a: (a) Text (1). (b) Currency (1). (c) Date (1).

pages.spec: Explain what a formula is and write formulas using arithmetic operators
pages.summary: A formula is a calculation that always starts with =. It can use numbers and cell references with the operators + - * / and ^, and Excel works it out using BODMAS. If a value changes, the formula recalculates automatically.

diagram.title: Predict the result
diagram.caption: Work out each formula using BODMAS, then click to check.
head: Formula
Result

blocks.text: A **[[formula]]** tells Excel to calculate something. Every formula **starts with an equals sign (=)**. Without the =, Excel thinks you have typed text.
These symbols are called **[[operators|operator]]**. Notice that Excel uses `*` for multiply (not ×) and `/` for divide (not ÷).
Use cell references, not numbers

You *could* type `=0.6*25`, but a good formula uses **cell references** instead. Then, if the price or the number sold changes, the answer updates by itself. This is called **[[automatic recalculation]]**.

blocks.title: Takings for crisps, in cell D2
blocks.output: Multiplies the price in B2 (0.60) by the number sold in C2 (25) and shows 15, formatted as £15.00.

blocks.title: Worked example: the tuck shop changes a price
blocks.context: D2 contains =B2*C2 and shows £15.00. The tuck shop raises the price of crisps in B2 from £0.60 to £0.70. What happens?
steps: The formula in D2 has not changed: it still says =B2*C2.
Excel recalculates straight away using the new value: 0.70 × 25 = 17.50.
Any other formula that uses D2 (such as the total in D7) also updates: 83.60 + 2.50 = 86.10.
blocks.answer: D2 changes to £17.50 and the total to £86.10, without retyping anything.

blocks.text: Order of operations (BODMAS)
Excel follows **[[BODMAS]]**, just like in Maths: **B**rackets, **O**rders (powers), **D**ivision and **M**ultiplication, then **A**ddition and **S**ubtraction.
To find the average of two marks in B2 and C2, `=B2+C2/2` is **wrong**: it divides only C2 by 2. You need brackets: `=(B2+C2)/2`.
Press **Ctrl + `** (the key above Tab) to switch between seeing the results and seeing the formulas in every cell. Great for checking your work.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A formula always starts with =.
Operators: + - * / and ^.
Use cell references so the answer recalculates automatically.
Excel uses BODMAS: use brackets to control the order.
The cell shows the result; the formula bar shows the formula.

check.q: Which is a correctly written Excel formula to multiply B2 by C2?
check.why: Start with = and use * for multiply.

check.q: What is the result of =20+10/2?
check.why: Divide first: 10 ÷ 2 = 5, then 20 + 5 = 25.

check.q: Why is it better to use cell references than typed numbers in a formula?
o: The result updates automatically when the data changes
check.why: This is automatic recalculation.

check.q: Which symbol means 'to the power of'?
check.why: =2^3 means 2³ = 8.

practice.q: Cell B4 holds the price of a pizza (£8.50) and C4 holds how many were ordered. Write a formula for D4 to calculate the total cost.
practice.a: =B4*C4 (2). Award (1) for B4*C4 without the = sign, or for a correct formula using the number 8.50 instead of B4.

practice.q: A pupil wants the average of two scores in E2 and F2. They write =E2+F2/2. Explain why this gives the wrong answer and write the correct formula.
practice.a: Excel uses BODMAS / division is done before addition (1), so only F2 is halved (1). Correct formula: =(E2+F2)/2 (1).

practice.q: Explain what is meant by **automatic recalculation** and why it is useful.
practice.a: When a value in a cell changes, every formula that uses that cell is worked out again automatically (1). This saves time / avoids mistakes, as nothing has to be recalculated by hand (1).

pages.spec: Use the functions SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX and COUNT on a range of cells
pages.summary: A function is a ready-made formula with a name, such as SUM or AVERAGE. You give it a range in brackets, e.g. =SUM(B2:B9), and it does the work. Functions are quicker and less error-prone than long formulas.

diagram.title: Match the function
diagram.caption: Match each function to what it does.
pairs: Adds up the numbers in a range
Finds the mean of the numbers
Counts the cells that contain numbers

blocks.text: Adding up 8 test scores with `=B2+B3+B4+B5+B6+B7+B8+B9` works, but it is slow to type and easy to get wrong. A **[[function]]** is a built-in formula with a name that does the job for you.
Every function has the same shape: **=NAME(what to use)**. The part in the brackets is called the **[[argument]]**, and it is usually a range.

head: A
B
blocks.caption: Class 9B's Digital Technology test scores (cells A1:B9)

head: Function
What it does
Formula for 9B
Result
blocks.caption: The five functions you need first

blocks.title: Worked example: check the AVERAGE
blocks.context: Show that =AVERAGE(B2:B9) gives 74.5 for class 9B.
steps: COUNT: there are 8 scores.
AVERAGE = SUM ÷ COUNT = 596 ÷ 8 = 74.5.
blocks.answer: 74.5, so AVERAGE is really SUM divided by COUNT.

blocks.text: AutoSum: the quick way

items: Click the empty cell just below your numbers (B10).
On the **Home** tab, click **AutoSum (Σ)**. Excel guesses the range: `=SUM(B2:B9)`.
Check the range is right, then press **Enter**.
Click the small arrow next to Σ for Average, Count Numbers, Max and Min.

blocks.text: **COUNT** only counts cells with numbers in them. If Jack's score was typed as *Absent*, =COUNT(B2:B9) would give **7**, not 8.
Spotting errors

head: Error
Usual cause
rows: Dividing by zero or by an empty cell
Trying to do maths with text, e.g. =B2*A2 where A2 says *Aoife*
blocks.caption: Common error messages

blocks.title: Key points
items: A function is a ready-made formula: =NAME(argument).
SUM adds, AVERAGE finds the mean, MIN smallest, MAX largest.
COUNT counts cells containing numbers only.
Write ranges with a colon: B2:B9.
#NAME? usually means a typing mistake in the function name.

check.q: Which formula adds up every number from C2 to C20?
check.why: SUM with a colon range.

check.q: Cells A1:A4 hold 10, 20, 30 and 40. What does =AVERAGE(A1:A4) give?
Cells A1:A5 hold 4, 9, Absent, 7, 2. What does =COUNT(A1:A5) give?
check.why: COUNT ignores the text 'Absent', so 4.

check.q: A cell shows #NAME?. What is the most likely cause?
check.why: Excel does not recognise the name, e.g. =AVRAGE.

practice.q: Using class 9B's sheet, write formulas to find (a) the highest score (b) the lowest score.
Explain **one** advantage of using =SUM(B2:B9) instead of =B2+B3+B4+B5+B6+B7+B8+B9.
practice.a: Any one: quicker to type (1); less chance of missing a cell / typing mistakes (1); easier to read/check (1).

practice.q: A teacher's sheet shows #DIV/0! in the cell meant to show the average. Suggest why.
practice.a: The formula is dividing by zero / by an empty cell (1), e.g. no marks have been entered yet so the count is 0 (1).

pages.spec: Use IF and COUNTIF to make decisions and count values that meet a condition
pages.summary: IF checks a condition and shows one result if it is true and another if it is false, e.g. =IF(B2>=70,"Pass","Fail"). COUNTIF counts the cells in a range that meet a condition, e.g. =COUNTIF(C2:C9,"Pass").

diagram.title: How =IF(B2>=70,"Pass","Fail") decides
diagram.caption: Only one of the two results is ever shown.

nodes.label: Read B2
nodes.detail: Excel looks up the score in B2, e.g. 72.

nodes.label: B2 >= 70?
nodes.detail: The condition is either TRUE or FALSE.

nodes.label: Show "Pass"
nodes.detail: Value if true: 72 is 70 or more.

nodes.label: Show "Fail"
nodes.detail: Value if false, e.g. for Niamh's 64.

nodes.label: Done
nodes.detail: If B2 changes, the IF is checked again automatically.

blocks.text: Sometimes a spreadsheet has to make a **decision**: has this pupil passed? Does this order get free delivery? The **[[IF]]** function does this.

blocks.title: The IF function
blocks.code: =IF(condition, value if true, value if false)

blocks.text: The **[[condition]]** is a test that is either TRUE or FALSE. It uses a **[[comparison operator]]**:

blocks.title: Worked example: pass or fail?
blocks.context: Class 9B's pass mark is 70. Write a formula for C2 that shows Pass or Fail for Aoife (score in B2), then copy it down to C9.
steps: Condition: is the score 70 or more? `B2>=70`.
Value if true: "Pass". Value if false: "Fail". Text must go in **speech marks**.
C2: `=IF(B2>=70,"Pass","Fail")`. Aoife has 72, so C2 shows **Pass**.
Copied down, Niamh (64), Erin (58) and Ryan (69) get **Fail**; the other five get **Pass**.
blocks.answer: =IF(B2>=70,"Pass","Fail")

blocks.text: IF can give back numbers or calculations too. A tuck shop pre-order sheet could charge £2.50 delivery only on small orders: `=IF(B10>=20,0,2.50)` gives 0 if the order total in B10 is £20 or more, and 2.50 if it is less.
COUNTIF: count the ones that match
**[[COUNTIF]]** counts how many cells in a range meet a condition. It has two arguments: the range, and the condition in speech marks.

head: Formula
What it counts
Result for 9B
rows: Cells in C2:C9 that say Pass
Cells in C2:C9 that say Fail
Scores of 80 or more (Ciarán 85, Jack 90, Grace 81)
blocks.caption: COUNTIF examples using class 9B

blocks.text: Watch the speech marks. `=IF(B2>=70,Pass,Fail)` gives a **#NAME?** error because Excel thinks Pass and Fail are names of something. In COUNTIF, a condition with an operator also needs speech marks: `">=80"`.

blocks.title: Key points
items: IF has three parts: condition, value if true, value if false.
Conditions use = <> > < >= <=.
Text results go in speech marks.
COUNTIF(range,condition) counts cells that meet a condition.
IF decides for one cell; COUNTIF counts across a range.

check.q: B2 holds 65. What does =IF(B2>=70,"Pass","Fail") show?
check.why: 65 is not 70 or more, so the false value is shown.

check.q: Which operator means 'not equal to' in Excel?
check.why: Excel uses <>.

check.q: Cells A1:A6 hold Yes, No, Yes, Yes, No, Yes. What does =COUNTIF(A1:A6,"Yes") give?
check.why: Four cells say Yes.

check.q: Why does =IF(B2>50,Good,Poor) give an error?
o: The text values need speech marks
check.why: Text must be written as "Good" and "Poor".

practice.q: A school charges £5 for a club, but pupils with a sibling in the club (C2 = "Yes") pay £3. Write an IF formula for D2.
practice.a: =IF(C2="Yes",3,5): correct condition C2="Yes" (1); correct true/false values 3 and 5 in the right order (1); correct syntax with = and commas (1). Accept =IF(C2<>"Yes",5,3).

practice.q: Column D (D2:D30) holds each pupil's house: Erne, Lough or Castle. Write a formula to count how many pupils are in Erne.
practice.a: =COUNTIF(D2:D30,"Erne"): correct range (1); correct condition in speech marks (1).

practice.q: Explain the difference between the IF function and the COUNTIF function.
practice.a: IF tests a condition and returns one of two results for a single cell (1). COUNTIF counts how many cells in a range meet a condition (1).

pages.spec: Explain the difference between relative and absolute cell references when replicating formulas
pages.summary: Replicating (copying) a formula with the fill handle changes relative references, so =B2*C2 becomes =B3*C3 on the next row. An absolute reference such as $F$1 has dollar signs and never changes when copied.

diagram.title: What does it become?
diagram.caption: Each formula is copied from row 2 down to row 5. Predict the new formula, then click to check.
head: Formula in row 2
After copying to row 5

blocks.text: You do not need to type the same formula 30 times. Write it once, then **replicate** it: drag the **[[fill handle]]** (the small square at the bottom right of the cell) down the column. This is called **[[replication]]**.
Relative references
Normal cell references are **[[relative|relative reference]]**: when you copy the formula, they change to match the new position. That is usually exactly what you want.

head: Cell
Formula after copying
Result
blocks.caption: The tuck shop takings formula copied down from D2 to D6

blocks.text: Absolute references

Sometimes every formula must use the **same** cell, such as one exchange rate or one pass mark. An **[[absolute reference]]** has a **$ sign** before the column letter and row number, e.g. **$F$1**. It stays fixed however far you copy it.

blocks.title: Worked example: the Dublin trip in euros
blocks.context: Year 10 are going to Dublin. Prices in pounds are in B2:B5 (£20, £8, £14, £5). The exchange rate, 1.15 euros to the pound, is in F1. Write a formula for C2 that can be copied down to C5.
steps: C2 needs £20 × 1.15, so start with `=B2*F1`.
If copied down, C3 would become `=B3*F2`. F2 is empty (worth 0), so the answer would be **0**. Wrong!
Fix F1 with dollar signs: `=B2*$F$1`.
blocks.answer: =B2*$F$1 in C2 gives €23.00, and copies down correctly.

head: Relative reference
Absolute reference
rows: Changes to match the new position
Data that is different on every row
One value used by every formula (a rate, price or pass mark)

blocks.text: Click on a reference in the formula bar and press **F4** to add the dollar signs automatically.
You may also see *mixed* references such as $A1 or A$1, where only the column or only the row is fixed. You will meet these again at GCSE.
A tell-tale sign of a missing $: the first answer is right, but the copied cells show **0** or **#VALUE!**. Click a copied cell and look at the formula bar to see which reference moved.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Replication means copying a formula, usually with the fill handle.
Relative references (B2) change when copied.
Absolute references ($F$1) stay fixed when copied.
Use absolute for a single value every row needs.
Press F4 to add $ signs.

check.q: D2 contains =B2+C2. It is copied to D3. What is in D3?
check.why: Relative references move down one row.

check.q: Which is an absolute reference?
check.why: Dollar signs before the column and row.

check.q: C2 contains =B2*$H$1. It is copied to C6. What is in C6?
check.why: B2 is relative (becomes B6); $H$1 is absolute (stays).

check.q: What is the fill handle used for?
o: Copying a formula into neighbouring cells
check.why: Drag the small square to replicate.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a **relative** and an **absolute** cell reference.
practice.a: A relative reference changes/adjusts when the formula is copied to a new cell (1). An absolute reference (with $ signs) stays the same when copied (1).

practice.q: Cell E1 holds the pass mark, 70. A teacher writes =IF(B2>=E1,"Pass","Fail") in C2 and copies it down. Every pupil from row 3 onwards shows Pass, even those with low marks. Explain why and correct the formula.
practice.a: E1 is relative, so it changes to E2, E3 and so on when copied (1); those cells are empty (0), so every score is >= 0 / passes (1). Correct formula: =IF(B2>=$E$1,"Pass","Fail") (1).

practice.q: Give **one** advantage of replicating a formula instead of typing it into every cell.
practice.a: Any one: quicker (1); fewer typing mistakes / consistent formulas (1).

pages.spec: Sort and filter data and use conditional formatting to highlight important values
pages.summary: Sorting puts rows in order (ascending A to Z, smallest to largest, or descending). Filtering hides the rows you do not need. Conditional formatting changes a cell's colour automatically when it meets a rule, such as scores under 60.

diagram.title: Sort or filter?
diagram.caption: Two ways of making a big table easier to use.

states.label: Sort
points: Every row is still shown
Rows are rearranged into order
Ascending (A to Z, 1 to 9) or descending
Great for rankings, e.g. top scorer first

states.label: Filter
points: Only matching rows are shown
Other rows are hidden, not deleted
Choose values or a rule, e.g. greater than 80
Great for finding, e.g. only form 9B

blocks.text: When a sheet has lots of rows, you need ways to find what matters quickly. Excel gives you three tools: **sort**, **filter** and **conditional formatting**.
Sorting
To **[[sort]]** means to put the rows in order of one column. **Ascending** is A to Z or smallest to largest; **descending** is Z to A or largest to smallest.

items: Click any cell in the column you want to sort by (e.g. B2 for test scores).
On the **Home** tab, click **Sort & Filter**, or use the **Data** tab.
Choose **Sort Largest to Smallest** to put the top score first.
For more than one level (e.g. by form class, then by surname), use **Custom Sort**.

blocks.text: Never select **just one column** and sort it. The names would stay put while the scores moved, so every pupil gets the wrong mark! Click one cell inside the table and Excel sorts whole rows together.

blocks.title: Worked example: ranking class 9B
blocks.context: Sort class 9B's scores (A1:B9) from largest to smallest. Who is first, who is last, and what position is Aoife?
steps: Descending order of scores: 90, 85, 81, 77, 72, 69, 64, 58.
Matching names: Jack, Ciarán, Grace, Oisín, Aoife, Ryan, Niamh, Erin.
Aoife's 72 is the 5th value.
blocks.answer: Jack is first (90), Erin is last (58), Aoife is 5th.

blocks.text: Filtering

A **[[filter]]** hides the rows that do not match what you want, without deleting them. Click **Sort & Filter > Filter**: a drop-down arrow appears on each heading. Untick values, or use **Number Filters** such as *Greater Than…*.
A funnel symbol on a heading shows a filter is switched on. If data seems to be missing, check for one and choose **Clear Filter**.
Conditional formatting

**[[Conditional formatting]]** changes how a cell looks (fill colour, font colour, icons) **automatically** when its value meets a rule. If the value changes, the colour updates too. Find it on the **Home** tab.

head: Rule
Example use
rows: Score cells turn light red so the teacher spots who needs help
Highlight Cells Rules > Text that Contains "Fail"
Every Fail in column C is shown in red
A bar inside each cell, longer for bigger numbers, like a mini chart
Green for high takings, red for low takings at the tuck shop
blocks.caption: Useful conditional formatting rules

blocks.title: Key points
items: Sort puts whole rows in order: ascending or descending.
Click one cell in the table before sorting so rows stay together.
Filter hides rows that do not match; nothing is deleted.
Conditional formatting colours cells automatically by a rule.
All three are on the Home tab.

check.q: Sorting names from Z to A is…
check.why: Z to A (or largest to smallest) is descending.

check.q: What happens to rows hidden by a filter?
o: They are hidden but still there
They are moved to a new sheet
They are sorted to the bottom
check.why: Clear the filter and they come back.

check.q: A teacher wants marks below 40 to turn red automatically. Which tool should she use?
check.why: A rule such as Less Than 40 with a red fill.

check.q: Why should you not select only the scores column before sorting?
o: The scores would no longer line up with the right names
check.why: Rows must move together.

practice.q: Describe how conditional formatting could be used in a spreadsheet of tuck shop stock levels.
practice.a: e.g. a rule that turns the stock cell red (1) when it falls below a set number, e.g. less than 10, so staff know to reorder (1).

practice.q: Explain the difference between **sorting** and **filtering** data.
practice.a: Sorting rearranges all the rows into an order, e.g. ascending/descending (1). Filtering hides the rows that do not meet a condition so only matching rows are shown (1).

practice.q: A spreadsheet lists 200 pupils with their form class. Describe how a teacher could show only the pupils in 9B.
practice.a: Turn on Filter (Home > Sort & Filter > Filter / Data > Filter) (1). Use the drop-down arrow on the Form class heading and tick only 9B (1).

pages.spec: Create a chart from spreadsheet data and choose the right type of chart
pages.summary: A chart turns numbers into a picture. Column or bar charts compare categories, line graphs show change over time and pie charts show parts of a whole. A good chart has a title, axis titles and, if needed, a legend.

diagram.title: Match the data to the chart
diagram.caption: Match each set of data to the best chart.
pairs: Takings for each tuck shop item
Temperature each hour of a school day
Hours of revision v test score

blocks.text: A **[[chart]]** makes patterns in data easy to see at a glance. A head of year would much rather look at one chart than read 200 numbers!
Choosing the right chart

head: Chart
Best for
Example
rows: Takings for each tuck shop item
Showing how something changes over time
Temperature in Enniskillen each day for a week
Showing parts of a whole (adds up to 100%)
How pupils travel to school: bus, car, walk, cycle
Seeing if two sets of numbers are linked
Hours of revision against test score
blocks.caption: Which chart should I use?

blocks.text: A pie chart only makes sense if the parts add up to one whole. Never use a pie chart for things like monthly temperatures, and do not use one with lots of tiny slices.
Making a chart

items: Select the data **including the headings**, e.g. A1:A6 and D1:D6 for item and takings.
To select two columns that are not next to each other, select the first, then hold **Ctrl** and select the second.
On the **Insert** tab, choose a chart, e.g. **Clustered Column**.
Click the **+** (Chart Elements) next to the chart to add a **chart title**, **axis titles** and **data labels**.
Drag the chart so it does not cover your data.

blocks.text: Parts of a chart

head: Part
Job
rows: Says what the chart shows, e.g. *Tuck shop takings, Monday*
Label the x-axis (across) and y-axis (up), with units, e.g. *Takings (£)*
A key showing which colour is which data series; needed when there is more than one series
The actual values written on the bars or slices
blocks.caption: What a good chart needs

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing a chart for the tuck shop
blocks.context: The tuck shop manager wants (a) to compare Monday's takings for the five items and (b) to see how total takings changed from September to June. Which charts should she use?
steps: (a) Five separate items being compared: a **column chart**, one column per item. Water (£22.50) will be the tallest column and fruit juice (£10.80) the shortest.
(b) The same thing measured over time: a **line graph**, months along the x-axis and takings (£) up the y-axis.
Both need a title and axis titles with units.
blocks.answer: (a) Column chart; (b) line graph.

blocks.text: Charts are linked to their data. Change a number in the sheet and the chart redraws itself instantly.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Column/bar: compare categories.
Line: change over time.
Pie: parts of a whole.
Always add a title and labelled axes with units.
Use Ctrl to select columns that are not next to each other.

check.q: Which chart is best for showing how a plant's height changed each day over a month?
check.why: Change over time suits a line graph.

check.q: Which chart best shows the percentage of pupils who walk, cycle, take the bus or come by car?
check.why: Parts of one whole: a pie chart.

check.q: What is a legend?
o: A key that explains the colours or series
check.why: It shows which colour is which series.

check.q: Which key do you hold to select two columns that are not next to each other?
check.why: Hold Ctrl while selecting the second range.

practice.q: A pupil has recorded how many goals each of six players scored this season. Name the most suitable chart and give a reason.
practice.a: Column/bar chart (1), because it compares separate categories / players (1).

practice.q: State **three** features that should be added to a chart to make it easy to understand.
practice.a: Any three: chart title (1); x-axis title (1); y-axis title with units (1); legend (if more than one series) (1); data labels (1); sensible scale (1).

practice.q: Explain why a pie chart would **not** be suitable for showing a town's rainfall each month over a year.
practice.a: A pie chart shows parts of a whole (1); monthly rainfall is change over time, so a line or column chart would show the pattern better (1).

pages.spec: Use a spreadsheet model to answer 'what if' questions
pages.summary: A spreadsheet model uses formulas to represent a real situation, such as a school trip budget. Changing the input values (what if more pupils go?) instantly shows the effect on the outputs, which helps people make decisions.

diagram.title: Try it: the trip budget model
diagram.caption: Change the inputs to answer your own what-if questions about the W5 trip.

blocks.text: A **[[model]]** is a spreadsheet that represents a real-life situation using **inputs** (values you can change), **formulas** (the rules) and **outputs** (the answers). Because Excel recalculates automatically, you can try out ideas without any risk. This is called asking **[[what if questions|what-if question]]**.
Example: the Year 9 trip to the W5 science centre

head: A
B
blocks.caption: A simple trip budget model. Inputs in B1:B3, outputs in B4:B5.

blocks.text: The coach costs the same however many pupils go, so it is shared between them. More pupils means a cheaper trip for everyone.

blocks.title: Worked example: what if more pupils go?
blocks.context: The teacher wants the trip to cost less than £30 per pupil. What if 45 pupils go instead of 30?
steps: Change only the input B2 from 30 to 45.
B4 recalculates: 450 ÷ 45 = £10.00 coach cost per pupil.
B5 recalculates: 10 + 18 = **£28.00**, which is under £30.
blocks.answer: With 45 pupils the trip costs £28.00 each, so it meets the target; with 25 it rises to £36.00.

blocks.text: Example: tuck shop profit

The tuck shop buys crisps for **£0.35** a packet and sells them for **£0.60**. Profit per packet = `=B2-B1` = £0.25. If 25 packets are sold, profit = `=B3*B4` = 25 × 0.25 = **£6.25**. What if the price goes up to £0.70? Profit per packet becomes £0.35, but would pupils still buy as many? A model only answers the maths; people still have to make the judgement.
Why use a model?

items: **Fast**: try lots of ideas in seconds.
**Cheap and safe**: no money is spent until the best plan is found.
**Accurate**: the formulas never make arithmetic mistakes.
**Limitation**: a model is only as good as its data and rules. If the coach company puts its price up, or pupils drop out, the real answer will be different.

blocks.text: Excel also has a tool called **Goal Seek** (Data > What-If Analysis) that works backwards: *how many pupils are needed to make the trip cost exactly £30?* (Answer: 450 ÷ 12 = 37.5, so 38 pupils.)
Keep all your **inputs together** in one clearly labelled area and colour them, so it is obvious which cells people are allowed to change.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A model uses inputs, formulas and outputs to represent a real situation.
What-if: change an input and see the outputs update.
Models are fast, cheap and safe for testing ideas.
A model is only as accurate as its data and formulas.
Goal Seek works backwards from the answer you want.

check.q: In the trip model, which cell is an input?
check.why: B2 (number of pupils) is a value you change; B4 and B5 are calculated.

check.q: Coach hire is £450 and 50 pupils go. What is the coach cost per pupil?
What is a 'what if' question?
o: Changing input values to see the effect on the results
check.why: Try different inputs and watch the outputs.

check.q: Which is a limitation of a spreadsheet model?
o: It can only be as accurate as the data and rules put into it
check.why: Real life may not match the model.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by a **spreadsheet model**.
practice.a: A spreadsheet that represents a real-life situation (1) using formulas so that inputs can be changed to predict/see what happens (1).

practice.q: Using the trip model, calculate the total cost per pupil if 36 pupils go. Show your working.
Give **two** advantages of using a spreadsheet model to plan a school event instead of working it out on paper.
practice.a: Any two: results recalculate automatically when values change (1); quick to try many what-if options (1); fewer calculation errors (1); can be saved/shared and reused (1); can produce charts (1).

pages.spec: Plan, build and test a spreadsheet so that it is accurate and easy for others to use
pages.summary: A good spreadsheet is planned first, built with clear labels and formulas, then tested with data whose answers you already know. Data validation, such as a drop-down list or a number range, stops users typing in impossible data.

diagram.title: Plan, build, test, improve
diagram.caption: Good spreadsheets are made in a cycle.

items.label: Plan
items.detail: Decide the outputs, the inputs and the formulas that link them.

items.label: Build
items.detail: Enter headings, data and formulas; format it clearly; add validation.

items.label: Test
items.detail: Try normal, boundary and invalid data and compare with the answers you expected.

items.label: Improve
items.detail: Fix any formula that gave a wrong result, then test again.

blocks.text: Real spreadsheets are used by other people: the tuck shop volunteers, a teacher, a parent. They need to be **accurate** and **hard to break**. Good spreadsheet designers follow a cycle: **plan, build, test, improve**.
1. Plan

items: What **outputs** are needed? (e.g. total takings, profit, best-selling item)
What **inputs** must be typed in? (e.g. price, cost, quantity sold)
What **formulas** link them? Write them down before you start.

blocks.text: 2. Build

items: Give the sheet a **title** and every column a clear **heading**.
Keep inputs in one area; use **cell references**, never typed numbers, in formulas.
Use **absolute references** for single values like a pass mark.
**Format** money as currency and widen columns so nothing shows #####.
**Rename** the worksheet tab, e.g. *Monday*, and save with a sensible file name.

blocks.text: 3. Test
Use **[[test data]]**: values where you already know the right answer, so you can check the formula is correct. Test three kinds:

head: Type of test data
Meaning
Example for a test score out of 100
rows: Sensible data that should be accepted
Values right at the edge of what is allowed
0 and 100, and 69/70 either side of the pass mark
150, -5, or the word *Absent* in a number column
blocks.caption: Three kinds of test data

blocks.title: Worked example: testing the pass/fail formula
blocks.context: C2 contains =IF(B2>=70,"Pass","Fail"). Choose boundary test data and give the expected results.
steps: The boundary is the pass mark, 70, so test either side of it.
B2 = 69: expected **Fail**.
B2 = 70: expected **Pass** (this checks >= was used, not >).
If 70 shows Fail, the formula wrongly uses `>` and must be fixed.
blocks.answer: 69 → Fail, 70 → Pass. Testing exactly 70 catches the most common mistake.

blocks.text: Data validation
**[[Data validation]]** (Data tab > Data Validation) checks what a user types **before** it is accepted, and shows an error message if it breaks the rule.

head: Validation rule
Example
rows: Form class: choose 9A, 9B or 9C from a list, so nobody types *9 b*
Prices: a negative price is rejected
Trip date must be in this school year
blocks.caption: Useful data validation rules

blocks.text: Validation stops *impossible* data, not *wrong* data. If a pupil scored 64 but 46 is typed, validation will still accept it, because 46 is between 0 and 100.
To stop people overwriting your formulas, you can **lock** those cells and **Protect Sheet** (Review tab), leaving only the input cells unlocked.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Plan outputs, inputs and formulas before building.
Use clear headings, cell references and sensible formatting.
Test with normal, boundary and invalid data.
Data validation rejects impossible data as it is typed.
Protect formula cells so they are not overwritten.

check.q: Which is boundary test data for a mark that must be 0 to 100?
check.why: 100 is right at the edge of the allowed range.

check.q: A drop-down list of form classes is an example of…
check.why: It restricts what can be entered.

check.q: Why test with data where you already know the answer?
o: So you can check the formula's result is correct
check.why: Compare the expected result with the actual result.

check.q: A score of 46 is typed instead of 64. Will validation 'whole number between 0 and 100' stop it?
o: No, because 46 is still within the allowed range
check.why: Validation checks data is sensible, not that it is correct.

practice.q: A spreadsheet records pupils' ages in Years 8 to 10 (11 to 15). Give an example of normal, boundary and invalid test data for the age column.
practice.a: Normal, e.g. 13 (1). Boundary, e.g. 11 or 15 (1). Invalid, e.g. 30 / -2 / text such as 'twelve' (1).

practice.q: Describe how **data validation** could be used on the form class column of a pupil spreadsheet, and explain one benefit.
practice.a: Use a List validation rule / drop-down with the allowed form classes, e.g. 9A, 9B, 9C (1). Benefit: stops spelling/typing mistakes so data is consistent / can be sorted, filtered and counted correctly (1).

practice.q: Explain why a spreadsheet designer should use cell references rather than typing numbers into formulas.
practice.a: If an input value changes, the formula recalculates automatically (1), so the designer does not have to edit every formula and errors are avoided (1).

glossary.def: Computer systems that can do tasks that would normally need human intelligence, such as recognising faces, understanding speech or making predictions.
A set of step-by-step instructions for solving a problem or completing a task.
Facts, figures, text, images or sounds that a computer can store and process.
A test proposed by Alan Turing in 1950 in which a judge has typed conversations with a hidden person and a hidden computer and tries to tell which is the computer.
A program that holds a conversation with a person using text or speech.
AI designed to do one specific task, or a small set of related tasks, very well. All AI today is narrow AI.
A possible future AI that could learn and do any intellectual task a human can. It does not exist yet.
AI that predicts what a user will want next (a video, song or product) from their history and that of similar users.
AI software that listens to spoken requests and carries them out, often on a phone or smart speaker.
Technology that turns spoken words into text a computer can use.
AI that identifies or checks a person from an image of their face, e.g. face unlock.
AI that predicts whether an email is junk (spam) and moves it out of the inbox.
A type of AI in which a computer learns patterns from examples (data) instead of following rules written by a programmer.
Something that repeats or links examples together, which a machine learning model can learn and use to make predictions.
The correct answer attached to a training example, e.g. cat or dog, spam or not spam.
The labelled examples a machine learning model learns from.
What machine learning produces after training: the learned patterns used to make predictions about new data.
New labelled examples, not used in training, that are used to check how accurate a model is.
The percentage of test examples a model gets right: number correct ÷ number tested × 100.
A detail or measurable property the model uses to make a decision, e.g. the words in an email or the shape of an ear in a photo.
A type of machine learning model loosely inspired by the brain, made of layers of simple connected units.
Machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers.
A machine learning model that sorts each input into one of a set of groups (classes), e.g. spam or not spam.
AI that creates new content, such as text, images, music, video or code.
A very large neural network trained on huge amounts of text that writes by repeatedly predicting a likely next word. It powers AI chatbots.
The instruction or question you give to an AI tool.
When an AI tool produces false or made-up information but presents it as true.
When an AI system gives results that are unfair to certain groups of people, usually because of unbalanced or unfair training data.
Deciding what is morally right and wrong, e.g. whether and how AI should be used.
Presenting someone else's work (including work written by AI) as your own.
Information that identifies you, such as your name, address, phone number, photos or passwords.
A fake image, video or audio clip made with AI that shows a real person saying or doing something they never said or did.
A note saying where information came from, including when and how an AI tool was used.
A microscopic electronic switch on a chip that is either on (1) or off (0). Processors contain billions of them.
The base 2 number system, which uses only the digits 0 and 1. Computers store and process all data in binary.
A binary digit: a single 1 or 0. The smallest unit of data.
The base 10 number system people normally use, with the digits 0 to 9. Also called decimal.
The left-most bit of a binary number, which has the largest place value (128 in a byte). Shortened to MSB.
An error that happens when the result of a calculation needs more bits than are available, so the extra bit is lost and the stored answer is wrong.
A group of 4 bits (half a byte). One nibble can be written as one hexadecimal digit.
A group of 8 bits. One byte can store a whole number from 0 to 255 or one ASCII character.
1024 bytes (KB).
1024 kilobytes (MB).
1024 megabytes (GB).
1024 gigabytes (TB).
How much data the main memory (RAM) can hold at once, usually measured in gigabytes. More RAM lets more programs and data be used without slowing down.
How quickly a processor can carry out instructions, affected by its clock speed (in GHz) and number of cores.
The base 16 number system, using the digits 0 to 9 and the letters A to F (A = 10, F = 15). One hex digit represents one nibble.
A list of all the characters a computer can use, with a unique binary code for each one.
American Standard Code for Information Interchange: a 7-bit character set of 128 characters, e.g. A = 65, a = 97.
A large character set that aims to include every character from every writing system, plus emoji, using up to 32 bits per character. Its first 128 codes match ASCII.
The kind of data a value is, such as integer, float, string or Boolean. It decides how the value is stored in binary and what can be done with it.
A data type for whole numbers, positive or negative, stored as a binary number.
A data type for numbers with a decimal part (called real at GCSE), stored as the digits plus the position of the decimal point.
A data type for text: a sequence of characters, stored as one character code after another.
A data type that can only be True or False, so it needs only one bit.
Short for picture element: the smallest single point of colour in a digital image.
An image stored as a grid of pixels, with a binary colour code for each pixel.
The number of bits used to store the colour of each pixel. n bits give 2ⁿ colours.
The number of pixels in an image, written as width × height, e.g. 1280 × 720.
A signal that changes smoothly and continuously, such as a sound wave. It must be converted to digital before a computer can store it.
The number of samples of a sound taken every second, measured in hertz (Hz). CD quality is 44,100 Hz.
The number of bits used to store each sound sample. CD quality uses 16 bits.
The number of bits used for each second of sound: sample rate × bit depth (× channels).
Making a file smaller so it uses less storage and transfers faster.
Compression that makes a file smaller without losing any data, so the original can be rebuilt exactly, e.g. png, gif, zip.
Compression that permanently removes some data to make a file much smaller, e.g. jpeg, mp3, mp4.
A simple lossless compression method that stores runs of repeated values as a count and the value, e.g. WWWWBB becomes 4W2B.
The abilities needed to use, understand and create with digital technology, from using software confidently to writing code.
A skill that can be used in many different jobs or subjects, such as problem solving or communication.
Using computers and machines to do tasks automatically that people used to do by hand.
A person who designs, writes, tests and improves computer programs. Also called a programmer or software engineer.
A person who watches an organisation's systems for signs of attack and responds when something goes wrong.
A person who collects, cleans and analyses data to find patterns, and often builds AI models that make predictions.
A person who designs, builds and maintains the networks that connect computers.
Storing data and running software on servers in data centres, reached over the internet, instead of on your own device.
A user experience designer: someone who researches users' needs and designs products that are easy and accessible to use.
A person who plans the rules, levels, characters and story of a game, and tests that it is fun.
A person who sets up, maintains and fixes technology and helps users with problems. Often a first job in tech.
All the businesses whose main product is software, digital services or technology.
Splitting the working week between the workplace and home.
Working from home, or anywhere away from the office, for all or nearly all of the time.
Coursework completed in school under set conditions, marked by the teacher and moderated by the exam board.
A number used to compare qualifications: GCSEs are level 2, A levels level 3, a bachelor's degree level 6.
A paid job that includes training towards a recognised qualification.
An NI apprenticeship at levels 4 to 7, from foundation degree up to master's level, combining paid work with study.
Personal skills that help you work well with others, such as communication, teamwork and resilience.
The ability to keep going when things go wrong and to learn from mistakes.
A way of giving evidence of a skill: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
A collection of your best work, with explanations, that shows what you can do.
A legal cyber security competition where players solve puzzles to find hidden 'flags'.
An event where people work in teams for a short time to build a solution to a challenge.
The trail of data you leave online, such as posts, likes, comments and photos.
What other people think of you based on what they can find about you online.
Behaving in a reliable, respectful and appropriate way for work or study.
Curriculum vitae: a short document summarising your skills, education and experience for an employer.
A CV that puts your skills first, each backed by evidence, instead of a list of past jobs.
Writing that explains why you want a course or job and why you would be good at it.
A fixed, over-simple idea about what a group of people is like.
Including people of different genders, backgrounds, ethnicities, ages, abilities and ways of thinking.
A plan setting out your possible career goals and the steps you will take towards them.
A goal that is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
Time spent in a real workplace to find out what a job is like.
A way of solving problems clearly and logically so that a computer or a person could carry out the solution. It has four parts: decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithms.
Breaking a large, complex problem down into smaller, more manageable sub-problems.
A smaller part of a bigger problem, produced by decomposition, that can be solved on its own.
Spotting similarities within or between problems so that an existing solution can be reused.
Removing or hiding detail that is not needed, to focus on what matters for solving the problem.
A simplified version of something real, made by abstraction, e.g. the London Underground map.
A precise, ordered, finite set of step-by-step instructions for solving a problem or completing a task.
A diagram that shows an algorithm using standard symbols joined by arrows.
The flowchart symbol (a rounded rectangle) used for Start and Stop.
The flowchart symbol (a rectangle) used for an action or a calculation.
The flowchart symbol (a diamond) used for a Yes/No question. It has two labelled exits.
The flowchart symbol (a parallelogram) used when data goes in from the user or out to the screen.
An arrow in a flowchart that joins the symbols and shows the order to follow them in.
Structured, code-like English used to plan an algorithm. It is not a real programming language.
Instructions carried out one after another, in order.
Choosing which path to follow depending on a condition, e.g. IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF.
A question or comparison that is either true or false, e.g. mark >= 50.
Repeating a set of instructions; looping.
A loop that repeats a set number of times, e.g. FOR i ← 1 TO 10 ... NEXT i.
A loop that repeats while a condition is true, e.g. WHILE ... ENDWHILE.
A named store that holds a value which can change while an algorithm runs.
Putting a value into a variable, replacing any value it held before, e.g. score ← 10.
A table used to record the value of each variable, condition and output, line by line, as an algorithm is worked through by hand.
Working through an algorithm by hand, step by step, usually with a trace table.
A collection of items stored in order under one name, each at its own position.
A search that checks each item in a list in turn, from the start, until the target is found or the list ends.
A search on a sorted list that checks the middle item and throws away half of the remaining list each time.
Smallest to largest, or A to Z. The opposite is descending order.
Exchanging the positions of two items, using a temporary variable so neither value is lost.
One trip through the whole list in a bubble sort, comparing each neighbouring pair.
A sorting algorithm that compares neighbouring pairs, swaps them if they are in the wrong order, and repeats passes until a pass makes no swaps.
How much time (number of steps) and memory an algorithm needs to solve a problem.
The greatest number of steps an algorithm could ever need, e.g. a linear search when the target is last or missing.
An error in an algorithm or program that stops it working correctly.
Finding and fixing bugs: test, trace, fix, then retest.
An error that breaks the rules (grammar) of a language, so the program will not run.
An error that lets the algorithm run but makes it give the wrong result.
A logic error where a loop runs one time too many or too few, often from using < instead of <=.
A loop that never ends because its condition never becomes false.
Values chosen to test an algorithm: normal, boundary (at the edge) and erroneous (invalid).
The methods, tools and habits used to protect computers, networks, accounts and data from attack, damage or unauthorised access.
The three goals of security: Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability.
Making sure only authorised people can see data.
Making sure data is accurate and has not been changed without permission.
Making sure data and systems work and can be accessed when authorised people need them.
Malicious software: any program designed to cause harm to a computer, its data or its user.
Malware that attaches itself to a file or program and spreads when that file is opened or shared.
Standalone malware that spreads across networks by itself, without a user opening a file.
Malware disguised as a useful or wanted program, which hides something harmful inside.
Malware that encrypts or locks files and demands payment to release them.
Malware that secretly monitors what a user does and sends the information to someone else.
Software that shows unwanted adverts and may track browsing.
Tricking or manipulating people into giving away information or access.
Fake emails or messages pretending to be from a trusted organisation, sent to steal details or spread malware.
Phishing using SMS text messages.
Phishing using voice calls or voicemail.
Inventing a believable story to persuade someone to give information or access.
Watching someone enter a password, PIN or other details.
Using software to try every possible password until the right one is found.
A long password made of several words, such as three random words.
An app that creates and stores strong, unique passwords, unlocked with one master password.
Proving that a user is who they claim to be.
Logging in using two different types of factor, such as a password and a code from your phone.
Logging in using two or more different types of factor.
Scrambling data using a key so it cannot be understood without the key.
Turning ciphertext back into readable plaintext using the key.
The original, readable message before encryption.
The scrambled, unreadable message after encryption.
A simple cipher that shifts every letter a fixed number of places along the alphabet.
HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure: the encrypted way of sending web pages, shown by a padlock in the browser.
Hardware or software that checks network traffic in and out against rules and blocks anything not allowed.
Software that scans for, detects and removes or quarantines malware.
A software update that fixes a bug or security weakness.
A separate copy of data that can be used to restore it if the original is lost or damaged.
UK law that makes unauthorised access to computers, and impairing or damaging them, a crime.
Any information that can identify a living person.
The UK General Data Protection Regulation: rules on how organisations must collect, use and protect personal data.
UK law that works alongside UK GDPR to control how personal data is used.
Legally testing a system for weaknesses, with the owner's permission, so they can be fixed.
A planned, agreed attack on a system by an ethical hacker, followed by a report.
A National Cyber Security Centre programme of competitions, courses and bursaries for young people.
An organised collection of related data, stored so that it can be easily searched, sorted and updated.
Raw facts and figures with no context, e.g. 14, Smith, 07/09/2025.
Data that has been processed and given context so that it has meaning, e.g. 'Ben Smith is 14'.
Software that a school or business uses to store and manage information about its people and activities, e.g. pupils, attendance and timetables.
Software used to create, manage and search a database, e.g. Microsoft Access.
A collection of records about one type of thing (e.g. Pupils or Books), organised in rows and columns.
All the data about one person or thing in a table; one row.
One item of data stored about every record, e.g. Surname; one column.
The heading of a field, e.g. DateOfBirth. It should be short, clear and unique within the table.
The view in Access that shows a table's data in rows and columns, like a spreadsheet, for entering and viewing records.
The kind of data a field will hold (e.g. Short Text, Number, Date/Time, Currency, Yes/No), which controls what can be entered and what can be done with it.
An Access data type that gives each new record a unique number automatically (1, 2, 3...). Often used for the primary key.
A data type that can only hold one of two values, e.g. Yes/No or True/False. Also called Boolean.
A field that holds a unique value for every record in a table, so each record can be identified, e.g. PupilID.
The view in Access used to set up a table's structure: field names, data types, descriptions and field properties such as validation.
An automatic check made by the computer when data is entered, to make sure the data is sensible and reasonable. It cannot check that data is correct.
The condition set on a field in Access that data must meet, e.g. Between 8 And 14.
A validation check that data is between a lowest and highest value, e.g. a year group between 8 and 14.
A validation check that a field has not been left empty.
A validation check on the number of characters entered, e.g. a surname of no more than 30 characters.
A validation check that data is of the correct data type, e.g. only numbers in a Number field.
A validation check that data follows a set pattern, e.g. a postcode of letters and digits in the right places.
An Access field property that forces data to be typed in a set pattern, used to carry out a format check.
A validation check that data matches one of a list of allowed values, often chosen from a drop-down list.
Checking that data has been copied or entered accurately from its original source, e.g. by double entry or a visual check.
A verification method where data is typed in twice and the computer compares the two versions; if they do not match, the user must re-enter it.
A verification method where a person compares the data on screen with the original source document to spot mistakes.
A question you ask a database to find all the records that match certain criteria. In Access a query shows only the matching records and chosen fields.
The conditions a record must meet to be included in the results of a query, e.g. "Enniskillen" or >50.
A symbol used to compare values in criteria: = (equal to), <> (not equal to), < (less than), > (greater than), <= and >=.
A symbol that stands in for unknown characters in a search: in Access * means any number of characters and ? means exactly one character.
A logical operator used in a query when a record must meet all of the criteria to be found. It narrows a search.
A logical operator used in a query when a record only has to meet one of the criteria to be found. It widens a search.
To put records into order using one or more fields, either ascending or descending.
A user-friendly screen for entering, viewing and editing records, usually one record at a time.
A professional, printable layout of data from a table or query, often grouped and with totals.
A database that stores all its data in one single table.
When the same data is stored more than once unnecessarily, wasting space and causing extra work.
When copies of the same data do not match, e.g. a teacher's room number is updated in one record but not in another.
A database that stores data in two or more tables linked together by key fields.
A field in one table that is the primary key of another table, used to link the two tables.
A way of designing where the needs of the people who will use a product come first at every stage, with users involved in research and testing.
How easy it is for users to use a product to get a task done.
How the whole experience of using a product feels to the user: easy, quick and pleasant, or confusing and frustrating.
The parts of a product that users see and interact with, such as screens, buttons, menus and icons (UI).
The group of people a product is designed for.
Collecting information yourself, directly from users, e.g. by interviews, surveys or observation.
A research method where a designer talks to one user at a time, asking open questions to get detailed answers.
A list of questions (questionnaire), often online, used to collect quick answers from lots of people.
A research method where designers watch people doing a task or using a product to see what they really do.
A realistic, made-up character, based on research, who represents one important group of users.
A short description of a feature from the user's point of view: As a [user], I want [goal], so that [reason].
Specific, testable checks that must all be true for a user story to count as done.
A usability principle: things that do the same job look and behave the same way everywhere in a product.
A usability principle: the system shows users straight away what is happening or what their action has done.
A usability principle: designing so mistakes are hard to make, and easy to recover from when they happen.
A simple outline of a screen's layout using boxes and labels, without colours, images or real text.
An early model of a product that users can try out, so ideas can be tested before the real thing is built.
How detailed and realistic a prototype is: low fidelity is quick and rough, high fidelity looks like the finished product.
Removing unnecessary detail to focus on what matters, e.g. a wireframe leaves out colours to focus on layout.
Designing products so that everyone, including disabled people, can perceive, use and understand them.
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines: the international accessibility standard from the W3C, with levels A, AA and AAA.
The four WCAG principles: content must be Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust.
A short text description of an image, read aloud by screen readers and shown if the image does not load.
How much text stands out from its background. WCAG AA needs at least 4.5 : 1 for normal text.
Software that reads out what is on the screen, used by blind and partially sighted people.
Devices or software that help disabled people use computers, e.g. screen readers, magnifiers, voice control.
Designing for the full range of people who might use a product: different ages, abilities, languages, cultures and devices.
When a design works well for some groups of people but badly for others, often because designers assumed users are like them.
Watching real users try to complete real tasks with a product, to find problems.
Usability testing where users say out loud what they are thinking as they use the product.
Showing two versions of a design to different groups of users and measuring which one works better.
A development approach where each stage (analysis, design, implementation, testing, deployment) is done once, in order.
Repeating a cycle of design, building, testing and refining, improving the product each time round.
An iterative way of developing software in short sprints, with working versions shown to users for feedback after each one.
In agile development, a short fixed block of time (usually 1 to 4 weeks) in which a team builds and tests some features.
The ideas people use to decide what is right and wrong; digital ethics applies them to how technology is made and used.
Gaining something but losing something else; every technology brings both benefits and harms.
Anyone affected by a technology, including people who did not choose to use it.
Creations of the mind, such as writing, music, art, inventions, designs and brand names, that the law can protect.
The automatic legal right of a creator to control copying, sharing, performing, adapting and selling of their original work.
Protection for a new invention that must be applied for; it lasts up to 20 years.
A registered sign, such as a name, logo or slogan, that identifies a brand.
The main UK law covering copyright and other intellectual property.
Using a small, fair part of a copyright work without permission for purposes such as study, review, teaching, news or parody, usually with credit.
Permission from a copyright owner to use their work, usually with conditions.
The default position: the owner keeps all rights, so you must ask permission to use the work.
Free, ready-made licences that let people reuse work if they follow conditions such as BY, SA, NC and ND.
Work with no copyright, because it has expired or been given away; anyone can use it.
Software whose source code is kept secret by its owner; users buy a licence to use it.
Software whose source code is available for anyone to read, change and share under its licence.
Presenting someone else's work, words or ideas as if they were your own.
A short note in your work showing which source an idea or quotation came from.
The full details of every source used, listed at the end of a piece of work.
AI that creates new text, images, audio or video from a prompt.
The large set of examples an AI model learns patterns from.
A realistic but fake image, video or audio clip made with AI, often showing a real person.
Any information that can identify a living person.
The UK General Data Protection Regulation: the main rules on how organisations must handle personal data.
The UK law that works alongside the UK GDPR to protect personal data.
A request to an organisation for a copy of the personal data it holds about you.
The right to ask for your personal data to be deleted in some situations; also called the right to be forgotten.
The UK data protection regulator; it replaced the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) on 30 September 2026.
The UK law that makes unauthorised access to computers, damaging or disrupting them, and supplying hacking tools illegal.
A building full of servers that store data and run online services such as the cloud, streaming and AI.
The total amount of greenhouse gases released because of something, such as making and using a device.
Thrown-away electrical and electronic equipment.
Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment: UK rules that require electrical items to be collected and recycled separately.
A unit of energy (kWh): the energy used by a 1,000 watt device in one hour.
Designing products to have less environmental impact over their whole life.
A set of steps used to think through a hard ethical question and reach a justified decision.
Storage, software and services on servers in data centres that you use over the internet instead of on your own device.
Saving files on a provider's servers so they can be reached over the internet from any device.
Storage that is somewhere other than the device you are using, such as cloud storage or a school server.
Saving files on the device itself (its hard drive or SSD) or on a USB stick plugged into it.
A large building full of servers that store data and run cloud services 24 hours a day.
Using software that runs on remote servers over the internet, such as Google Docs in a web browser.
The harm to the environment from using technology, e.g. the electricity, water and carbon emissions of data centres.
A website and app where teachers post work, notes and announcements, and pupils hand in their work.
A code of 6 to 8 letters and numbers that a pupil types in once to join a Google Classroom class.
The page in a Classroom class showing announcements and posts about new work.
The page in a Classroom class listing all assignments, questions and materials, grouped into topics.
A piece of work set in Google Classroom for pupils to complete and hand in.
To hand in an assignment in Google Classroom so the teacher can mark it.
To take back turned-in work so it can be changed; it must then be turned in again.
Google's cloud storage, where Google files and uploaded files are saved and organised into folders.
Where deleted Google Drive files go; they can be restored for 30 days before being permanently deleted.
The software that manages a computer's resources, peripherals, files and security, e.g. Windows.
An everyday choice that reduces the energy and storage your digital activity uses, e.g. deleting files you no longer need.
Google's online word processor for letters, essays and reports.
A feature that saves every change automatically as you work.
A record of earlier versions of a file, showing who changed what and when, which can be restored.
The level of access given to a person when a file is shared: viewer, commenter or editor.
A sharing permission that only lets someone open and read a file.
A sharing permission that lets someone read a file and add comments and suggestions, but not edit it directly.
A sharing permission that lets someone change anything in a file.
A mode in Google Docs where changes appear in colour as suggestions for the owner to accept or reject.
Working together at the same time, in real time, e.g. live co-editing or a video call.
Working together at different times, e.g. shared folders, comments, online workspaces or email.
Portable Document Format: a file type that looks the same on every device and is hard to edit.
The Google Classroom page that gathers work from all classes into Assigned, Missing and Done.
Using technology safely, responsibly and respectfully.
Agreed rules for how to communicate, chosen to suit the audience, such as how formally to write to a teacher.
Copying someone else's work, words or ideas and passing them off as your own.
Any information about a living person that could identify them, such as name with address, phone number or photo.
The UK law (with the Data Protection Act 2018) that controls how personal data is collected, stored and shared.
The trail of data left behind by everything you do online, including posts, searches and data collected about you. It can be permanent.
Data you deliberately choose to share online, such as posts, comments, photos and likes.
Data collected about you without you actively sharing it, such as search history, location data and cookies.
What other people think of you based on what they can find about you online, including what others post about you.
Showing each person adverts chosen using the data collected about their interests and behaviour.
A small text file a website stores on your device to remember information about you, such as a login or settings.
A cookie set by a company other than the website you are visiting, usually an advertiser, to track you across many sites.
Access an app asks for to parts of your device or data, such as your camera, microphone, contacts or location.
Data about data. In a photo it can include the date, time, device and GPS location where it was taken.
A request to an organisation, under UK GDPR, for a copy of the personal data it holds about you.
False or misleading information shared by someone who believes it is true.
False information created or shared deliberately to deceive or influence people.
A set of rules or steps a computer follows. Social media algorithms decide which posts to show you, often favouring content that gets lots of reactions.
Checking a source by leaving the page and opening new tabs to see what other trusted sources say about it.
Artificial intelligence that creates new content, such as text, images, audio or video, from patterns learned from large amounts of data.
AI-generated video, image or audio that shows a real person doing or saying something they never did.
Using AI to copy a person's voice from a recording so it can say new things.
Someone who lets criminals move money through their bank account. This is money laundering, a serious crime.
When personal data, such as usernames and passwords, is lost, stolen or accessed without permission.
Proving who you are in two different ways, such as a password plus a code from your phone. Often shortened to 2FA.
HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure: the encrypted version of HTTP, shown by https:// and a padlock, which keeps data secret as it travels between a browser and a website.
Encryption where only the sender and receiver can read messages, not even the company running the app.
A paid mystery item in a game that gives a random reward.
In-game money such as gems or coins, bought with real money and spent in the game.
A game design where paying real money gives players an advantage over others.
Designing technology to change how people behave, such as keeping them on an app for longer.
Constantly measuring your own life, looks or achievements against what others post online.
Brands paying or rewarding people with large online followings to promote products. In the UK it must be clearly labelled as advertising.
Clear permission given freely, without pressure, which can be withdrawn at any time.
A form of blackmail where someone threatens to share an intimate image unless the victim pays money or sends more images.
A free tool from Childline and the Internet Watch Foundation that helps under-18s in the UK get nude images of themselves removed from the internet.
UK law that makes it illegal to access or damage computers, accounts or data without permission.
Northern Ireland law that makes it an offence to send indecent or grossly offensive messages intended to cause distress or anxiety.
UK law that makes online platforms protect users, especially children, from harmful content, regulated by Ofcom. It also created new communications offences.
Child Exploitation and Online Protection: part of the National Crime Agency, where you can report sexual contact, grooming or sextortion aimed at young people online.
A simplified representation of a real system, used to understand it or predict what will happen.
The actual thing or situation in the real world that a model represents, such as the weather or a school canteen.
Running a model, often step by step over time, to imitate what would happen in the real system.
A model's estimate of what will happen. It may turn out to be wrong.
Removing details that do not matter for the question, keeping only what is important.
Something a modeller treats as true to simplify a model, e.g. every pupil takes 15 seconds to be served.
Breaking a big problem down into smaller parts that are easier to solve.
A named value in a model that can change, such as speed or number of pupils.
A value fed into a model that the user can change.
A formula or instruction in a model that describes how the system behaves.
A result produced by a model from its inputs and rules.
A value that stays the same every time a model runs, e.g. 60 minutes in an hour.
The kind of value a variable stores, such as integer, float, string or Boolean.
A data type for whole numbers, e.g. 12 stops.
A data type for numbers with a decimal point, e.g. 0.5 or 2.75. Also called real.
A data type for text, e.g. "Belleek route".
A data type with only two values: TRUE or FALSE.
Changing an input in a model to see the effect on the outputs.
Typing a fixed number into a formula instead of referring to an input cell, so the formula does not update.
An Excel tool that works backwards: it finds the input value needed for an output to reach a target.
Where income exactly equals costs, so the profit is £0.
A saved set of input values describing one possible situation, such as a worst case or best case.
One jump forward in a simulation over time, such as one day or one year.
Repeating a set of steps; in a simulation, applying the rules again for each time step.
A number chosen by chance, used in simulations to model events such as dice rolls.
How likely something is to happen, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
Checking a model by comparing its predictions with real data.
The difference between the real value and the value a model predicted.
Garbage in, garbage out: if the data put into a model is wrong, its outputs will be wrong too.
Gaining one thing by giving up another, e.g. a simpler model is quicker but less accurate.
When a model's results are unfair to, or less accurate for, some groups of people.
A model that has learned patterns from a large set of data so it can make predictions or generate content.
The examples an AI model learns its patterns from.
Statements used to judge whether a model or product does its job.
Values chosen to check a model gives correct results, including normal and extreme values.
Two or more computers or devices connected together so they can communicate and share data and resources.
A computer that is not connected to any network.
Local Area Network: a network covering a small area, such as one school, home or office building.
Wide Area Network: a network covering a large geographical area, often linking LANs together. The internet is the largest WAN.
A global WAN made of millions of smaller networks joined together.
Network Interface Card: the hardware inside a device that lets it connect to a network, by cable or wirelessly.
A device that connects devices together within a LAN and sends data only to the device it is meant for.
A device that connects different networks together (e.g. a LAN to the internet) and forwards packets towards their destination.
A device that lets wireless devices connect to a wired network using Wi-Fi.
A device that converts digital data from a computer into signals that can travel along a phone line or cable, and back again.
A copper cable with twisted pairs of wires, used to connect devices in a wired LAN.
A cable that carries data as pulses of light along thin strands of glass; very fast and works over long distances.
A wireless technology that uses radio waves to connect devices to a LAN and the internet, usually over tens of metres.
A short-range, low-power wireless technology for connecting devices directly to each other, usually within about 10 metres.
The layout of a network: how the devices are connected to each other.
A network layout where every device has its own connection to a central switch.
A network layout where all devices are connected to one main cable called the backbone.
A network layout where devices are connected to several other devices, so data has many possible routes.
A powerful computer that provides a service (such as storing files, printing or hosting websites) to other computers on a network.
A computer or device that requests and uses services from a server.
A network where clients request services from one or more central servers, which manage files, logins and security.
A network with no central server, where every computer is equal and shares its own files and resources directly with the others.
A small chunk of data sent across a network, with a header containing information such as the sender's and receiver's addresses and the packet number.
A way of sending data where it is split into packets that may take different routes and are put back in order when they arrive.
A set of rules that devices follow so they can communicate with each other, e.g. TCP/IP or HTTP.
A number that identifies a device on a network so data can be sent to it, e.g. 192.168.1.25. It can change if the device moves to another network.
A unique, permanent address built into every NIC when it is made, written as 12 hexadecimal digits, e.g. 3C:22:FB:9A:41:07.
The human-friendly name of a website, such as bbc.co.uk, that is easier to remember than an IP address.
Domain Name System: a system of servers that translates domain names such as bbc.co.uk into IP addresses.
Internet Service Provider: a company that connects homes and businesses to the internet, e.g. BT or Virgin Media.
Uniform Resource Locator: the full web address of a page, e.g. https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport.
A server that stores web pages and sends them to browsers that request them.
The maximum amount of data that can be sent across a network connection each second.
Megabits per second: one million bits per second. The usual unit for broadband speeds.
The delay between data being sent and it arriving, measured in milliseconds; also called lag or ping.
Services, software and storage provided over the internet from servers in data centres, instead of on your own device.
Saving files on servers owned by a company and accessed over the internet, e.g. OneDrive or Google Drive.
A large building full of servers that store data and run online services.
Everyday objects with sensors and network connections that let them collect and share data over the internet.
An everyday device, such as a speaker, doorbell or thermostat, that connects to the internet and can be controlled remotely.
