A program that shows information as a series of slides, usually to support a speaker, e.g. Microsoft PowerPoint, Google Slides or Apple Keynote.
The people who will watch or use a presentation. Their age, knowledge and needs affect every design choice.
What a presentation is meant to achieve, e.g. to inform, persuade, entertain or advertise.
Designing a product around the needs of the people who will use it, found by asking or observing them.
The accepted rules for communicating with a particular audience, e.g. how formal the language is, a title slide and a sources slide. Also called communication protocols.
A plan of every slide made before building a presentation, showing layout, text, images and their sources, effects, links and notes.
The strip of tools across the top of the PowerPoint window, organised into tabs (Home, Insert, Design…) and groups.
A ready-made arrangement of placeholders for a slide, e.g. Title Slide, Title and Content, Comparison.
A dotted box on a slide layout that holds a title, text or other content, e.g. 'Click to add title'.
A slide design guideline: no more than about six bullet points per slide and about six words per bullet point.
The difference between the colour of text and its background. High contrast makes text easier to read.
The top slide in a hidden set of master layouts (View > Slide Master). Changes to it, such as a logo or font, appear on every slide.
The legal right of a creator to control how their work is copied and used. In the UK it is automatic and protected by the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988.
Something a person creates with their mind, such as a photo, song, design, logo or invention, that they own. Protected by copyright, trade marks and patents.
Permission from the owner of a work setting out what others may and may not do with it, e.g. a Creative Commons licence.
Artificial intelligence that creates new content, such as text, images, audio or video, from a prompt. AI-generated images should be clearly labelled.
Using someone else's work or ideas and presenting them as your own.
Free licences that let creators allow others to use their work under set conditions, e.g. BY (credit the creator), NC (non-commercial).
Giving credit to the creator of a work you use: Title, Author, Source and Licence (TASL).
A PowerPoint feature that turns a list into a ready-designed diagram such as a process, cycle or hierarchy.
An effect that plays when moving from one slide to the next, e.g. Fade or Morph.
An effect applied to an object on a slide: entrance, emphasis, exit or motion path.
A presentation where the user chooses which slide to go to next by clicking links or buttons, e.g. a quiz or menu.
Clickable text or an object that jumps to another slide, a web page, a file or an email address (Insert > Link, Ctrl + K).
A ready-made shape, such as Home, Back or Next, that performs an action like going to a slide when clicked (Insert > Shapes).
A slide show setting (Browsed at a kiosk) where the show runs full screen, loops, and can only be moved on with links, buttons or timings.
Designing something so that everyone can use it, including people with a disability.
Software that reads aloud the text on a screen, including alt text, for people who are blind or partially sighted.
Alternative text: a short written description of an image or chart that a screen reader reads aloud.
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines: the international standard for accessible digital content, from the W3C. Its four principles are Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust.
A PowerPoint tool (Review > Check Accessibility) that lists errors, warnings and tips, such as missing alt text or slide titles.
Notes for the presenter about what to say for each slide. The audience does not see them.
A slide show view where the presenter sees the current slide, next slide, notes and a timer while the audience sees only the slide.
A checklist of what a good piece of work must do, used to plan and evaluate it.
How easy a product is for its users to use. Refining a product based on testing improves its usability.
The kind of value a variable holds, such as int, double, string, char or bool. It decides what can be stored and what can be done with it.
A whole number with no decimal part, positive or negative. In C# the data type is int.
A number with a decimal point, also called a real number. In C# use double, or float with an f on the end of the value.
Text: a sequence of characters, written inside double quotes in C#.
A data type with only two possible values, true or false. In C# the data type is bool.
A named block of code that carries out one task and runs when it is called. Also called a function, procedure or subroutine.
Running a method by writing its name followed by brackets (and any arguments), e.g. ShowBanner();
Breaking a large problem down into smaller parts that are easier to solve; each part can become a method.
A variable listed in a method's header that receives a value when the method is called.
The actual value passed into a method when it is called.
The value a method sends back to the place it was called from, using the return keyword.
A keyword in a method header meaning the method does not return a value.
A subroutine that returns a value. In C# this is a method with a return type such as int or bool.
A subroutine that carries out a task but does not return a value. In C# this is a void method.
The part of a program where a variable exists and can be used: the { } it was declared in.
A variable declared inside a method or block; it can only be used there and disappears when that code ends.
A variable that can be used by every method in a program. In C# the nearest thing is a static variable declared in the class, outside every method.
A way of storing and organising a collection of related data under one name, such as an array or a list.
A data structure that holds a fixed number of elements of the same data type, each found by its index.
The number that gives an element's position in an array or list. In C# the first index is 0.
A logic error where a loop runs one time too many or one time too few, e.g. using <= instead of < with an array.
A data structure that can grow and shrink while the program runs, e.g. List<int> in C#.
A loop that visits every item in a list or array in turn, without needing an index.
A table showing the value of each variable at each step as an algorithm runs; used to check code by hand (a dry run).
A search that checks each item in a list in turn, from the start, until the target is found or the list ends.
AI that creates new content, such as text, images or code, by predicting what is likely based on patterns in its training data.
The instruction or question you type into a generative AI tool.
When an AI tool confidently produces something false or made up, such as a method that does not exist.
Passing off someone else's work, including AI-generated work, as your own.
Developing software in repeated stages of planning, development, testing and refinement.
A table that plans and records tests: the test data, its type, the expected result, the actual result and whether it passed.
Values chosen to test a program: normal (sensible values), boundary (at the edges of what is allowed) and erroneous (values that should be rejected).
Test data at the very edge of the allowed range, such as 0 and 20 for a score out of 20.
Test data that should be rejected by the program, such as 25 or the word ten for a score out of 20.
Checking that input is sensible and allowed before the program uses it, e.g. rejecting a score above 20.
A free, block-based programming language from the MIT Media Lab. Programs are built by snapping blocks together.
A character or object on the stage that can be programmed with its own scripts, e.g. the Scratch Cat.
The area of the Scratch window where the project runs. It is 480 steps wide and 360 steps tall.
A background picture for the stage. Switching backdrops can show a new level or screen.
The part of the Scratch window that lists the blocks in the chosen category, ready to drag.
A stack of joined blocks that runs from top to bottom, usually started by a hat block.
Something that happens, such as clicking the green flag or pressing a key, that starts a script.
Carrying out instructions one after another, in order. A Scratch script runs from top to bottom.
A pair of numbers (x, y) giving an exact position on the stage. The centre is (0, 0).
One of the pictures a sprite can show. Switching costumes changes how the sprite looks.
A block that repeats the blocks inside it, such as [repeat (10)], [repeat until] or [forever].
Repeating a set of instructions using a loop.
A loop that repeats a set number of times, known before it starts, e.g. [repeat (4)].
A loop that repeats until a condition becomes true, e.g. [repeat until <touching (edge)?>].
Choosing which instructions to run depending on a condition, using if or if-else blocks.
A test whose answer is either true or false, e.g. <(score) > (10)>.
A value or block that can only be true or false. Boolean blocks have pointed (hexagon) ends.
Scratch blocks that find out what is happening, such as touching, key pressed, mouse position, timer and ask/answer.
A named store in memory that holds a value which can change while the program runs, e.g. score.
The kind of value stored, such as integer, float, string (text) or Boolean (true/false).
A block or symbol that does something with values: maths (+ - * /), comparisons or joining text.
An operator that compares two values and gives true or false: <, = or >.
A message sent to every sprite and the stage; scripts with a matching [when I receive] block then start.
Hiding detail that is not needed and giving a set of instructions a simple name, to reduce complexity.
A custom block you define yourself in the My Blocks category and can use as often as you like.
An input to a custom block or function that lets it do slightly different jobs, e.g. the number of sides.
A simplified representation of a real system that keeps only the parts that matter.
Running a model to see what happens over time or to test a prediction.
An error in a program that stops it working as it should.
Finding and fixing bugs in a program.
An error where the program runs but does the wrong thing, e.g. blocks in the wrong order.
Making software in repeated cycles of planning, developing, testing and refining.
A short sentence describing what a user needs: As a ... I want ... so that ...
A table listing each test with its expected result, actual result and whether it passed.
Values or actions used to test a program: normal, boundary and erroneous.
A program that stores data in a grid of cells and carries out calculations on it automatically, e.g. Microsoft Excel.
An Excel file. It can contain one or more worksheets.
One page (tab) of a workbook, made of rows, columns and cells.
A single box in a spreadsheet, where a column and a row meet. It holds one item of data or one formula.
A horizontal line of cells, labelled with a number.
A vertical line of cells, labelled with a letter.
The address of a cell: its column letter followed by its row number, e.g. B3.
A rectangular block of cells, written as first cell:last cell, e.g. A1:D6.
The currently selected cell, shown with a thick border. Its reference appears in the Name Box.
The bar above the grid that shows the real contents (value or formula) of the active cell.
The kind of data in a cell, such as text, number, currency, percentage or date.
Changing how a cell looks (font, colour, borders, number of decimal places) without changing the value stored.
A number format that shows a value as money, e.g. 0.6 is shown as £0.60.
A calculation in a cell. It always begins with =, e.g. =B2*C2.
A symbol that tells Excel which calculation to do: + - * / or ^.
When a value changes, every formula that uses it is worked out again straight away.
The order Excel works out a calculation: Brackets, Orders (powers), Division and Multiplication, Addition and Subtraction.
A ready-made formula with a name, such as SUM or AVERAGE, e.g. =SUM(B2:B9).
The value or range given to a function inside its brackets, e.g. B2:B9 in =SUM(B2:B9).
A function that adds up all the numbers in a range.
A function that finds the mean of the numbers in a range (total divided by how many).
A function that counts how many cells in a range contain numbers.
A function that tests a condition and gives one result if it is true and another if it is false.
A function that counts how many cells in a range meet a condition, e.g. =COUNTIF(C2:C9,"Pass").
A test that is either TRUE or FALSE, e.g. B2>=70.
A symbol used to compare two values: = <> > < >= <=.
The small square at the bottom right of the active cell, dragged to copy its contents into neighbouring cells.
Copying a formula into other cells so the same calculation is done on each row or column.
A cell reference such as B2 that changes to match the new position when a formula is copied.
A cell reference with $ signs, such as $F$1, that does not change when a formula is copied.
To put the rows of data in order of one column, ascending (A to Z, smallest first) or descending.
To show only the rows that match a condition, hiding the others without deleting them.
Formatting that is applied automatically when a cell's value meets a rule, e.g. red fill for scores under 60.
A visual display of spreadsheet data, such as a column chart, line graph or pie chart.
One of the two lines of a chart: the x-axis runs across and the y-axis runs up.
The key on a chart that shows which colour or symbol represents each data series.
A spreadsheet that represents a real-life situation using inputs, formulas and outputs.
Changing one or more input values in a model to see the effect on the results.
Data with known expected results used to check a spreadsheet works: normal, boundary and invalid.
Rules that check data as it is entered and reject values that break them, e.g. a whole number between 0 and 100.
